The four-job `bkit-tests-scope` / `bkit-tests` / `bkit-tests-live` / `bkit-tests-check` scaffold is now per-tier lanes ending in `bkit-tests-check`. `@smoke` / `test:smoke` exists only as the separate post-deploy Smoke tier (`docs/testing.md` § Smoke) and as a tag home `bkit check` warns on (`TAG_SCRIPT_HOMES` in `.bkit/core/engine/checks/after/ci-yml.ts`), not as a live-test layer.
rationale: The rename was the plan's named top blast-radius risk and #203 already shipped a working naming/CI standard, so re-litigating it via a breaking rename throws away dev work for no functional gain. Reusing the `@live`/`test:live` vocabulary keeps one coherent convention in bkit instead of two overlapping live-test layers; the gates are vocabulary-agnostic (they probe for whatever live script the consumer declares). The `.bkit/` remap is mechanical.

summary: install-module mechanics: separate opencode/codex model lookups, .agents doctrine files from the core template list only, deferred version write, Claude allow grants pruned only when bkit recorded writing them, opencode provider blocks replaced in existing order, Codex workflows as skills, cloud footprint opt-in
description: `.bkit/core/engine/install/modules/`: opencodeModelLookup and codexModelLookup are separate from the cursor modelLookup; `.agents/*.md` doctrine files come only from the core template list (`CORE_AGENT_FILES`) and are block-merged; the `.bkit/version` write waits for postDispatch; canonicalHashes drops paths bkit no longer keeps; the Claude derived `permissions.allow` grants (`WebFetch(domain:…)`, `mcp__…`) are added and pruned after the contained settings merge, and only a grant recorded in `claudeAllowDerived` is ever removed; opencode.json provider blocks are replaced (not merged) and rebuilt in the existing file's key order; `.claude/bkit-cloud.md` stays out of drift; opencode.yml provider drift is advisory only; Codex renders workflows as `.agents/skills/bkit-<wf>/SKILL.md` and writes no `.codex/config.toml`; deeper test tiers without a gate get an advisory, never a seeded stub.
rationale: Reshaping the shared cursor modelLookup would be a high-risk change touching every module signature for no functional gain. Deferring the version write keeps a mid-install crash from suppressing the first-install banner on retry. A stale canonicalHashes key would keep exempting the file from checks such as the floating-tag check. The settings merge is additive, so a grant bkit stops deriving stays forever without an explicit prune; recording authorship in `claudeAllowDerived` means a grant the consumer added by hand is never touched. Pruning before the additive merge would re-seat the pruned row. Replacing provider blocks stops a hijacked npm/baseURL surviving reinstall (deepContains treats a corrupted superset as satisfied); template-first ordering made install and upgrade render different orders so `bkit check` never settled. bkit-cloud.md holds machine-local secret values, so drift there is expected. opencode.yml is self-installed and bkit does not own it; bkit-cloud.yml self-syncs on a provider switch via one fanned-out secret. Codex has no project-scoped command surface: custom prompts are user-level, deprecated for skills, and openai/codex#4734 / #9848 asking for `.codex/prompts` were closed NOT PLANNED; `.agents/skills` is on Codex's search path and already bkit's canonical directory, and cross-host visibility of those skills is accepted deliberately. Codex has one gateway because the ChatGPT subscription is what makes it cheap to run. A seeded gate stub for a deeper tier would exit 0 and claim coverage while the agent loop silently stops at static-unit. Reasons moved out of code comments (owner rule 2026-10-10).
alternatives: Auto-rewrite opencode.yml — not adopted: file not bkit-owned. Pattern-based prune of allow grants — rejected: would touch consumer rows.

summary: OpenCode network allows stay unanchored *{base}* globs, covering apex and every subdomain; the URL-smuggling match is an accepted risk
description: OpenCode matches permission keys as anchored globs over the whole URL or command (* becomes .*, crossing / ? @ #). Derived keys are *{base}* in permission.webfetch and curl|wget *{base}* in permission.bash, for each allowlist base. These match the base anywhere in the URL, so https://evil.tld/?x=github.com and https://github.com.evil.tld/ are allowed without a prompt. A host-anchored https://{host}/* shape closes that, but no OpenCode glob can express 'any subdomain' safely (https://*.{base}/* matches https://evil.tld/?a=.{base}/), so it drops subdomain coverage and every subdomain fetch prompts. Maintainer accepted the smuggling risk to keep apex + subdomain parity with Claude's WebFetch(domain:{base}) + WebFetch(domain:*.{base}). Claude Code's domain: rule checks the real hostname and is not affected.
rationale: Keeps apex + subdomain parity with Claude's WebFetch(domain:{base}) + WebFetch(domain:*.{base}): an allowlisted host's subdomains fetch without a prompt on OpenCode too. No OpenCode glob can express a single DNS label, so the only safe subdomain-free shape (host-anchored https://{host}/*) would make every subdomain fetch prompt; the maintainer accepted the URL-smuggling match instead.
alternatives: https://{host}/* host-anchored - rejected (closes the smuggling match but drops subdomain coverage, so every subdomain fetch prompts). https://*.{base}/* - rejected (matches https://evil.tld/?a=.{base}/, so it is not safe either).

summary: pnpm + package.json required in every consumer repo as bkit tooling; consumer stack stays free behind bkit:gate:* scripts
description: Every consumer repo needs Node, a `package.json` and pnpm. They are bkit tooling, like `git`, `gh` and `jq`. The consumer stack (language, framework, database, host) stays free: gates are `bkit:gate:*` scripts that wrap any command, e.g. a Python repo declares `"bkit:gate:static-unit": "ruff check && pytest"` in a stub `package.json`. Commands that run the consumer package manager build the call in one module, `.bkit/core/engine/shared/package-manager.ts` (`PACKAGE_RUNNER`); no other command spells `pnpm` literally, so reversing this decision is a one-file change for the workflow commands. A gate that cannot run (exit 126/127) makes `bkit tests run` exit 4, which routes to the Failure Path, never `TEST_VERDICT=FAIL`.
rationale: bkit installs and upgrades itself with pnpm: `bkit upgrade --latest` shells out to `pnpm view` / `pnpm add` (`.bkit/core/engine/commands/install/upgrade.ts`), and cloud setup activates pnpm through corepack from `package.json` `packageManager` (`.bkit/core/engine/install/cloud-env.ts`). Installing bkit as a devDependency with pnpm makes the consumer repo a pnpm repo, so "bkit uses pnpm, project uses npm" is not a real option: the choice is pnpm everywhere or no pnpm assumption anywhere (about 10 source files). Both consumers already use pnpm. Cost: a JS team on npm / yarn / bun must switch to pnpm to adopt bkit; revisit when one appears.
alternatives: Package-manager agnostic everywhere (detect from lockfile; `bkit branches rebase` already keys lockfile regeneration on the lockfile name for 7 ecosystems via `LOCKFILE_REGENERATE`): rejected for now, needs bkit install / upgrade / cloud setup / auth docs reworked with no consumer needing it. Agnostic gate runner only, pnpm for bkit itself: rejected, incoherent because installing bkit with pnpm already makes the repo a pnpm repo.

summary: Workflow mechanics run as `bkit <noun> <verb>` commands under one contract: kebab-case flags, one JSON object on stdout, `[bkit-<noun>]` logs on stderr, fixed exit-code bands
description: Every mechanical workflow step is a `bkit <noun> <verb>` command in `.bkit/core/engine/commands/{workflow,ci,setup}/`, listed in `commands/registry.ts`; `conventions.test.ts` fails on an unlisted source file and holds every command to the contract in `commands/lib.ts`. Flags: kebab-case, `--flag=value` or `--flag value`, one name for one thing everywhere (`--workflow --step --fid --month --sub-plan --attempt --verdict --artifact`). stdout: ONE JSON object, camelCase keys matching `status.jsonl`. stderr: human log lines tagged `[bkit-<noun>]`. Exit: 0 ok / 1 the answer is no (gate failed, max attempts, lock held) / 2 usage error or missing dependency; 3-79 command-specific, listed in that verb's `--help`; 80 do it via MCP (`gh` unavailable); 81 hand the wait back to the agent turn loop; 82 needs a human. `--help` renders from the verb's own spec. Nouns are plural where a repo has many (`counters`), singular where it has one (`status`). `bkit <noun> <verb>` is tried before the older top-level commands; a noun that is also a command (`status`) routes only when the second word is one of its verbs. Workflow blocks run `"{BKIT}" <noun> <verb>`, `{BKIT}` held from Step 1 `repo info`’s `bkit` key: the main checkout’s `node_modules/.bin/bkit`, else `bkit` on PATH; the bkit repo links itself as a dev dependency for the same path. A value a later step needs is held from the JSON by key, never re-derived; `jq` in a workflow block only picks one key out of a command's output in that block. The slop plugin `bkit-slop-type-suppression.mjs` is a template at `.bkit/templates/scripts/slop/`, not a script a workflow runs.
rationale: Stated in the #467 commits and code: the contract is fixed once in `commands/lib.ts` so flag names, output shape and exit codes are not copied per command (8d3c3dcf); `--help` and the convention test read the same spec, so help text cannot drift from what a command accepts (`commands/lib.ts` header). Repo facts each workflow worked out by hand — repo root from any worktree, UTC month, where `status.jsonl` lives, skip-CI tokens — now have one answer (8d3c3dcf); porting surfaced hand-derived bugs, e.g. macOS reading UTC timestamps as local time, which made a live run look ten hours idle and lose its lock (8dc60537). Logic lives in commands, not workflow shell, because the host shell is not guaranteed bash and a workflow body cannot take shell positional parameters — slash-command argument substitution rewrites `$N` (`.agents/rules.md` § Project Rules › Workflow bash blocks; `.bkit/workflows.md` § Workflow Authoring Rules) — and because a workflow that runs an installed script by path breaks when the consumer renames or deletes it (`.bkit/core/engine/audits/templates/template-path-refs.test.ts`). The main-checkout binary works before and without a worktree `node_modules`, since design and plan worktrees never install (`.bkit/workflows.md` § Workflow commands).
alternatives: Shell scripts that workflows source or run — rejected for the reasons in the rationale. Not written down anywhere: why one JSON object rather than shell `KEY=value` lines, and why exit codes 80-82 specifically.

references: docs/deployments.md § One CI run per dev commit (release PR mirrors the `dev` push run)
summary: Template offers a release-PR mirror mode: a same-repo promotion PR (`dev` or `release/*` head) into the default branch skips its lanes and its capstone copies the dev push run's verdict
description: Adopted from a consumer; bkit's own CI runs it too. bkit-tests-scope (`Decide Release Mirror`) sets mirror_push_run (run_level=none, every lane off) for a same-repo PR into the default branch whose head is a promotion branch: `dev`, or `release/*` when the repo promotes via a release branch. bkit-tests-check (`Mirror Push Run`) runs `bkit runs mirror --head=<PR head> --branch=dev --max-minutes=170`, which polls `bkit runs gate --event=push` at the PR head SHA and passes only on a green push-run capstone; a `release/*` head with no green `dev` push run at that SHA fails red (exit 3). Opt-in reference in the template scaffold, with three stated preconditions: dev pushes run full, push runs diff against the last green push run, and promotion hangs off the default-branch push run.
rationale: The release PR head is the dev tip the push run already tests, so a full PR run repeats the slowest run in the repo. Reusing the ship gate keeps one run-selection and capstone-lookup implementation; --event push stops the PR's own run at the same SHA from counting or masking a red push run. A real, non-skipped required check is kept because a skipped required check can read as passed while the push run is red. The default-branch push run still re-runs full and gates promotion, so the mirror only gates the merge.
alternatives: Skip the release PR's required check outright — rejected: a skipped required check can pass the PR while the push run is red
Rely on the existing Check SHA Cache step — rejected: it only short-circuits after the push run finished green; an in-flight or red push run still triggers a full duplicate
Inline poll loop in the workflow YAML — rejected: the required check's logic must be unit-tested code
New standalone run-lookup implementation — rejected: duplicates `bkit runs gate` run selection and capstone lookup

summary: `bkit workflows close` grades compliance before writing its report; workflows no longer call `bkit comply`
rationale: One writer, and the grade always lands in the close commit; before, the grade could be written after the commit.

summary: `{BKIT}` is the bkit path `repo info` prints, held and filled in by the orchestrator; it is not an install-time token
rationale: No install or render change is needed, and the placeholder guard (a flag still holding `{UPPER}` exits 2) catches a missed substitution.

summary: `bkit comply` labels rows with `resolveRepoSlug`, like every other telemetry writer
rationale: `bkit.repoSlug` was a second source for the same value. No further reason is written down.

summary: The set of files checked for a stale marker is derived from what install writes, and a test asserts every written file carries one
description: `listStampedFiles(cwd)` (`.bkit/core/engine/install/modules/index.ts:188`) joins the core templates install writes, every manifest entry that is neither JSON nor generated, and the rendered agents, commands and skills on disk. `upgrade.integration.test.ts` installs every host into a fresh repo, asserts every tracked non-JSON, non-template file carries the marker at the installing version and that the set equals `listStampedFiles`, then rewinds every marker and checks `check` flags them and `upgrade` restamps them with no conflicts. A real install exits 1 when a written file lacks a marker.
rationale: A hand-kept list misses new file types; a derived set plus a test that fails on any unstamped file keeps the next one from shipping without a marker.

summary: The template-name table is `NPM_STRIP_REMAP` in `shared/package-roots.ts` (read backward by `templateRelPath`), so drift checks map `.gitignore` to the `gitignore` template
rationale: The `.gitignore` block was never drift-checked because the template file is named `gitignore`.

summary: Ship lands docs, summaries, ledgers and skill removals on the PR before the merge, and the merge gate carries CI forward from the last tested commit past bookkeeping-only commits
description: bkit-ship.md runs Deferred Sweep (Step 5), Update Docs & Summary (Step 6), Prune Skills (Step 7) and Commit + Push Bookkeeping (Step 8: one `bkit ledgers commit --scope=pr` `[skip ci]` commit, plain push to {SHIP_BRANCH}) before Re-validate (Step 9) and the merge. Re-validate (`bkit runs revalidate`) resolves VALIDATED_HEAD = the head before that commit while the PR head is it plus bookkeeping only (`onlyBookkeeping` in `.bkit/core/engine/commands/workflow/runs.ts`) and dev requires no status checks; `bkit runs gate --validated=` checks CI there (exit 17 otherwise). Close Workflow records a `ship-merge-ci` verdict row (`bkit runs gate --squash-of --capstone-only --record=`) and, without dev pushes, publishes its commit from a close worktree off origin/dev, falling back to a `ship-close/{FID}` PR.
rationale: The post-merge close commit had no publish channel on a cloud runtime (dev not pushable, --delete-branch removes the feature branch), which lost #380 SHIPPED row, and its pathspec never covered docs/*.md on any runtime. Carrying CI forward means a PR that arrives green spends no extra CI run on ship own docs commit.
alternatives: Keep the post-merge flush and publish it via dev push or a close PR only (smaller, but a crash between merge and close still loses docs); re-run CI after the bookkeeping push (one extra full CI run on every Path A ship).

references: .bkit/workflows.md § Routing state — durable mode / verdict / strategy
summary: #58 follow-up — durable routing state (DEBUG_MODE / PUSH_MODE / verdicts / STRATEGY ladder) re-read from status.jsonl
description: P0: debug / push mode transitions write `workflow-meta` rows via `bkit status meta --debug-mode=` / `--push-mode=`; every block that branches on `$DEBUG_MODE` / `$PUSH_MODE` re-reads it in that block via `bkit status route` (`.bkit/core/engine/audits/workflows/counter-prose-audit.test.ts` rule 8). P1: a step's last verdict / failures across blocks (active run) via `bkit status route --step= [--sub-plan=]`; same-block artifact extraction stays with `bkit steps verdict`. P2: the step's prior strategy (all runs) and `nextStrategy` (`''→STANDARD→PIVOT→FINAL→FINAL`) from the same `route` call replace prose STANDARD→PIVOT→FINAL. Fail-closed: `--require=` on a missing or invalid field exits 4. Does not replace judgment authorship or bootstrap identity vars.
rationale: Counters fixed misremembered integers; mode/verdict/strategy still drifted across fenced Bash process boundaries and resume. Append-only meta + fold reads match #58 discipline without a stored mutable blob.
alternatives: (1) Keep session-only mode/verdict — REJECTED, resume/cross-block drift. (2) Stored routing object — REJECTED, same drift class as stored counters. (3) Replace artifact extraction with status in the producing step — REJECTED, status mirrors judgment after write.

summary: #167 — rules.md equality gate is block-scoped to the managed bkit:start→bkit:end region
description:
- **Category:** infra
- **Status:** active
- **Decision:** The CI gate asserting byte-equality between bkit's own `.agents/rules.md` and the canonical template `.bkit/core/.agents/rules.md` compares the `<!-- bkit:start -->` … `<!-- bkit:end -->` managed block ONLY (inclusive of both markers). It does NOT compare the files whole. The `### bkit Repo Authoring` section that follows the closing `<!-- bkit:end -->` marker in `.agents/rules.md` (line 98+) is bkit-repo-only content — it documents bkit-internal authoring conventions (template sync, preflight advisory rules, etc.) that never ship to consumers and must never trip the equality gate. Implemented as `.bkit/core/engine/audits/repo/rules-sync.test.ts` (Vitest unit test) using `extractManagedBlock()` to isolate the block before comparison.
- **Why:** The `### bkit Repo Authoring` section intentionally diverges from the template (it contains bkit-repo-specific instructions that would be noise in a consumer's `rules.md`). A whole-file comparison would require either (a) duplicating the section into the template (wrong — it would then ship to consumers), or (b) permanently stripping it from `.agents/rules.md` (wrong — agents authoring bkit need it). Block-scoped comparison is the only design that keeps the two files in sync on consumer-facing rules while allowing the bkit-repo section to exist freely.
- **Discarded:** Whole-file comparison — forces either shipping bkit-repo-only content to consumers or deleting the authoring-convention section that bkit's own agents rely on. Neither is acceptable.
- **Source:** phase
- **Related:** #167, #160, D3 (rules.md block-scoped gate in 160-centralise-install-code-plan.md), `.bkit/core/engine/audits/repo/rules-sync.test.ts`, `.agents/rules.md` § Project Rules › Repo Authoring, `.bkit/core/.agents/rules.md`
- **Current (checked 2026-09-23):** The repo-only tail is now `## Project Rules` (heading `#### Repo Authoring`) after `<!-- bkit:end -->` in `.agents/rules.md`; there is no `### bkit Repo Authoring` heading and no fixed line anchor.
rationale: The `### bkit Repo Authoring` section intentionally diverges from the template (it contains bkit-repo-specific instructions that would be noise in a consumer's `rules.md`). A whole-file comparison would require either (a) duplicating the section into the template (wrong — it would then ship to consumers), or (b) permanently stripping it from `.agents/rules.md` (wrong — agents authoring bkit need it). Block-scoped comparison is the only design that keeps the two files in sync on consumer-facing rules while allowing the bkit-repo section to exist freely.

summary: Gate checks run inside `bkit steps finish`; `bkit steps gate` is called only where no finish writes the row: Step 1 gates, close gates (build also gates `build-create-pr`, written by `steps done`), debug Step 4 (`context-fetch`, written by `context finalise`), ship Step 2 (`ship-worktree-setup`, written by `steps done`), ship Steps 3 and 9, auto
rationale: One code path checks a row's fields, right after it is written; a second call at every gate would repeat it.

summary: `bkit workflows fail` changes lock, status-row, sentinel and rebase state only when given a lock token; an empty token counts as none. The label set it prints (`bkit:failed` added) is computed with or without a token
rationale: A failure before Step 1 takes the lock must not touch another run's lock.

summary: Record files are created by the commands that first write them; install never creates them
description: `docs/failures.jsonl`, `docs/deferrals.jsonl`, `docs/roadmap.md`, `.bkit/issues.jsonl`, `.bkit/friction.jsonl` and `.bkit/stats.jsonl` are not install outputs: the step or command that first appends a row creates the file (`bkit roadmap feature` renders `docs/roadmap.md`). `.bkit/core/engine/commands/install/install.integration.test.ts` pins that install never creates `docs/roadmap.md`. Only the `bkit:gate:*` / `bkit:deps:*` package.json script names are add-if-missing; `.agents/skills.md` is a managed block (`489-skills-md-is-a-managed-block`).
rationale: Not written down: the owner chose lazy creation on 2026-10-10 over the 2026-10-07 plan, and the record states the choice without a reason.
alternatives: Create the record files if missing at install (settled plan 2026-10-07 §1) — not adopted 2026-10-10; no reason recorded.

summary: .bkit/issues.jsonl is the canonical feature ledger; docs/roadmap.md is its regenerated projection
description:
Design Addendum 3 § N-O (owner, 2026-07-27) inverted the authority model a second time: .bkit/issues.jsonl (kind: "feature", append-only, six-state status ladder) is canonical, appended at every phase close; docs/roadmap.md is fully regenerated from it on every fold, never upserted.
- **Current (checked 2026-10-09):** The ledger is `.bkit/issues.jsonl` (`kind:"feature"`). `bkit roadmap fold` (`.bkit/core/engine/commands/workflow/roadmap.ts`) reads it as the sole input; every phase close appends its row and re-renders through `appendFeature` (`bkit branches land` for design / plan, `bkit roadmap mirror` for build / debug, `bkit roadmap feature` for ship). Shape unchanged: append-only JSONL is canonical, `docs/roadmap.md` is a full regenerate.
rationale: A full-regenerate projection over an append-only merge=union ledger is reproducible from scratch and sidesteps the per-FID upsert + KN-42 duplicate-collapse invariant entirely.
alternatives: Per-FID upsert on docs/roadmap.md as canonical (Directive 1, design Addendum 1) — REJECTED: build/debug rows on feat/{FID} are not re-derivable from dev, so a blind regenerate would revert them; the ledger removes the need for upsert semantics altogether.

summary: Why specific bkit test guards exist: block-locality audit, frozen ship step keys, ctx-step bash extraction, whole-second ts gate, deferral reason/writer/unjustified gates on live ledgers, ungated workflow/step fields, telemetry spec-example validation, real-install provenance check
description: Test files under `.bkit/core/engine/` assert: every `$VAR` in a workflow/prompt fence is assigned in that fence (`audits/workflows/block-locality-audit.test.ts`, sources only); the 15 canonical `ship-*` keys never change (`audits/workflows/ship-invariants.test.ts`); bkit-cloud.yml's ctx step runs as extracted bash against a stub gh (`audits/templates/cloud-ctx-step.integration.test.ts`); live ledgers carry no whole-second `ts` after the cutoff, deferral `reason` on the folded state, `unjustified` carried forward, only listed writers (`audits/repo/ledger-integrity.test.ts`); `.bkit/jsonl.md` examples pass the real codec (`ledgers/telemetry.test.ts`); `.bkit/version` provenance survives a real install (`commands/install/install.integration.test.ts`).
rationale: Shell state does not persist between Bash tool calls, so an unassigned `$VAR` expands empty and `jq --arg v "$X"` writes an empty field while exiting 0; it never fired (244 committed verdict rows carried values) only because the orchestrator substituted held values — correctness rested on undocumented model inference with nothing to detect when it stopped holding (#440). Auditing host mirrors would double-report and hold CI red until a re-install, turning a regenerable artifact into a merge blocker. Renaming a ship step key resets attempt counters across three repos and orphans the Tier-3 detector corpus. The ctx-step test exists because #363's plan called for bash-unit verification, none was committed, and build-challenge found H1 (FID truncation) and M1 (jq fail-open treating unparseable status.jsonl as zero rows, defeating the cap forever) only by manual dry-runs; extraction is by indentation because the repo ships no YAML parser. A hand-typed ts is round because a model reaches for `T00:00:00Z` and increments: stats.jsonl (shell idiom) was 0-for-63 whole-second while agent-appended ledgers were 44-for-270; pre-cutoff rows stay because re-minting history would invent data. `validate()` never sees `jq >>` appends, so the file is the only place to enforce the reason enum; `fold()` is last-write-wins, so the next append decides whether a reviewer's `unjustified` survives and the judged party is usually the appender. Backfilling `workflow` on manual rows would put invented data into analysis. Spec examples are what agents copy; `severity` and `references` were lost by examples drifting from the type. The provenance write path is a fresh object literal, so a field addition can silently drop it and a mocked install would never notice. Each workflow's own bash summary was wrong (`grep -c || echo 0` printing `0\n0`, jq `//` keeping empty strings, `wc -l` counting lines). Reasons moved out of test comments (owner rule 2026-10-10).

summary: bkit's own CI validates `.github/workflows/*` with actionlint
description: `Run actionlint` in `bkit-tests-static` (`.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml`; the same step ships in `.bkit/templates/.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml`) downloads actionlint 1.7.12 through a SHA-pinned installer script and runs it over the workflows.
rationale: A YAML linter accepts workflows that are valid YAML but invalid GitHub Actions; actionlint checks `${{ }}` expression syntax and runs shellcheck on `run:` blocks, catching that class. Reasons moved out of `.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` comments (owner rule 2026-10-10).

summary: bkit CI warns on dev pushes when the default branch serves stale Renovate config or workflows; the step ships in the template and bkit runs it unchanged
description: `Check Default Branch Lags Dev` in `bkit-tests-static` of `.bkit/templates/.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml`, identical in `.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml`, diffs `.github/renovate.json5`, `.github/renovate.json` and `.github/workflows` between `origin/<default>` and HEAD on dev pushes and writes a run-summary block + `::warning::`; it never fails and skips when the default branch is dev or unset.
rationale: CI on dev proves the code, but nothing else checks that the code reached the default branch, and Renovate config plus scheduled / default-branch Actions are read live from the default branch. Reasons moved out of `.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` comments (owner rule 2026-10-10).

summary: bkit's own CI keeps one run per branch or pull request, as the template does
description: `.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` concurrency: group `ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && format('pr-{0}', github.event.pull_request.number) || github.ref }}`, `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}` (the default branch queues, every other ref cancels), same as `.bkit/templates/.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` with `{{DEFAULT_BRANCH}}` filled.
rationale: Owner 2026-10-10: bkit uses its own templates completely. A push plans from the last green run on the branch, so a cancelled run's changes stay in scope of the run that replaced it; `bkit-cloud.yml` routes only success/failure conclusions, so a cancelled run is simply not routed. bkit's `ci-yml-capstone-contract-drift` advisory already asked consumers for this shape.

summary: Why further bkit test guards exist: archive subdirectory for superseded plans, template/repo action-pin parity, summary output-format verbs, closed-vocabulary backticks, one gate table per host family, single-emit and no-literal-list hook checks, preflight graded against the installed tracker, verdict vocabularies linked from files
description: Tests under `.bkit/core/engine/`: superseded design/plan documents move into `docs/plans/{YYYYMM}/archive/` (`audits/workflows/workflow-archive-snippet.integration.test.ts`); repo and template workflows pin the same action SHAs (`audits/templates/template-action-pins.test.ts`); summary prompts use one of three coverage verbs (`audits/workflows/summary-output-format.test.ts`); closed-vocabulary tokens are backticked outside fences (`audits/workflows/prompt-notation.test.ts`); every gate holds on every host (`install/modules/index.integration.test.ts`, `audits/hooks/gateguard-parity.integration.test.ts`); preflight sees the tracker being installed (`checks/before/index.integration.test.ts`); producer and consumer verdict vocabularies agree (`audits/workflows/verdict-vocabulary.test.ts`); this repo's .gitattributes carries a union rule for .bkit/friction.jsonl that the template does not (`audits/templates/telemetry-gitattributes.integration.test.ts`).
rationale: The close step once copied a fresh document over the canonical one, so re-running design or plan destroyed the previous document (#417); a rename in place would match the sub-plan and plan-presence globs in bkit-build.md / bkit-ship.md, while a subdirectory is invisible to every exact-name or non-recursive read; deriving the bucket with `date +%Y%m` broke a design crossing a month boundary (#416). Renovate ignores `.bkit/templates/**`, so template pins silently rotted until a consumer's CI broke; the snapshot pinned the stale value as expected. Summary prompts carried three unnamed contracts, and nothing separated do-not-drop-items from be-brief, so a summariser could drop rows; restating the rule twice on one line is how two statements drift apart. The predecessor notation rule (backtick only when compared) was undecidable and the corpus split 86% vs 68% bare for the identical construct; bracketed instructions inside fences were left behind in the first sweep. Per-host gate suites drifted (Cursor was missing gate-config, ALLOW_CONFIG_EDIT, deny-retry and docs-density cases). The install path resolved the tracker ~70 lines after preflight, so a linear → github switch told the consumer to add github but never to drop linear. bkit-ship.md gated DIAGNOSE_VERDICT as PASS|FAIL while dispatching the same agent other workflows gate as PASS|CONCERNS|FAIL, so a legitimate CONCERNS failed the ship gate; two verdict variables one edit apart let a typo silently read the wrong step's verdict. Union on friction.jsonl can resurrect rows harvest drained, so bkit does not impose it on consumers; this repo accepts the trade-off. A literal host list in a hook would drift unnoticed because nothing compares it to the registry. Asserting a test gate rather than the corpus stops a loosened checker looking like an honest pass. Reasons moved out of test comments (owner rule 2026-10-10).
alternatives: Rename superseded documents in place — rejected: matches workflow globs.

summary: The Renovate example disables updates for `@cbartens/bkit`; bkit is upgraded with `pnpm bkit upgrade`
description: packageRule `{ matchPackageNames: ["@cbartens/bkit"], enabled: false }` in `.bkit/templates/.github/renovate.json5`.
rationale: `pnpm bkit upgrade --latest` bumps the pin and re-syncs bkit's files and `.bkit/templates/` in one step; a bare version bump skips the re-sync and leaves the consumer split-brain. `@cbartens/bkit` is public on npmjs, so without this rule Renovate resolves it and opens those bare bumps. Reasons moved out of the Renovate example's comments (owner rule 2026-10-10).

summary: Every template bkit ships is adopted in this repo verbatim or with a listed set of edits, and a test enforces it
description: `.bkit/core/engine/audits/repo/dogfood-templates.test.ts` holds one entry per template: identical, adopted with an ordered list of labelled edits (`placeholder` / `adapt` / `bkit-only`), not adopted (`.github/dependabot.yml`: this repo uses Renovate), or generated (`docs/capabilities.md`). The repo copy must equal the template after the listed edits, byte for byte. `.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` is the template (which already ships the `bkit-tests-check` capstone) with these edits: placeholders for the default branch and the `.nvmrc` Node version; the `bkit-tests-scope` planner lane added, with the static and unit lanes waiting on it, slop delta on every event against the planner base, and `actions: read` for the planner and the capstone's Mirror Push Run; the `bkit-tests-integration` lane added, the unit coverage stub and Mirror Push Run enabled, and the capstone also asserting the planner and integration lanes; no tenant lease or deploy job, no turbo, no `Detect Direct Push`, and the migrations-immutable, auto-force-e2e, supabase-migrate, test-db and test-presence stubs dropped. Its bkit-only steps are `Assert Dist Freshness` and `Check Status Holes` (the one `bkit-only` edit) and `Run Shell Tests (bats)` (inside the unit-lane `adapt` edit). `.github/renovate.json5` carries one `bkit-only` edit holding vite and pnpm majors. `package.json` carries no inline `lint-staged` key, so `.lintstagedrc.json` is the config lint-staged loads.
rationale: Owner 2026-10-10: "we need to COMPLETELY eat our own dogfood". A template improvement found here goes into the template so consumers get it; a difference with no label fails the test.

summary: Templates carry no `bkit:start` / `bkit:end` blocks; only files bkit writes do
description: `bkit-ci.yml`, `bkit-cloud.yml`, `.vale.ini`, `.vale/styles/House/*.yml`, `.prettierignore` and `.cursor/Dockerfile` under `.bkit/templates/` hold plain content. The bkit-ci.yml advisories `ci-yml-missing-actionlint` and `ci-yml-run-injection` recognise an adopted bkit-ci.yml by an uncommented `bkit-tests` or `bkit-tests-<lane>` job (`ADOPTED_CI_JOB_RE`); `ci-yml-capstone-contract-drift` keys on the `bkit-tests-check` job.
rationale: bkit never writes a template, so a block in one signals ownership bkit does not have.

summary: The template bkit-ci.yml ships the `bkit-tests-check` capstone, without a planner
rationale: Owner 2026-10-10: ship the template with it switched on if required for bkit-ship to work. `runs gate`, `runs wait` and `setup protect-main` read only the capstone job and its result; no bkit command reads planner output. The executed-test count check applies only when the unit lane writes a count, which keeps the template stack-agnostic.

summary: The Renovate example caps pnpm's worker pool in Renovate's runner and enforces release age in Renovate, with pnpm's own `minimumReleaseAge` set to 0
description: `env: { PNPM_WORKERS: "1", PNPM_MAX_WORKERS: "1" }` and `minimumReleaseAge: "7 days"` in `.bkit/templates/.github/renovate.json5`; consumers set `minimumReleaseAge: 0` in pnpm-workspace.yaml.
rationale: On a large pnpm-11 monorepo, `pnpm update --lockfile-only`, especially alongside a pnpm-level `minimumReleaseAge` gate that verifies publish timestamps for every lockfile entry, can exceed the physical memory of Mend's hosted microvm and fail with `kernel-out-of-memory` (a physical OOM, not a V8 heap limit), blocking every dependency PR; CI and Vercel pass because their runners have far more RAM (KN-CORE-10, KN-41). The worker cap is cheap and reversible and scoped to Renovate's runner, but may not clear a metadata-driven OOM on its own because `--lockfile-only` barely engages the worker pool. Enforcing release age in Renovate holds young dependencies out of PRs with no per-install timestamp check, removing the memory spike at the source and speeding every CI and Vercel build; security and OSV PRs bypass it, so CVE fixes are never delayed. pnpm 11 defaults the gate to 1440, so deleting the key leaves it active and drops the `@cbartens/*` exclusion, breaking same-day bkit upgrades; only 0 turns the per-entry check off. The trade-off is losing pnpm-level defence against fresh manual or transitive installs. Reasons moved out of the Renovate example's comments (owner rule 2026-10-10). The release age is 7 days, and Dependabot's `cooldown.default-days` matches it (owner decision 2026-10-14): a week gives a wider margin than a 1- or 3-day wait for a bad or compromised publish to be detected and pulled before its update PR opens; security updates bypass both, so the longer wait never delays a CVE fix.

summary: Build proves each task's tests failed before its code existed: the execute agent calls `bkit tests red` once per test, which runs it itself and records the red only on a real failure
rationale: A test written after the code tends to match what the code does; one seen failing first proves it exercises the new behaviour. Build makes one commit per sub-plan and subagents never commit, so there is no per-task starting point to check out afterwards; checking at the moment of the red is the only per-task proof. An agent that writes the code first sees the red refused because the test passes.
alternatives: Re-run the test at the task's starting commit in a throwaway worktree (no per-task commit exists); temporarily remove the task's source changes (sub-plan granularity only, a crash leaves code missing); accept failure output the agent records (the agent can fabricate it, the weakness of Task Master's TDD mode).

summary: Red and green are judged by the named test's own outcome in a JUnit report written by the consumer-declared `bkit:test:file` script, never by exit code
rationale: Spike 2026-10-14 (vitest): a misspelled path, a syntax error and an import of unwritten code all exit 1 like a real assertion failure; a test-name filter matching nothing exits 0 with the test skipped; vitest reports load errors as a failure named after the file path, so failure-vs-error cannot separate them. Only 'the named test ran and failed / passed' does. JUnit XML is the format most runners write (vitest, pytest built in; jest via jest-junit). bkit passes the full repo-relative path because vitest matches short paths as substrings.
alternatives: Exit code alone; JUnit failure vs error split; a runner-specific JSON report; a test command written into the plan (an agent could write one that always fails).

summary: A test failing only because the code it imports does not exist is not a valid red; the execute agent writes a stub first so the red is the assertion failing
rationale: An import failure never shows the assertion failing, so `expect(true).toBe(true)` would pass the moment the module exists. The named-test rule enforces this mechanically: the runner reports the load error as a case named after the file, never the test name.
alternatives: Accept import-missing as red (classic TDD counts a compile failure).

summary: Test-first covers unit and integration tiers, has no plan-wide opt-out, and reports itself as not enforced (never silently passes) when there is nothing to check
rationale: Build never runs E2E or @live locally, so those rows stay planned up front in the Derived Test Matrix. Per-task `Test first: n/a — {reason}` covers docs, config, pure refactors and prototypes; plan scope-check rejects an unjustified n/a. A plan-wide switch is a setting nobody asked for. Brief builds (no plan), plans predating `Test first:` lines, and repos without `bkit:test:file` get `Enforced: false` with the reason, so in-flight plans keep working after upgrade.
alternatives: Require test-first for every tier; a per-plan opt-out flag; fail builds whose plan predates the `Test first:` line.

summary: A red's evidence is a `build-task-red` status row (test, test name, file hash, failure message) plus a `.snapshot` copy of the test file beside the runner log; nothing pins a git object
rationale: Spike 2026-10-14: an unreferenced tree snapshot is deleted by gc; refs/bkit or refs/worktree pins survive gc but a plain push or clone never carries them, so a build resumed in a fresh cloud container would lose them. The row and snapshot ride the plan-execute commit and survive push and resume. The row is written with --commit=none because the default commit runs `git add -A` and would commit the half-written task.
alternatives: Temporary-index tree snapshot pinned under refs/bkit/* or refs/worktree/*.

summary: `bkit tests green` reports any change to a test file since its red with the diff; the verify agent judges it — added tests, formatting or a renamed test is fine, a weakened, removed or rewritten assertion is a gap gap-remediate cannot fix
rationale: A later task adding tests to the same file and the pre-commit formatter both change the file legitimately, so an exact-match rule would fail honest builds; detecting the change is mechanical, judging its meaning is not.
alternatives: Exact file-hash match (false failures); additions-only line check (breaks on formatter reflow).

summary: `bkit:test:file` is a consumer-declared script bkit never seeds; install's `test-file-script-missing` advisory hands over the contract and a vitest example until it exists
rationale: No single command runs one test file on every stack, and a monorepo must route the path to the owning package and config. Spike on consumer-a: running it through turbo crashed (the package's existing `--outputFile` clashed with the JUnit flag) and turbo's test tasks are cached and depend on upstream suites, so the script must call the runner directly. The implementation is each consumer's, per the stack-agnostic rule.
alternatives: Seed a vitest default; name it `bkit:gate:*` (it is not a chained tier gate).

summary: bkit is MIT across the whole package: engine, core, shared and templates alike. The root `LICENSE.md` is the MIT text; install writes the same text to the consumer `.bkit/LICENSE.md`. The managed marker names no licence. No folder carries its own licence. Contributions come in under MIT with no CLA
rationale: Owner decision 2026-10-14; no rationale recorded for the move to MIT. The marker dropped its licence because MIT's condition is the full copyright and permission text, which `.bkit/LICENSE.md` carries; a URL in each file (what PolyForm's Notices section accepted) satisfies nothing under MIT.

summary: Superseded by `mit-licence-everywhere`: one licence (MIT) for every payload folder, and the marker names no licence
A red for an unchanged test stands on resume; a red refused as `passed` blocks the task; already-landed and moved tests are not gaps when the evidence says so
description: `bkit tests red` returns `already: true` without running when a red exists for the same task, test file and test name and the file hash is unchanged. Refusals carry a kind (`no-report`, `not-run`, `passed`, `skipped`, `exit-mismatch`); execute blocks on `passed` and never undoes code to force a red. Execute skips reds for tasks logged `DONE — already landed`; verify reads the plan-currency report and maps that `no-red` to no gap. `tests green` reports whether a recorded test the plan does not name passes now, so verify can clear a renamed or moved test.
rationale: Execute never ticks tasks, so a resumed build re-runs it from the first task and every finished task would otherwise be refused and loop. Work that already landed cannot show a red. A test moved by plan-currency `Reword` leaves the planned path missing, which gap-remediate cannot fix. Found by a full read of every workflow and prompt that touches plan tasks.

summary: bkit ships no context-compression proxy (caveman, Headroom) and no proxy template; token cost is cut by reading less (`.agents/rules.md` `Code reads` / `Narrow text search first`, ReadGuard)
description: Measured in `tests/compression/bkit-caveman-headroom-compression-proxy-comparison.md`: 456 Claude Code transcripts from one consumer repo, 500 tool results replayed offline with their real tool call and user message. Projected share of total cost saved, bootstrap 95% range: caveman 1.8% (1.0–2.6%), Headroom with Kompress off 0.8% (0.4–1.4%), Headroom with Kompress 2.7% (2.2–3.2%). Both proxies keep the prompt cache intact: each tool result is compressed once on arrival and the same compressed form is resent on later requests. Tool results >= 2 KB, re-reads included, are 26.9% of cost; the rest (agent messages, system prompt, rules, tool definitions) is not rewritten while the cache is warm. Exact repeats of an earlier result are 2.1% of cost, bounding lossless de-duplication. Not measured: Headroom's default `--mode token` and its opt-in `HEADROOM_DEDUPE` / `HEADROOM_COLD_RECOMPACT`.
rationale: About 1–3% saving does not justify an extra process in every session that sees all LLM traffic. The larger savings are lossy: Kompress changed code syntax (`(preset) => void` became `(preset) void`), caveman elides function bodies, and one live caveman run produced a wrong answer from a compressed log. Reading less is lossless and reaches the share a proxy cannot.
alternatives: Ship Headroom `--mode cache --disable-kompress` as an optional template (rejected: 0.8% saving, one more moving part); caveman (rejected: every bkit agent's `tools:` needs its retrieve tool, voice harms written artifacts); Headroom with Kompress (rejected: rewrites code).

summary: Audit reports record their audited commit in the same `bkit:anchor` block as design and plan docs; filenames keep the UTC timestamp suffix, not a commit hash
description: `@bkit-audit-generate` stamps `<!-- bkit:anchor -->` (`baseSha` = HEAD at stub creation, `baseRef` = audited branch via `bkit branches anchor-stamp --base-ref=`) on top of the report right after creating it, so the commit is machine-readable at the top of the file instead of in Step 1 prose. Each template Step 1 reads the previous report commit from its anchor, falling back to the HEAD its `Previous Run` recorded. A hash in the filename was rejected: the same commit is audited more than once (re-runs, audits of live outside state such as open dependency PRs, model catalogues, CI timings) so it is not unique, and hashes do not sort by time, which Step 1 relies on to find the newest prior report. Plan and design filenames stay fixed (`{FID}-plan.md`, `{FID}-design.md`): workflows open them by exact name, `-plan-*` means split sub-plans, and they already carry `baseSha` in their anchor.

summary: `maxTurns` gets a fourth tier, XL=300, held only by `@bkit-audit-generate`
description: One agent runs all 35 audit templates and the cap is set per agent, so the audit runner moves from L=150 to a new XL=300 tier rather than splitting into per-template agents. Measured local runs: log-triage 177 turns (cut off with no final reply, work also split across four helper agents of 47-98 turns), security 175, prompts 141, friction 139, harvest 60. Big audits do real work past 150, so L was acting as a workload budget for them; XL sits at about twice the largest measured run, the same doubling the 3600s step timeout uses.
alternatives: 200 (rejected: the largest measured runs already reach ~177); a second XL audit agent for the big templates only (rejected: a second agent rendered per host, a launcher that must pick per template, and a big-template list that goes stale, for no gain beyond stopping a stuck small audit sooner)

summary: Script-host guardrails (Cursor, Codex, Antigravity) classify git by the parsed command; Claude and opencode carry glob rows for the common git reorderings in the same tier; --no-verify is ask-tier everywhere; shell reads of secret files are gated on the script hosts only
description: `hooks/guardrails-tiers.js` parses each segment, `sh -c` script and `$(…)` substitution: git global options skipped, flags in any order, short clusters expanded, option values never read as flags. DENY: `git push` with `--force`, an `f` in a short cluster, or a `+refspec`; `--force-with-lease` never. ASK: `git reset --hard`, any `git clean` that is not `-n` / `--dry-run`, whole-tree `git checkout` / `git restore` (not `--staged` alone), `git stash drop`, `git rebase -i` / `--interactive`, `git filter-branch`, `--no-verify` on any git subcommand, `git commit -n`; plus a `secret` tier for a shell read of `.env` / `.env.*` (not `.env.example`), `*.pem`, `*.p12`, `id_rsa` — redirect targets, copy destinations, grep / rg patterns, comments and `ls` / `mv` / `test`-style commands are not reads. Cursor and Antigravity ask on it, Codex advises. Claude `permissions` and opencode `permission.bash` add glob rows for the same tiers (`git push * --force`, `git push * -f*`, `git push * +*`, `git reset *--hard*`, `git clean -*f*`, `git checkout *.`, `git restore *.`, `git * --no-verify`, …); they carry no rows for shell secret reads. The Claude guardrails hook stays advisory-only.
rationale: Prefix rows and literal regexes let `git reset -q --hard`, `git clean -df`, `git push origin +dev` and `git push origin dev --force` through on every host. Claude globs take `*` anywhere, so reordered force-push is expressible as deny without touching `--force-with-lease`; the Claude hook therefore needs no deny / ask decision, which keeps `guardrails-shell-advisory-scope-and-detection`. Only force-push is deny: the permissions deny list is global to every agent Bash call, and `.agents/rules.md` permits `--force-with-lease` on personal branches. opencode is last-match-wins, so its new ask rows for `--no-verify` sit after the `git push --force-with-lease*` allow and its anywhere-force deny rows after those, keeping the existing keys so no consumer migration is needed. Claude and opencode get no shell secret-read rows because a command-text glob such as `Bash(* .env *)` also matches `cp .env.example .env`, `git add .env.example`, grep patterns and commit messages, and an ask stalls autonomous and cloud runs on those harmless commands, which costs more than the read it would catch.
alternatives: Make the Claude PreToolUse hook return deny / ask — rejected: globs express the force-push cases, and a hook decision is a second policy source. Shell secret-read glob rows on Claude and opencode (`Bash(* .env *)`, `Bash(*.pem *)`, `Bash(* id_rsa *)`) — rejected: they cannot tell a read from a mention and stall unattended runs. Mass-promote the PROHIBITED git list to deny — rejected by the tier split above.

summary: bkit-audit-generate appends MEDIUM+ findings to docs/failures.jsonl, reusing any open row that names the same problem whichever workflow wrote it, and closes only its own audit-{slug}-* rows a rerun no longer finds
description: Audit findings lived only in the report, so /bkit-plan saw them only when the issue named the report (AUDIT_PATHS), and they dropped out of sight once the next run replaced the report. The audit agent now writes each MEDIUM+ finding as a failure row. Matching runs against every open row, not only audit-{slug}-* keys: debug runs, triage and other workflows already record most flakes and many bugs under their own keys, and a prefix-only match wrote a second row for the same problem on every run (worst on the flakes audit, whose subject is rows the ledger already holds). Same problem = same file:line, test title or error signature; a match reuses that key, otherwise a new audit-{slug}-{content-slug} key is minted. Closing stays scoped to audit-{slug}-* rows so a rerun that misses an intermittent flake never closes a row another workflow opened. The failures and deferrals audits write nothing. Templates that named failure rows as a later step now say the audit agent writes them. AUDIT_PATHS stays for plans that fix one report.
alternatives: Plan Step 4 scans docs/audits/ and matches finding Location against the draft plan files - rejected: new search step, own staleness filter (baseSha), and findings still vanish when a report is replaced. Exempting the flakes audit from ledger writes like failures and deferrals - rejected: flakes no other workflow recorded would never reach the ledger, and security and testing hit the same duplication.

summary: Audits probe every tool they need before the probe steps but never stop on a blocked call; they run everything the remaining tools allow and list blocked calls, their narrow allow rules and the skipped work under Not Checked
description: `@bkit-audit-generate` has no tool for asking a human, and in Claude Code auto mode its frontmatter `permissionMode` is ignored, so each action goes to the classifier. Each template Pre-Flight opens with a `Permissions` item: one cheap read-only call per tool the run uses. A blocked call, there or in any later step, is recorded verbatim with the narrow allow rule that clears it in `Not Checked`, `Process Improvements` and `Project Instructions` `Permissions`, never retried or reworded; the run carries on with every step the remaining tools allow and lists the work it could not do under `Not Checked`. Blocked calls persist in `Project Instructions` `Permissions` so the next run probes them first and the owner has one list of rules to grant. The earlier stop-and-resume pause is dropped: some blocks are deliberate (an owner who will not grant a production read), and a pause assumes every block is cleared by an allow rule, so those runs stopped before Step 1 on every run and an unattended run waited forever. Allow rules over chat approvals: a chat approval clears one named action, and whether a subagent classifier reads approvals given to the parent session is undocumented.
alternatives: Stop before Probe Steps and hand back allow rules to grant, or resume with continue (rejected: stalls every run on a deliberately blocked call and every unattended run); a known-gap marker in Project Instructions that exempts a call from the pause (rejected: keeps the pause and adds a per-project switch to fix a problem not stopping removes); an up-front ask by the launching session in `.agents/rules.md` (rejected: audit-runner behaviour belongs in the audit prompt and templates, not the universal rules).

summary: The outdated-bkit warning lives in `bkit repo info` and the anchor stamp, not in a rules.md rule or a prose step per workflow / audit template
description: Every phase workflow's Step 1 already runs `bkit repo info`, and every design, plan and audit doc is already stamped by `stampAnchor` (`bkit workflows promote` / `bkit branches anchor-stamp`). Both compare `.bkit/version` `pinnedVersion` (the release the workflow, prompt and template text was rendered from) with the newest published `@cbartens/bkit`, compared as numbers with a prerelease older than its release. `repo info` returns `bkitAdvisory`, which Step 1 shows the user; the stamp records `bkitVersion` / `bkitLatest` in the anchor block and, when outdated, writes a visible tool-owned `Outdated bkit` line under it, so a doc read later shows it came from stale templates. Warning only: no registry answer, no pin, or `BKIT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` means no warning, never a failure. The registry is asked at most once a day (cache in the git common dir, failures remembered for an hour) so parallel runs and offline runs add no wait. The pinned version is compared rather than the installed package because the rendered text, not the binary, is what an agent reads.
alternatives: A rule in `.agents/rules.md`: an instruction the agent may skip, the semver comparison is error-prone by hand, and it loads in every session including ones that run no workflow. A prose step in each phase workflow and each `docs/templates/bkit-audit-*.md`: the same steps copied into every file and every consumer, drifting apart. An opt-in `--bkit-version` flag on `anchor-stamp` for audits only: leaves design and plan docs without the record.

summary: `maxTurns` tiers are S=50 / M=100 / L=200 / XL=400; S holds only `*-summary`, L adds every codebase-sweeping investigator and whole-doc rewriter, XL holds the audit runner, every `bkit-utility-update-*` agent and both maintainer release agents
description: Human-set brackets; the cap is a runaway-loop guard, so agents with any recorded early stop or codebase-wide work move up one bracket. 100 to 200: `@bkit-build-plan-verify` (stopped at 50 tool uses, findings unwritten), `@bkit-ship-deferred-sweep` (70 + 75 tool uses across a resume), `@bkit-debug-failure-diagnose` (56 and 74 tool uses, only the template saved), `@bkit-plan-generate` (budget spent on research, skeleton only), `@bkit-plan-update` and `@bkit-design-update` (whole-doc rewrites ending at Verdict: PENDING), `@bkit-build-challenge-1/-2` (cut off in final bookkeeping), `@bkit-build-challenge-reconcile`, `@bkit-build-challenge-tests`, `@bkit-build-plan-current` (same diff surface), `@bkit-design-spike` (runs probe code), `@bkit-ship-update-docs` (per-cycle twin of update-documentation). 50 to 100: `@bkit-plan-scope-check-1/-2`, `@bkit-plan-complexity-check` (read the whole plan against code), `@bkit-debug-abort-handover`, `@bkit-build-install-skills`. L also rises 150 to 200 for the test-loop modifiers; XL rises 300 to 400 for `@bkit-audit-generate`; all six `@bkit-utility-update-*` agents move 100 to 400 because each sweeps a whole ledger, the roadmap board or the doc catalog; `utility-new-release` (100) and `utility-pre-release-check` (200) move to 400. Early-stop counts come from `.bkit/friction.jsonl` and `harvest/friction.jsonl` and count tool uses, not turns, mostly from runs under the older 25/50 caps. Replaces `audit-generate-xl-turn-tier` on the cap value only.
alternatives: raise only agents with a recorded cap hit (rejected by human: the cap is only a ceiling, so codebase-wide work moves up without waiting for a hit); keep the reviewers and ideators at 100 too (kept: they read a few docs and write one, no recorded hit); L=150 so the `@bkit-build-plan-execute` cap stays a sharp signal that a plan should have been split (#463 body; superseded by the human choice of 200 — the cap still bounds an oversized plan and `@bkit-plan-complexity-split` remains the upstream control)

summary: `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json` and `.opencode/opencode.json`: bkit owns only its tracker entry, and inside it only the keys and toolsets the template sets; extra keys, headers and toolsets are the consumer's
description: Install and upgrade reset each key the template sets in the tracker entry and keep the consumer's other keys and headers (`mergeTrackerEntry`, `.bkit/core/engine/install/write.ts`). `headers["X-MCP-Toolsets"]` keeps the consumer's list in its order and appends any template toolset it lacks, so a toolset bkit adds still reaches every consumer. The entry is in sync, and `bkit check` reports no drift, when it already holds everything that merge would write (`trackerEntryInSync`). Used by `reconcileMcpJson` (`.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`) and `reconcileOpencodeJson` (`mcp.<tracker>`). The rest of each file stays the consumer's, as before. Uninstall is unchanged: it removes the entry only while it still equals the template, so an extended entry stays.
rationale: bkit owns the entry because tracker steps run through it, and those steps need only what the template sets: the URL, the `Authorization` header and the `issues` / `projects` toolsets. The whole-entry exact match also refused additions that cannot break any step, so enabling one more toolset (consumer-a adding `actions` in Cursor and OpenCode) needed a bkit release, and `bkit check` failed pre-push and CI until then (#613).
alternatives: Exact match on the whole entry (the previous rule) — replaced: it refused harmless additions. Template wins on the toolset list — rejected: the list is one comma-separated string, so a plain merge drops every consumer toolset. Consumer list replaces the template list — rejected: a toolset bkit adds would never reach existing installs, and an old install missing `projects` would stay broken.

summary: Vulnerability, config and secret scanning ships as one copy-and-own Trivy workflow, `bkit-trivy.yml`, running the official image pinned by tag and digest
description: `bkit-trivy.yml` runs `trivy fs --scanners vuln,misconfig,secret --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 --include-dev-deps --skip-dirs .bkit/templates` on push, pull request and a daily cron, through `uses: docker://ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy:<tag>@sha256:<digest>`. Acceptances live in `.trivyignore.yaml` (`statement` + `expired_at`), passed only when the file exists. With `scripts/ci/check-dependency-audit.mjs` adopted the scan skips `pnpm-lock.yaml`, so a pnpm advisory is accepted in `accepted-advisories.json` only. No `bkit check` advisory and no setup tip for an absent scanner.
rationale: Renovate and Dependabot propose fixes and never fail CI; the pnpm audit gate covers pnpm lockfiles only. Trivy is the one open-source tool covering lockfiles in every language, container and IaC config, and secrets in a single pinned binary. The docker image pinned by digest lets Renovate bump tag and digest together, where a binary download needs a sha256 no updater refreshes. `aquasecurity/trivy-action` and `setup-trivy` tags were re-pointed at a credential stealer in March 2026, so no tag-referenced action. `--include-dev-deps` is required: measured on this repo, Trivy 0.75.0 without it read 0 of 193 pnpm packages and passed.
alternatives: OSV-Scanner: lockfiles only; image scanning less mature; a second tool once containers arrive
Grype + Syft: comparable image scanning; ignore rules carry no expiry
Extend check-dependency-audit.mjs to read Trivy JSON: one acceptance file for every stack, but more code; deferred until a non-pnpm consumer needs a dated-acceptance gate
trivy-action / setup-trivy pinned by SHA: still runs the action install path hijacked in March 2026

summary: The capstone's pass/fail verdict is `scripts/ci/check-capstone.mjs`, required with `bkit-ci.yml`; the template capstone step reds with a copy-the-script message when the file is missing, and never skips itself
description: `check-capstone.mjs` reads the lanes from `LANES` plus `<LANE>_RESULT` / `<LANE>_RAN` / `<LANE>_CACHE_SKIP`, an optional `PLAN` and `SCOPE_RESULT`, and `EMPTY_COUNT`. It reds on a lane whose result is not `success`, a lane that ran under `run_level=none`, a lane that succeeded with 0 tests or a non-numeric count, a plan that does not parse, a failed scope job and an empty `LANES`. `cache_skip=true` and `run_level=none` with every lane skipped assert nothing. No `PLAN` means every listed lane is expected to run. The template sets `EMPTY_COUNT: warn` so a lane that writes no count yet stays a warning; bkit's own workflow leaves it unset, so an unreported count reds. Both workflows run it after an ungated checkout without `continue-on-error`. `ci-scripts.test.ts` runs the script's test file and asserts both capstone steps call it with every `needs` lane wired in; bkit's `scripts/ci/` copy stays byte-identical to the template (`dogfood-templates.test.ts`). The whole-file snapshot of the template workflow is replaced by targeted assertions.
rationale: The assert is the only required check and a shell block inside YAML cannot be unit-tested: changing the 0-test arm survived the full suite in bkit's workflow and was caught in the template only by the whole-file snapshot. A missing script must red because skipping the step would leave a green that proves nothing. The template and bkit's copy are copy-and-own files that `bkit install` and `bkit upgrade` never write, so no migration exists to add the script to a consumer; a consumer sees the changed template path on upgrade and copies it.
alternatives: Skip the step when the script is absent: rejected, green proves nothing
Keep the inline shell and test it by extracting it from YAML: rejected, the test would copy the code it guards
Migration that writes the script into a consumer's scripts/ci/: rejected, the workflow and scripts are copy-and-own and no install path writes them
Gate the checkout on the plan: rejected, a run with no script exits on a missing module before reading the plan

summary: Shell guardrails flag off-allowlist curl/wget URL hosts and shell-as-edit-channel writes as advisories; Claude's hook never denies or asks; detection is head-of-command-line, scheme-strict, host-only, quote-aware, covers nested commands on every host and is quiet on scratch sinks
description: `.claude/hooks/bkit-guardrails.cjs` covers only what a command-prefix permission table cannot express: URL hosts and shell edits into source files. It emits `additionalContext` only. Cursor's twin asks on off-allowlist fetches and allows shell edits with an agent_message; Codex's emits its ask tier as advisory. All hosts share one shell parser (`hooks/guardrails-shell.js`: `shellWords`, `commandWords`, `commandLines`) and match the program of every command line it yields — each list / pipeline segment, `sh -c` script and `$(…)` / backtick body — not a bare token, so a fetch or in-place edit inside a wrapper is caught. They count only explicit-scheme URLs, consult only each URL's host, and report only unquoted redirects into repo-looking paths with source extensions.
rationale: Claude rules match a command prefix, never a URL host, and a blanket ask row would force a prompt on every shell fetch in every mode — unanswerable in a cloud session; the hook gives the signal without the prompt. `deny` already lives in settings.json and is evaluated before any hook, so a duplicate would be dead code with a second place to drift. A content-scoped `ask` is evaluated before the auto-mode classifier and always forces a prompt — the stall the host is configured to avoid. Shell edits stay advisory on every host because the edit-tools rule has sanctioned exceptions (bkit's plan workflow does a `sed -i.bak -E` bulk rewrite) and a gate that blocks a documented exception gets switched off. Matching a bare token fires on `grep 'curl'`, and a gate that fires on noise or constantly is one consumers disable. A scheme-less token cannot be told apart from a local path without guessing, and guessing turns a flag into an allow. Matching the allowlist against the whole command string is defeated by `?src=github.com` or `github.com.attacker.io`; the host alone decides where bytes go. On Codex the ask tier informs rather than stops; every command in it is already PROHIBITED in all bkit workflow headers, so only a human driving Codex by hand reaches it. Two shell parsers (a segment-head splitter for fetch / edit, a quote-aware one for git tiers) let `sh -c 'curl …'`, `$(curl …)` and `(curl …)` slip past the fetch gate and read a `>` inside quotes as a file write; one parser in the part every host includes closes both.
alternatives: Ask row on Claude shell curl — rejected: prompt on every fetch. Block shell edits — rejected: sanctioned exceptions. Whole-string allowlist match — rejected: trivially defeated. Keep the segment-head splitter beside the quote-aware parser — rejected: wrapped fetches bypass the gate and a quoted > reads as a write.

summary: The local static gate (bkit:gate:static) and the CI bkit-tests-static job run the same steps, including pnpm lint; a test fails when they diverge
description: bkit:gate:static chains typecheck, lint, format:check, lint:prose and slop:delta. The template bkit-ci.yml static job runs a Run Lint step (pnpm lint) after Run Typecheck, so a push that skips the hooks (cloud agent, --no-verify, web edit) is still linted. template-ci-yml.test.ts splits the gate into its pnpm scripts and asserts each has a run: pnpm <script> step in bkit-tests-static (slop:delta may carry an argument); exceptions live in a named list with a reason each. An adopted bkit-ci.yml is copy-and-own, so existing consumers keep their copy; no migration ships.
rationale: The template already told non-Node users to replace its typecheck / lint / test steps, and the local gate runs pnpm lint unconditionally, so any repo that passes the local gate has a lint script and the CI step cannot break it. Keeping lint local-only leaves every push that bypasses hooks unlinted.
alternatives: Keep lint local-only and document the gap: unlinted pushes land from cloud agents, --no-verify and the web UI.

summary: The gate-config file-name list lives only in .bkit/core/hooks/gateguard-engine.js, the code every host hook inlines; the TypeScript copy, its generator and the generated .cjs are gone
description: gateguard-engine.js holds GATE_CONFIG_PATTERNS and isGateConfig and is inlined into each host hook, so it is the list that decides whether an edit gets the weaken-the-gate advisory. shared/protected-paths.ts keeps only MIRROR_PATH_PREFIXES and isMirrorPath for the compliance grader. Gate-config cases are asserted in audits/hooks/gateguard-parity.integration.test.ts against the generated hook of every host, so a pattern dropped from the engine fails a test. The removed .claude/hooks/gate-paths.generated.cjs existed only in bkit's own repo, install never wrote it and .claude/ is not in the npm package, so no consumer migration is needed.
rationale: The TypeScript list had 13 patterns against the engine's 23 and no production caller; its drift test compared a generated file nothing executes, so it stayed green while the live list changed. One list tested through the real hooks cannot diverge from itself.
alternatives: Generate the engine's pattern list from the TypeScript table at render time: adds a build step and a second place to edit for a list the hooks already own.
Keep both lists and widen the drift test to compare them: the TypeScript copy would still have no caller.

summary: bkit-cloud.yml is disabled in bkit's own repo (repo setting) rather than wired to runner secrets; the workflow file is unchanged
description: The dogfood copy of the cloud lane no-ops unless ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENCODE_PROVIDER_KEY is set, and neither is. It is disabled with gh workflow disable bkit-cloud.yml (gh workflow list --all shows disabled_manually) and re-enabled with gh workflow enable bkit-cloud.yml once a key is set as a repo secret. docs/deployments.md records this under the bkit-cloud.yml section.
rationale: Putting an LLM provider key into repo settings is a credential decision for the owner. Disabling needs no credential and is undone with one command.
alternatives: Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENCODE_PROVIDER_KEY as repo secrets so the lane runs live: needs the owner to choose and store a credential.
Delete .github/workflows/bkit-cloud.yml: loses the dogfood copy of the shipped template.

summary: The unit coverage gate lives in one package.json script that both bkit's CI unit lane and /bkit-build Run Tests run; its branch floor lives in vitest.unit.config.ts
description: `test:coverage:unit` in `package.json` carries `--coverage.include` and `-c vitest.unit.config.ts`, which holds `coverage.thresholds.branches`; `Run Unit Tests` in `.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` and the /bkit-build Run Tests step (via `bkit:gate:static-unit`) both call it; the CI step only appends the JSON reporter + outputFile for the executed-count. `Report Unit Coverage` reads the same file via `vite-config-path` and runs on every event, so the job summary shows the measured figure against the floor on pushes as well as PRs.
rationale: vitest stays the gate (one run, no custom gate script), and the floor has one file read by both the gate and the report: a CLI flag in package.json cannot be scraped by the report action, and a floor written twice drifts. A coverage drop still fails in the build worktree before CI sees it.

summary: The shipped bkit-stub:coverage unit report runs on every event and reads the unit floor from vitest.unit.config.ts
description: `.bkit/templates/.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` bkit-stub:coverage: `Report Unit Coverage` has `if: !cancelled()` plus a `hashFiles` guard on the unit summary, `vite-config-path: vitest.unit.config.ts`, and `comment-on: pr` on same-repo PRs else `none`. The stub and `.bkit/shared/docs/testing.md` § Coverage on PRs put the unit floor in a `vitest.unit.config.ts` loaded with `-c` by the unit run only; the `--coverage.thresholds.branches` CLI flag is no longer the recommended form. The `coverage` advisory in `.bkit/core/engine/checks/after/tools.ts` says the same.
rationale: davelosert/vitest-coverage-report-action always writes its table to the job summary and shows a floor only when it can scrape `<metric>: <number>` from a file; a CLI flag cannot be scraped, and the PR-only guard left pushes with no statement of the floor at all. vitest stays the gate, reading the same file, so the shown floor is the one that gates. Copy-and-own template: no migration.

summary: One readInstallingVersion() in shared/package-json.ts throws when bkit's own package.json is missing, not a JSON object, or has no string version
description: `readInstallingVersion(root = getPkgRoot())` in `.bkit/core/engine/shared/package-json.ts` is the only reader of the version of the bkit package doing the install, built on `readPackageJson`. It throws an Error naming the file and saying to reinstall `@cbartens/bkit` when `package.json` is missing, is not a JSON object, or has no non-empty string `version`. Every former copy (`install/placeholders.ts`, `checks/after/managed.ts`, `install/modules/core.ts` x2, `commands/install/install.ts` x2, `checks/before/index.ts`, `commands/install/upgrade.ts`) calls it; the install.ts `getInstallingVersion` and core.ts `readInstallingVersion` wrappers are gone. `commands/comply.ts` `readBkitVersion` keeps its own fail-open walk-up: the compliance grader never gates.
rationale: The file is bkit's own manifest inside the installed package, so a damaged one means a corrupt install, not a consumer mistake. The old `"0.0.0"` fallback fed a wrong value into the stamp, the pin and the gates: markers rendered as v0.0.0 while the `.bkit/version` pin write threw, and `detectManagedStale` returns null on `0.0.0`, which switches the stale-marker gate off exactly when the install is broken. Six readers fell back and two threw, so one run could stamp half the files and then abort. Throwing stops before any file is written, matches the existing `package corrupt?` exit in `runCoreModule`, and surfaces through the CLI's top-level handler as one clear message. The `0.0.0` / empty guard in `detectManagedStale` stays for an injected unreleased-tree version.

summary: Unit tests may drive real git, bash and node against an os.tmpdir() folder; no network, no backing service
description: The Unit row of the docs/testing.md Tiers table allows real git / bash / node subprocesses run against a throwaway os.tmpdir() folder. It keeps the bans on network, backing services and state outside that folder. Driving the bkit CLI via tsx and wired multi-module flows stay Integration. About 33 non-mocking *.test.ts files under .bkit/core/engine/ spawn such processes; the commands/** ones are labelled Unit (boundary: real temp git repo).
rationale: The commands/** sources are thin wrappers over git, so a test that fakes git proves little. test:coverage:unit excludes *.integration.test.ts and holds the 78% branch floor in vitest.unit.config.ts, so renaming these files would drop their coverage from the floor and break it. Their slowness and timeouts belong to the flakes audit, not the tier line.
alternatives: Rename the files to *.integration.test.ts: drops them out of test:coverage:unit and breaks the branch floor.
Split the pure logic out of each wrapper into separate unit tests: large rewrite that duplicates what the real-git tests already prove.

summary: Test files are linted by Oxlint with oxlint-tsgolint, not ESLint, running only five test-quality rules as errors
description: `pnpm lint` runs `oxlint -c .oxlintrc.json --type-aware --tsconfig tsconfig.test.json --deny-warnings .bkit/core/engine`. `.oxlintrc.json` turns the default categories off and enables, for `**/*.test.ts` only: `vitest/expect-expect`, `vitest/no-conditional-in-test`, `vitest/no-conditional-expect`, `vitest/valid-expect` with `maxArgs: 2`, `typescript/no-floating-promises`, all `error`. Both packages are exact devDependencies (oxlint 1.87.0, oxlint-tsgolint 7.0.2004). `pnpm lint` sits inside `bkit:gate:static` and the CI static lane. No baseline, no ignore list: every hit is fixed in the test.
rationale: typescript-eslint 8.71.2 supports only TypeScript below 6.1.0 and the repo is on TypeScript 7.0.2, so type-aware ESLint rules such as `no-floating-promises` cannot run. oxlint-tsgolint is built on TypeScript 7 and runs the same rule. `valid-expect` defaults to one argument; Vitest's `expect(value, message)` is legitimate, so `maxArgs: 2` removes 122 false hits. Only these rules run because the issue is tests that cannot fail, and the default categories flag many unrelated things. oxlint 1.88.0 was younger than the 7-day `minimumReleaseAge` when chosen.
alternatives: ESLint with @vitest/eslint-plugin and typescript-eslint: no type-aware rules on TypeScript 7.
ESLint without type-aware rules: drops no-floating-promises.
Baseline or ignore list for existing hits: tests that cannot fail stay in the suite.

summary: bkit's own pnpm install refuses releases younger than 7 days and runs with supply-chain protections on, set in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`; the shipped Renovate example stays unchanged
description: `pnpm-workspace.yaml` sets `minimumReleaseAge: 10080`, `trustPolicy: no-downgrade`, `blockExoticSubdeps: true`, `strictDepBuilds: true` and `onlyBuiltDependencies: [esbuild]`. Every install, including lockfile-maintenance and automerge-group PRs, skips versions published in the last 7 days, direct and indirect. `devDependencies` are exact versions. The shipped Renovate example does not set `minimumReleaseAge`; it remains the consumer's choice per `docs/deployments.md`.
rationale: pnpm 11 can run out of memory on Mend's hosted runner, so the shipped example leaves the setting to the consumer. bkit runs Renovate on its own `ubuntu-latest` runner, which has the memory, so the repo can take the 7-day gate. `onlyBuiltDependencies` rather than `ignoredBuiltDependencies`: with `strictDepBuilds` on, pnpm 10.34.6 still fails the install with `ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS` for an ignored package, and `allowBuilds` is not read by that version; esbuild's postinstall only verifies and swaps in the platform binary, so letting it run is harmless.
alternatives: ignoredBuiltDependencies: [esbuild]: install fails under strictDepBuilds on pnpm 10.34.6
Renovate-only minimumReleaseAge: leaves local and CI installs ungated
Set minimumReleaseAge in the shipped Renovate example: risks pnpm 11 out-of-memory on Mend hosted runners

summary: `engines.node` is `>=24`, matching `.nvmrc`, CI and `release.yml`; it ships in the next major release
