description: Node 20 and 22 are no longer supported. Consumers on them break on install, so the release carrying this change is a major version. `docs/technology.md`, `docs/setup.md`, `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `.bkit/README.md` state `>=24`; `CHANGELOG.md` lists it under Breaking Changes. `docs/migrations.md` does not list it because it registers code migrations only.
rationale: bkit is built, tested and released on Node 24 only, so a lower floor claims support nothing exercises.
alternatives: Keep >=20 and add Node 20 and 22 to the CI matrix: more CI cost for runtimes nothing needs
Raise the floor in a minor release: breaks consumers without a major-version signal

summary: The shipped Renovate example extends config:best-practices, rebases PRs only on conflict, holds majors for dashboard approval, runs lockfile maintenance monthly and tracks off-manifest pins through one regex custom manager
description: Both `renovate.json5` copies: `extends: ["config:best-practices", ":dependencyDashboard"]`; an npm packageRule restores `minimumReleaseAge: "7 days"` over the preset 3 days; `rebaseWhen: "conflicted"`; majors carry `dependencyDashboardApproval: true`; `lockFileMaintenance` runs before 6am on the first day of the month; `ignorePaths` repeats the `:ignoreModulesAndTests` entries and adds `docs/plans/**`; `packageManager` joins the non-major group; one `customManagers` regex reads `# renovate: datasource=... depName=...` comments in Dockerfiles, `.claude/bkit-cloud.md` and workflows. `bkit-renovate.yml` pins `renovate-version` and the github-actions lookup of `ghcr.io/renovatebot/renovate` is disabled.
rationale: The default rebase re-runs CI on every open automerge PR whenever the base branch moves. Majors otherwise open a branch and a CI run before anyone decides on them. ghcr.io image tags carry no publish date, so `minimumReleaseAge` would hold every renovate-version update as pending; GitHub releases are dated. A repo-level `ignorePaths` replaces the preset list rather than extending it. Checksum-paired pins get the version bump only; the sha256 is updated by hand in the same PR.
alternatives: Keep config:recommended: no digest pinning of Docker images and actions, no abandoned-package flags
Leave renovate-version floating: the action tag can sit a major behind the latest Renovate
rebaseWhen behind-base-branch: one CI run per open PR on every base push

summary: Push to dev blocked when docs/capabilities.md is not what the pushed commit builds; checked in a throwaway checkout of that commit; graphify absent only warns
description: graphify pre-push block: push to dev → bkit-graphify.sh check-at PUSH_DEV_SHA → exit 1 on drift. check-at builds in a git worktree of the pushed commit: graphify reads the working tree, so uncommitted edits (usually a concurrent session's) would otherwise decide the answer. graphify not installed → NOT-checked warning, push goes on: a cloud session that cannot install it must still push; CI Check Capability Register re-checks every push to dev. Revert pushes skip it, as they skip the test tiers. Other branches keep the warn-only staleness note. One graphify release (GRAPHIFY_SPEC in bkit-graphify.sh): register commands refuse others, CI installs it; another release draws different edges. Upstreamed from app-gether-life, whose owner decided the same on its #1467.
alternatives: Warn-only note (previous state: stale register reached dev, CI red on 08ecf9b6). Plain graph:check in the hook (reads uncommitted edits → another session can flip it red or green). Block when graphify absent (locks out cloud sessions without it).

summary: Network allowlist is core-owned .bkit/allowlist.json, written for every host set; a recorded .cursor/allowlist.json is migrated away, not kept as a fallback read
description: Cursor, Codex, Claude and Antigravity guardrail hooks read one allowlist. It lived at .cursor/allowlist.json and only the Cursor module wrote it, so a Codex-only or Antigravity-only install (or uninstall --cursor) flagged every fetch while bkit check stayed green. Core now writes .bkit/allowlist.json on every install and upgrade; it is a CORE_MANIFEST byte-equal entry, so bkit check drift-gates it and full uninstall removes it. Hooks find it from the payload workspace roots / cwd, walking up to the .git root, because Antigravity runs plugin hooks from the plugin directory. Upgrade deletes a .cursor/allowlist.json whose hash .bkit/version records and prunes the hash; an unrecorded file is left alone. Owner confirmed the layout change on 2026-10-19.
alternatives: Keep .cursor/allowlist.json and write it whenever any reader host is installed (host-named path owned by a different host; uninstall --cursor still has to know about readers). Read the old path as a fallback (stale copy never updated or removed).

summary: A production rollback moves production back to the last good deployment first (every production host, from a rollback workflow sharing the deploy job's concurrency group), marks the bad deployment in ROLLED_BACK_DEPLOYMENT_ID, then fixes forward with a revert through dev and a normal release. Force-resetting main is a last resort for commits a dev release cannot undo, run only after production is back. bkit-tests-deploy refuses a marked deployment and a commit that does not descend from the one production serves.
description: The runbook reset main first and moved the host last. The reset is a push to main, so with bkit-tests-deploy it started a release run before production moved; with an ancestry-checking deploy job (both consumers that adopted bkit-tests-deploy run one) every release refused until production moved, and without one the CI promote raced the manual host promote. Moving the already-built good deployment is the fastest mitigation and needs no git change; fixing forward keeps main equal to what was released and keeps branch protection on.
alternatives: Keep reset-first and add a warning (the ordering hazard stays the default path); reset main and let the reset's release run promote the good commit (rebuilds instead of reusing a proven build, and runs with branch protection off); ship a rollback.yml template (larger change; the runbook states what such a workflow must do, consumers own the host-specific switch).

summary: Every design / plan close builds its commit in a throwaway .worktrees/_land-{FID} off origin/dev and pushes HEAD:dev, retrying up to 10 times with 2s-doubling, 30s-capped, jittered backoff when dev moved; any other refusal falls back to the PR squash-merge, whose merge also retries after update-branch. The close takes no dev lock, local dev is only fast-forwarded (laptop, pure fast-forward, skipped otherwise), and Gate 12 reads status.jsonl from origin/dev.
description: Parallel design / plan sessions collided at close: each checked out, pulled and squashed into dev in the one shared main checkout, so another session's staged or uncommitted file, or a dev moved by a sibling close, failed the squash or the push. Building the commit off origin/dev in a private worktree removes the shared checkout from the critical section, so the only remaining race is the push itself, which a rebuild-and-retry absorbs. Cloud runtimes get the same routine: a runner that can push dev retries the race instead of failing, and a push GitHub refuses (branch protection or a ruleset on dev) falls back to the PR close with a retried merge. Because local dev may stay behind (local commits, an uncommitted edit the move would overwrite), the gate and the audit read the landed copy on origin/dev rather than the main checkout's file.
alternatives: Keep the local squash under the dev lock (serialises closes but still fails on another session's uncommitted or staged files in the main checkout); 3 push retries with no backoff (too few for several sessions closing together); make Gate 12 read the main checkout file and require the fast-forward (a skipped fast-forward would fail a close that landed).

summary: bkit workflows close --flush --branch= removes the workflow-created feature worktree and deletes the branch only after the close is on dev (kept while a close PR is unmerged); ship's Step 14 Worktree Cleanup and its ship-worktree-cleanup step key are retired, Close Workflow becomes Step 14 and ends with cd {REPO_ROOT}, and Gate 14 reads status.jsonl from origin/dev.
description: With the book in the worktree, removing the worktree before the close would delete the rows the close commit must carry. Folding the removal into the close is the only order that keeps the book until it is on dev. A separate cleanup step after the close would need its own status row with nowhere left to write it, so the key is retired rather than renumbered.

summary: Ship Step 13 runs bkit branches sync-dev: fetch, fast-forward local dev without a checkout (merge --ff-only plus frozen install only when the main checkout is on dev and dev moved); local dev commits missing from origin/dev are logged with the publish command and never pushed. The step key stays ship-switch-to-dev.
description: Local dev commits ahead of origin/dev are someone's unreviewed work; ship is not the place to publish them, and the old rebase-and-push of all-skip-CI commits could still publish them unreviewed. Keeping the frozen step key avoids resetting attempt counters and orphaning the status-hole corpus.

summary: A ship FAILED record whose dev push is refused or exhausted is not landed: workflows handover --flush exits 10 / 11 and the record stays in the book root, where the next ship of {FID} carries it into its own dev commit. No PR fallback and no dev lock.
description: A failure record is low value next to the failure comment already on the issue, and a PR per failure would add review noise. Accepted cost: in an ephemeral cloud container the book dies with the container, so a refused FAILED record there is lost.

summary: bkit roadmap mirror (build / debug close) lands its row through pushToDev in every runtime and skips only when the run's own checkout is on dev; any refusal skips with a log line and exit 0, never a PR.
description: The feat-side row already reaches dev with ship's merge, so the mirror only makes the board current sooner; it must never fail or block a close.

summary: Design / plan / build / debug Failure Paths always keep the run's record through one `workflows handover --push --worktree`: committed and pushed on the feature branch (never onto an open PR); from a dev / main / detached checkout only the logs and ledgers land on dev through pushToDev, nothing committed in the checkout. Ship keeps its --flush to dev.
description: Before, design / plan never committed a failure record and build / debug committed one only with a handover, so a record lived only in a local worktree and died with a cloud container. Debug adopting dev ran `git add -A` + push on dev, publishing the half-done fix and any local-only dev commits. The feature branch is the record's home because code and bookkeeping reach dev together only through ship's merge; dev / main has no feature branch, so only bookkeeping lands there.

summary: No close reads the tracker, because nothing on the board comes from the tracker
description: No phase close reads the tracker, runs a drift check, or evaluates a cadence. Every phase close appends its `kind:"feature"` row to `.bkit/issues.jsonl` and re-renders the roadmap-status block from the ledger through `appendFeature` (`.bkit/core/engine/commands/workflow/roadmap.ts`): design / plan inside `bkit branches land`; build / debug via `bkit roadmap mirror` (the feat-side row, then a dev-side copy landed through a throwaway `origin/dev` checkout, skipped with a log line when the push is refused or fails); ship Step 6 via `bkit roadmap feature --strict`. Rendering is fail-open. Only ship gates on it: `--strict` exits 1 when the `SHIPPED` row could not be appended, and the step routes that to the Failure Path.
rationale: The question of whether a close should enrich from the tracker disappears once the board holds no tracker-derived rows to enrich.

references: .bkit/workflows.md (One landing routine for every dev write; PR-mode design/plan closes MUST push before `bkit prs open`; `[skip ci]` scope; Cross-step invariants: Close squash)
summary: #341 OQ-A confirmed, OQ-D withdrawn: design/plan close lands through `bkit branches land` as a direct dev push of a squash built off origin/dev in every runtime, else (push refused) via a {BRANCH}->dev PR merged with gh (D5(a), not push_files); the landed subject keeps `bkit [skip ci]`, so a docs-only close dispatches no CI
description: Design and plan Close Workflow run one `bkit branches land --workflow=<design|plan>` (`landVerb` in `.bkit/core/engine/commands/workflow/branches.ts`). Every runtime first tries the direct close (`landDirect` / `buildClose`): `git merge --squash -X ours {BRANCH}` in a throwaway `.worktrees/_land-{FID}` off a fresh origin/dev, roadmap row, one path-scoped `docs({FID}): <phase> DONE bkit [skip ci]` commit (`--squash-of={BRANCH}`), `git push origin HEAD:dev`, rebuilt and retried when dev moved (decision `design-plan-close-throwaway-origin-dev-worktree`). Any other push refusal (branch protection or a ruleset on dev) takes `landPr`: commit the roadmap update on {BRANCH}, push it, open or reuse the {BRANCH}->dev PR (`existing: "reuse"`), and squash-merge it with subject `docs({FID}): <phase> DONE bkit [skip ci]` and an empty body via gh, retrying a refused merge after `update-branch`; exit 80 at stage `open` / `merge` hands either step to MCP `create_pull_request` / `merge_pull_request`, then re-runs with `--pr` / `--merged-sha`; the landed SHA is the PR merge commit. Both paths then scan the landed commit BODY (subject excluded) and cross-check the transport; the `close-transport` row (`closeTransportRow`) is written only on a runtime that does not push dev, whose checkout holds the branch; a runtime that pushes dev never writes the main checkout, logs the skip, and `bkit branches land`'s JSON output carries the same shape, SHA and scan result. The merge does not wait for CI: the landed subject carries `bkit [skip ci]`, so a docs-only close dispatches no run. The OQ-D CI-cost reversal accepted at build (drop `[skip ci]` from every phase-close and intermediate status subject) is withdrawn.
rationale: Spike B (closed, folded into the design) found push_files (D5) cannot express `merge --squash -X ours`, inlines full file content per call (non-repairable payload bloat), and inverts conflict semantics (branch-wins vs dev-wins) -- three defects that demote it from primary. D5(a) is uniform with ship's server-side merge and avoids the push_files payload/conflict/credential-coupling defects. OQ-D was reversed: a deliberate `bkit [skip ci]` on a docs-only SUBJECT is the CI-minutes convention. The real defect is a token inherited into a squash BODY; every close passes an explicit --body "" and `bkit prs scan-body` scans the landed BODY only. `.bkit/core/engine/audits/workflows/skip-ci-subject-audit.test.ts` asserts both halves.
alternatives: D5 (push_files) as shape-A primary -- REJECTED per Spike B (non-repairable payload bloat, conflict-semantics inversion, credential coupling shared with gh's own flaky mode-3 auth). Dropping `[skip ci]` from every phase-close and intermediate status subject (the original OQ-D) -- REJECTED on reversal: one full dev CI run per docs-only close; the inherited-token risk is met by an explicit empty squash body plus a landed-body scan.

summary: #384 ship-bookkeeping lands AFTER #341 (d64ef5be merged); 384 re-derives against the post-#341 bkit-ship.md — outcome: 341-first-landed
description: Pre-flight gate for #384 (ship bookkeeping mutates validated PR head). #341 (CLOSED, merged d64ef5be) landed the post-#341 ship markers first: the ship runtime-resolved row writer is present once at bkit-ship.md:320 at d64ef5be, now `bkit runtime row --workflow=ship` at .bkit/core/workflows/bkit-ship.md, RUNTIME_DEVPUSHES appears 10x. #384 takes the post-#341 bkit-ship.md as its diff base: `git log --oneline d64ef5be..HEAD -- .bkit/core/workflows/bkit-ship.md` is empty (no intervening rewrite). No concurrent PR/branch rewrites bkit-ship.md — feat/58-workflow-counters and worktree-374-test-lane-coverage carry 0 bkit-ship.md-touching commits past origin/dev. Ship never checks out dev: Step 13 runs `bkit branches sync-dev`, which fast-forwards local dev without a checkout (decision `ship-sync-dev-fast-forward-only-never-push-local-dev`). Comment corrections folded into issue context by design phase: (a) non-firing pull_request on a CONFLICTING PR is general GitHub behaviour, not a bkit token quirk; (b) cancel-in-progress is a second independent justification for the frozen head; (c) Path B2 is the common case, not the escape hatch.
rationale: Two workflows rewriting bkit-ship.md on the same clone would collide. Recording 341-first-landed makes the serialisation explicit and machine-checkable: any later task asserting it can grep docs/decisions.jsonl for outcome 341-first-landed on key 384-341-serialisation.
alternatives: Land 384 against pre-#341 bkit-ship.md — REJECTED: would re-derive RUNTIME_DEVPUSHES/worktree conventions that #341 already settled. Block 384 behind an open #341 PR — REJECTED: #341 is CLOSED (d64ef5be merged).

summary: Ship keeps its 14 step names (`ship-worktree-cleanup` retired by decision `ship-close-removes-worktree-after-landing`); Steps 3 and 9 write no row and check their values with `steps gate --placeholder`
rationale: The names are frozen by `ship-invariants.test.ts` and `checks/status-holes.ts`; new rows would break the status-hole check for every past ship.

summary: Flags only tests passed are removed; tests set `package.json` `bkit.*` values instead
rationale: Follows 489-no-code-without-a-production-caller. Removed: `runs wait|gate --capstone/--ci-workflow/--required-lanes`, `--tracker` on `prs open` and `issues labels`, `runtime row --at`, `branches switch --lock-wait`, `--context-file`.

summary: Ship's close (docs({FID}): ship DONE) and Failure Path record (chore({FID}): ship FAILED) are built by pushToDev in a throwaway .worktrees/_land-{FID} off origin/dev, carrying the run's book (md logs dev lacks or the run rewrote copied, ledgers unioned; from a dev / main checkout only the run's own record), and pushed as dev with rebuild-and-retry when dev moved. Ship books in {WORKTREE_PATH} in every runtime; its workflow lock stays in the main checkout. The repo-global dev lock, bkit branches switch and every --dev-pushes flag are removed.
description: A laptop ship switched the main checkout to dev and committed there under a dev lock, so it could sweep another session's uncommitted work into its commit and serialised every parallel close. The design / plan close already proved the throwaway-checkout routine; ship now uses the same one, which removes the shared checkout from every dev write and leaves the push as the only race. Logs the run rewrote are copied too, so a second handover updates dev instead of leaving the first copy. The book moves to the feature worktree because the main checkout is no longer a tree ship may write to; the lock stays in the main checkout because it is gitignored and must be one file whichever tree the run books in.

summary: pushToDev runs every git command of a landing with core.hooksPath pointed at the null device (one more GIT_CONFIG_* entry), and logs that hooks were skipped. It is the one named exception to 'workflows never bypass hooks' in .bkit/templates.md.
description: A landing commits only docs, logs and ledger rows under [skip ci], built on a fresh origin/dev the run did not edit. The consumer's pre-commit / pre-push hooks gate code (format, static, unit, bkit check); run in the throwaway they either re-check the whole of dev, which the landing cannot fix, or fail on a checkout with no installed dependencies, so a hook failure would strand a close that has nothing for the hook to check. Skipping them is logged so it is never silent.
alternatives: Run the hooks: a red dev or a missing node_modules in the throwaway blocks every close. --no-verify per command: misses hooks git runs outside commit / push (post-checkout on worktree add).

summary: A Failure Path run from a dev / main / detached checkout lands only the run's own record: its log folder (md logs plus that folder's uncommitted .jsonl lines) and shared-ledger lines that are uncommitted and carry workflow == this workflow and ts >= the run's workflow-started at. No start row → no shared-ledger row is carried, logged. The hand-back removes exactly the carried lines; staged or since-edited files are kept and named.
description: On a shared checkout the uncommitted ledger lines can belong to another session or to a half-finished fix; carrying every line would publish them as this run's FAILED record, and handing the whole file back would delete them locally. The same workflow-and-time rule already scopes ledgerCounts, so the record and the close telemetry agree on what the run wrote.
alternatives: Carry every uncommitted ledger line (publishes other sessions' rows). Carry only the log folder (loses the run's own decisions and friction rows).

summary: Ship Step 1 runs bkit worktrees setup and bkit workflows start (with status path, ship-start-workflow and runtime row) straight after the workflow lock, before tracker writes and the repo preflight. Step names are unchanged (467-ship-step-names-frozen); lock age is still never checked.
description: Ship books every row in the feature worktree, so a failure between the lock and the worktree had no book: the Failure Path could record nothing and the flush had nothing to land. Opening the run first means every later failure keeps its record. The ship-input file stays in Step 2 because it needs ISSUE_TEXT.

summary: bkit workflows close --flush releases the ship lock only once the close landed on dev or its ship-close/{FID} PR opened. Any other outcome (dev moved before every push, a push with no server answer, fetch / checkout / commit failure, PR not opened) exits non-zero with the lock kept, for the Failure Path.
description: The Failure Path's workflows fail --token releases the lock; a close that had already released it left the Failure Path running unlocked while another ship of the same FID could start.

summary: ghUnavailable counts a failed gh call whose stderr carries HTTP 403 as unavailable, like gh missing or not logged in, so the caller hands the call to the GitHub MCP.
description: The Claude cloud proxy answers gh pr and gh issue (GraphQL) with a 403 (cloud environments docs, GitHub proxy section; inferred, not tested in a session). Before, a 403 was exit 1 and stopped the close's PR route with an error instead of switching to the MCP, which has its own credentials.

summary: bkit install --tracker=<name> re-renders every installed host and needs no host flag.
description: When --tracker= is given, install dispatches the named modules plus every host detectInstalledModules finds. validateModuleFlagsForVerb accepts install with no module flag when --tracker= is set.
rationale: Each host renders tracker-specific commands, agents and MCP entries, while bkit.issueTracker is one value for the repo. Rendering only the named hosts left the others on the old tracker, so bkit check failed right after an install that exited 0. The documented onboarding command bkit install --tracker=github exited 1.
alternatives: (1) Reject a tracker switch unless every installed host is named: REJECTED, it makes the user list hosts bkit already knows. (2) Change the docs to name a host: REJECTED, the stale-host defect stays.

summary: {{DEFAULT_BRANCH}} is the production branch: origin/HEAD, but main when origin/HEAD is dev or unset.
description: resolveDefaultBranch reads git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD through a non-throwing spawnSync and keeps the whole branch name after refs/remotes/origin/. An empty result or dev gives main.
rationale: Every use of the token in managed docs and CI templates means the production branch, beside dev. A repo whose GitHub default is dev (PRs target dev) rendered dev/dev text, and since origin/HEAD is set by some git versions on fetch and not on others, two machines rendered different bytes and the drift gate flipped by machine.
alternatives: (1) A package.json bkit key naming the production branch: DEFERRED, it needs an upgrade migration for repos whose origin/HEAD names another branch. (2) Always main: REJECTED, it breaks repos whose production branch is master.

summary: A release re-runs no test or lint step: the Release workflow keeps only the on-main check, dist freshness and the CHANGELOG block, sets HUSKY=0, and bkit's own pre-push skips the gates for a tag-only push on commits origin already holds.
description: release.yml dropped typecheck, test, format:check, lint:prose and lint:slop and sets HUSKY=0 on the job. The repo .husky/pre-push exits 0 before the delete-only check when every pushed ref is a tag (or tag delete) whose commit a refs/remotes/<remote> branch contains; the shipped template is unchanged.
rationale: The release commit is already gated: its PR passed bkit-tests-check and the merge push to main runs the full CI suite, and release.yml refuses a tag not on origin/main. Measured on v5.3.0: the Test step took 101s and the sliding v{N} tag push took 176s because pnpm install ran husky and the pushed tag fired the full pre-push gate on the runner; the local tag push ran the full gate a third time, and a v5.4.0 tag push was once refused by it on a commit that passed seconds later.
alternatives: (1) Keep the release re-run as defence in depth: REJECTED, the on-main check plus main protection already block an untested commit and the re-run only adds time and flake exposure. (2) Ship the tag-only skip in the template: NOT DONE, consumers may tag commits their CI never gated. (3) git push --no-verify for the sliding tag: REJECTED, HUSKY=0 also stops the hooks being installed at all.

summary: bkit-utility-update-tracker is the one agent allowed to write tracker issue fields: title, labels, board status, priority, size, milestone, parent and blocked-by. It never creates, closes, reopens or comments, never touches bkit:* labels, never sets a done state and never removes a link.
description: Two-Layer Separation keeps tracker calls in workflows; the roadmap utility reads only. The tracker utility is a second, human-invoked exception with field-write grants. Priority and size come from the newest issues audit Proposal, then the template's Ranking Rules and Size Scale; own judgement fills empty fields only and proposes the rest. GitHub blocked-by is written to the body block build reads.
rationale: The issues audit and roadmap only propose; nothing applied their proposals, so the board drifted from the rules. A utility run by a human is the approval, and the hard limits keep its writes to fields a human can undo.
alternatives: Utility writes a change plan and the caller applies it: every run needs a second manual pass the utility could do itself.
Workflow command instead of an agent: tracker hygiene is not a phase and needs no lock, worktree or status row.

summary: /bkit-design Step 3 Grill ends with a draft scenario round: the orchestrator drafts the acceptance scenario (Narrative, Success Criteria, Key Edge Cases, Process Sketch) from the whole context, asks the human to confirm or refine the inferred parts, and records it under a `DRAFT only` label in design-grill-{RUN}.md. bkit-design-generate starts its Acceptance Scenario from the draft and records each change as a Decisions row.
description: The draft round is always the last round and counts toward the 10-round cap, so decision rounds stop at 9. Headless runs and a human stop record the draft labelled as not reviewed by a human. grill=false writes no draft. The plan template is unchanged: it still copies the design's Acceptance Scenario verbatim and the human confirms it at the plan's Acceptance Scenario confirmed box.
rationale: Owner 2026-10-21: the interview ended on a vague 'confirm shared understanding'; a concrete scenario built from the issue, the prompt and the answers gives the human something specific to confirm or correct before any design work. The DRAFT label tells the design agents they may amend it. Changes made by the design get a Decisions row only, no confirmation item, because the human reviews the scenario again at the plan checkbox.
alternatives: Plan may also amend the scenario with each change listed (rejected by owner: plan keeps copying the design verbatim).
Draft round outside the 10-round cap (rejected by owner: it counts).
Design changes to the draft also raise a Risks & Open Questions item for confirmation (rejected by owner: a second sign-off for the same scenario).

summary: Linear workflow writes send labels and state as separate save_issue calls, labels first; each label a transition adds is created first with save_issue_label (workspace label, `already exists` = done); phase start sets the state type `started`; hand-off keeps the state name `In Review` and a team without it logs Unapplied.
description: Verified live on a default Linear team (#646): save_issue rejects the whole call when any state or label name is unknown, valid fields included, and never creates the name. One combined call let a missing In Review state drop bkit:failed on every Failure Path. Separate calls keep labels landing when the state is missing. `started` is a state type every team has whatever its names; In Review has no type of its own, so it stays a name and its absence is tolerated because bkit:merged / bkit:failed carry the hand-off. Workspace labels need no team UUID (save_issue_label takes teamId as a UUID only, while bkit.linearTeam is a key) and apply to every team. Not verified live: workspace label creation and its permission requirements, and save_issue with a retired label.

summary: Template pre-commit only formats; template pre-push runs the deepest push gate package.json declares (`bkit:gate:static-unit-integration`, else `bkit:gate:static-unit`), skips the suite on revert branches, and blocks a [skip ci] HEAD on a branch with an open PR; bkit-repo pre-commit skips the dist check for test-only commits
description: `.bkit/templates/.husky/pre-push` runs `bkit:gate:static-unit-integration` when package.json declares it, else `bkit:gate:static-unit` (BKIT_PUSH_GATES in `.bkit/core/engine/install/manifest.ts`), plus the drift gate; E2E, @live and anything reaching a deployed service stay in CI. The integration tier may start local services (a database in Docker). `.bkit/templates/.husky/pre-commit` runs `bkit:gate:format` only, and the `gate-commit-repeats-push` advisory names any script it shares with the push gate. On a revert branch the test tiers are skipped while lint, typecheck, prose and slop:delta still run. A HEAD commit carrying a [skip ci]-class token is blocked when the branch has an open PR (dev/main exempt, gh absent → allow). bkit's own `.husky/pre-commit` runs `bkit:check:dist` only when a non-test `.bkit/core/engine/**/*.ts` is staged; its pre-push bats run self-skips when bats is absent. bkit's own `bkit:gate:static-unit` runs `test:coverage:unit` in place of `pnpm test`, and it declares `bkit:gate:static-unit-integration` (`test:integration`).
rationale: Integration runs on push, not on commit (owner, 2026-10-21): a commit stays seconds, and a push is where a slower check still costs nothing but local time, ahead of a CI round-trip. The gate is opt-in by declaring it, the same "declared = run it" rule `/bkit-build` uses, so a repo whose integration tier needs something only CI has keeps it CI-only by not declaring the gate. Each check runs once: a commit gate that repeats a push check, a unit gate that calls both `pnpm test` and a coverage run, or a unit config that also matches integration files runs the same work twice on every push (found in bkit, app-gether-life and visitfrasercoast-com, 2026-10-21). The hook mirrors CI's deterministic gates so a green push cannot red-CI on them. Gate content lives in package.json so a human push and an agent run enforce the identical set. A revert leaves the tree intentionally inconsistent (deleted files referenced by surviving tests), so the suite is skipped so recovery lands; prose is unaffected by deleted code and slop:delta reports removals as resolved, never added. The workflow CI-Dispatch gate only covers the push it makes at close; the HEAD guard backstops manual pushes, and is conditioned on an open PR so sanctioned [skip ci] pushes with no PR still pass. `bkit:check:dist` rebuilds from the working tree, so a test-only commit made while a source edit is uncommitted would fail on a diff it did not cause. bats is not a devDependency, and without the self-skip a contributor without bats could not push.

summary: Jira is the third tracker: `.mcp.json` server key `jira` (tools `mcp__jira__*`), issue IDs are project keys `KEY-N`, and the FID is the lowercased key plus slug, matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9]+-[0-9]+-[a-z0-9-]+$`.
description: Jira project keys may carry digits after the first letter (`AB1-12`), so the Jira FID regex allows `[a-z0-9]` after the leading letter where Linear's allows letters only; the any-tracker regex widens the same way. The server key is the tracker name so `mcpServers.<tracker>` ownership, permission rows and block rendering stay uniform across github, linear and jira.

summary: The in-progress and review states a workflow moves an issue to come from package.json `bkit.linear.progress` / `review` (defaults `started` / `In Review`) and `bkit.jira.progress` / `review` (defaults `In Progress` / `In Review`); `bkit issues labels` returns the target as `trackerState`, null under github and none. A missing review state logs Unapplied and the labels still land.
description: Jira workflows differ per project and Linear teams rename states, so hard-coded names would fail on most real boards. Resolving the state in the engine keeps workflow prose identical across trackers. A missing state is skipped rather than failing the run because tracker writes are best-effort.

summary: Linear settings live in one package.json object `bkit.linear = { team, project, progress, review }`; the old `bkit.linearTeam` key is migrated into `bkit.linear.team`.
description: One object per tracker (`bkit.linear`, `bkit.jira`) keeps every tracker's settings in one place and lets `bkit repo info` read them the same way. bkit is public, so the rename ships with a registered migration instead of breaking existing consumers.

summary: `bkit repo info` emits `trackerTeam`, `trackerProject` and `trackerSite` (Linear team / project, Jira project / site, else null); workflows and prompts read those instead of tracker-specific config keys, and a null scope runs the related-issue search unscoped.
description: Tracker-neutral names let one workflow sentence serve every tracker block; only the tool call inside each block differs.

summary: Jira status changes list the issue's transitions (`executeRead` `listJiraIssueTransitions`) and fire the one whose `to.name` equals the target state; no matching transition logs Unapplied. Workflows never move a Jira issue into status category `done`.
description: Transition IDs and names are per-workflow and per-project, while the target status name is what users configure, so matching on `to.name` is the only portable lookup.

summary: Jira drives local workflow runs only: there is no Jira-side cloud trigger, no Jira preflight hook, `--auto` cloud setup keeps requiring the github or linear tracker, `bkit-cloud.yml` no-ops unless `bkit.issueTracker` is `github` or unset, and Jira repos get no `cloud-router-none` nudge. Jira Server / Data Center is out of scope; only Jira Cloud through the Atlassian Rovo MCP server.
description: Scoped in #60. Cloud dispatch needs a tracker-side trigger (GitHub labels, Linear's Cursor integration); Atlassian offers no equivalent bkit can wire, and the Rovo MCP server only serves Jira Cloud.

summary: A release runs the full suite only before and in CI on each dev push, and in CI on the main push; every other step reuses those results.
description: The owner set the policy: the suite runs in the pre-push hook before a push to dev, in CI on that dev push, and in CI on the push to main after the release PR merges, and those runs must stay full even when the files match a tested tree. Everything else reuses them. The release agents read the bkit-ci push run on dev at HEAD instead of re-running the suite locally, and stop when it is missing or red. bkit's own pre-push hook skips a branch push other than dev/main whose tree equals origin/dev or origin/main (the release/X push), alongside the existing tag-only skip. CI never skips a lane on a cache: push runs always run the suite, and a release PR into main mirrors the dev push run.

summary: bkit-ci.yml (bkit's own and the template) has no step that skips a test lane on an earlier green run; Check Tree Cache and the capstone's cache_skip exemption are removed.
description: Check Tree Cache skipped a pull request lane when the PR merge preview's tree matched a green push run on dev or main. With push CI on dev and main only, a feature PR's merge preview is a tree no push run has had, and a release PR into main runs in mirror mode with every lane off before any cache step matters (release PR #649, run 39612373800). The step could fire only on edge cases: a PR whose changes are already on dev, an empty main-into-dev PR, or a promotion PR from a branch mirror mode does not recognise. Removing it drops one GitHub API lookup per lane per PR, the copy-and-own script and test, the lanes' job-level actions: read, and the capstone's <LANE>_CACHE_SKIP exemption, which now cannot excuse a lane that ran 0 tests.
rationale: Code that never fires still costs consumers adoption work and every PR an API call, and the cache_skip exemption is a path by which a lane reporting 0 tests passes the capstone.
alternatives: Push CI on feature branches so a PR could match the branch's own push run (doubles runs per push); keep the step dormant (dead code in a copy-and-own template).

summary: /bkit-ship never opens or merges a PR into main; bkit prs open refuses --base=main and bkit prs merge refuses any PR whose base is not dev
description: worktrees setup refuses ship on dev or main with text saying releases stay manual, keeping the refusing to ship prefix. prs merge reads the live PR base at merge time, so a PR retargeted to main after ship Step 2 is never merged; the ship Step 10 MCP fallback asserts the base first. Releasing dev into main stays manual and utility-new-release stays separate and bkit-internal.
rationale: Nothing re-checked a PR base after ship Step 2, so a PR retargeted to main mid-run would have been merged into main; prose asserts are not enforcement.
alternatives: Prose-only refusal in bkit-ship.md: rejected, not enforced
prs open refusing every non-dev base: rejected, the owner scoped the open guard to main (Q4)
Fold the release into /bkit-ship: rejected, releases stay manual

summary: `@bkit-plan-generate` moves from L=200 to XL=400 and writes each process group into the draft before researching the next
description: Seven app-gether-life `.bkit/friction.jsonl` rows on 5.3.0 and 5.4.0 record `@bkit-plan-generate` spending all 200 turns (241-324 tool calls, 30-48 min) and stopping with every or nearly every plan section still `PENDING`; each SendMessage resume finished the plan in ~39 more calls. The agent re-checks every citation in its design, audit and issue inputs against code before writing, which is the whole-surface sweep XL holds, alongside `@bkit-audit-generate`. Every stop had the same shape: all research first, nothing written. The prompt already said to replace `PENDING` as content arrives; it now updates the draft after each section group, before reading for the next group, and does not defer to a final pass. A cap or timeout stop then leaves the finished groups on disk.
rationale: The cap is a runaway guard; these runs were not looping, they were doing codebase-wide verification the L tier does not cover. Raising the cap alone keeps the failure shape: an overrun at 400 would still leave a blank skeleton, only later.
alternatives: raise the cap only (rejected: same empty-draft stop, ~1h in); keep 200 and only enforce write-per-group (rejected: the resumes show the work genuinely needs ~240-360 calls); cap the research budget per group (not chosen: no measured per-group numbers to set it from). Open risk kept as is: the slowest run reached 48 min at 200 turns, so a 400-turn run can meet the 3600s step timeout before the cap.

summary: Every subagent named as a `decision` / `deferral` / `failure` ledger writer carries Bash so `jq` can mint `ts`
description: `.bkit/jsonl.md` § Write Idiom requires `ts` minted by `jq` at append time and rejects literals, so a writer without a shell cannot write a valid row. `@bkit-plan-generate` (decisions, deferrals), `@bkit-design-generate` (deferrals) and `@bkit-debug-abort-handover` (failures, deferrals) were listed writers with no Bash; app-gether-life friction rows on 5.3.0 and 5.4.0 record the orchestrator appending plan-generate's 6 and 9 rows for it. Each now lists Bash; the existing ledger step's `.bkit/jsonl.md` format reference carries the `jq` idiom, so no extra prompt clause, matching the other Bash-carrying writers.
rationale: Ledger rows written by the orchestrator lose the subagent attribution and depend on the orchestrator noticing the hand-back.
alternatives: drop these agents from the writers list and have orchestrators append (rejected: the writer is the agent that knows the row content; the orchestrator relays it lossy); a `bkit` CLI append command usable without a shell (not available to a tool-less agent either).

summary: The GitHub board is `bkit.github.project`, the board URL, beside `bkit.github.progress` / `review` (defaults `In progress` / `In review`); `update_project_item` names the item by repo and issue number and sets Status by option name.
description: GitHub, Linear and Jira settings share one shape: a block per tracker with where issues live and the state name per moment. A URL is what a person can copy from the browser, and its `/orgs/` or `/users/` segment gives the MCP `owner_type`, so personal boards work where a hard-coded org owner returned 404. The hosted GitHub MCP accepts a Status option name and finds the item from item_owner / item_repo / issue_number, so the field id, option ids and the list-items step that found the numeric item id are no longer needed.

summary: Orchestrators run medium effort from the Claude Code default for the 5.5 models; bkit ships no `effortLevel` and documents per-session and per-repo overrides in prompts.md § Orchestrators.
description: Claude Code defaults claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5 to medium effort, which is the orchestrator recommendation, so a shipped key changes nothing on current models. Subagents carry their own effort: frontmatter, which outranks the session level, so the session setting reaches the orchestrator only.
rationale: writeTier2JsonContained makes the template win on key collisions: a shipped effortLevel would reset a consumer-set value on every upgrade, report it as bkit check drift, and stop /effort choices persisting in that repo, while buying nothing over the default.
alternatives: Ship effortLevel medium as a bkit-owned key in .bkit/shared/.claude/settings.json
Offer effortLevel as a bkit check tip, like autoCompactWindow
Pin orchestrator model and effort through Claude skill frontmatter rendered from § Orchestrators

summary: Ship Step 4 B1 refreshes the PR head from dev only when dev requires status checks; otherwise the PR merges at the head CI passed at
description: B1 runs `bkit prs update-branch --only-if-required`. With no textual conflict and no required status checks on dev (ruleset or classic protection, read by the shared `devRequiresChecks` in prs.ts), the head stays at ENTRY_HEAD, so Step 9 finds nothing to re-validate and the Step 10 gate passes on the existing green. B2 (conflict-resolve push) and a dev that requires status checks still refresh and re-run CI. gh unable to read the requirement exits 80, which maps to update_pull_request_branch (the refresh). Build, debug and ship pass `git diff origin/dev...HEAD` (three dots) to subagents, so a branch behind dev shows only its own changes.
rationale: The refresh changed only the dev side of the PR: the feature's own change stayed byte-identical (a consumer's feature branch: patch-id identical before and after), yet the new head forced a full CI run before the merge, and the dev push run tests the merged result again. GitHub refuses an out-of-date PR only on a textual conflict (which the refresh does not fix) or a required up-to-date rule. The refresh dated from 4c785ccd (fix(216)), on the premise that a moved base fails the squash. Trade-off: A semantic clash between the branch and newer dev commits (no textual conflict) surfaces as a red dev push run after the merge, not a red PR before it. Accepted by the maintainer on #661. GitHub may not apply merge=union to ledger files server-side; a refused merge goes through Steps 11-12.
alternatives: Keep the refresh and accept ENTRY_HEAD's green when the feature's patch-id is unchanged (the refresh still fires a pull_request run GitHub starts on its own)
Keep refreshing on every Path B ship

summary: /bkit-debug on dev works in place in the main checkout, commits only its own paths, pushes only the commits it made and waits for dev CI on the pushed commit
description: worktrees setup records local dev HEAD and the modified and untracked paths with content hashes (line counts for append-only jsonl ledgers) under the git dir when debug runs in place on a shared branch, and returns startSha as the debug diff base. steps finish, bookkeeping and workflows close commits stage only paths outside that set (recorded ledgers: only the rows the run appended), refuse when another recorded path changed, and append each commit SHA to the record. branches push in every mode on a shared branch with a record pushes exactly those SHAs: plainly when origin/dev..HEAD equals them, else replayed onto origin/dev through pushToDev in a throwaway checkout with hooks off; the CI-Dispatch re-trigger goes the same way. Debug Steps 9 and 10 push nothing on dev. Step 11 dispatches, waits for and gates the dev CI run on the landed SHA, then releases the workflow lock, which removes the record; the dev hand-back also removes it. Step 1 never probes for a PR on dev, so PUSH_MODE is LOCAL. Debug still creates no branch. Narrows failure-path-record-own-branch-dev-fallback: debug fix commits may now reach dev through pushToDev; the Failure Path from dev still lands bookkeeping only. Widens ship-dev-writes-through-throwaway-origin-dev-checkout: pushToDev also replays debug code commits.
rationale: git add -A swept unrelated files into debug commits (workflows close included), git push origin dev pushed unrelated local commits from Steps 9, 10 and 11 and the CI re-trigger, startSha..HEAD would still sweep in commits others make mid-run, Gate 11 claimed a CI check that never happened on dev, and the Step 1 PR lookup could pick up and retitle an open dev-to-main release PR.
alternatives: Worktree on feat/{FID} plus branches land: rejected by the owner (#650 Q1)
git stash around the run: rejected, the stash stack is shared across worktrees and sessions
Own commits = startSha..HEAD: rejected, sweeps in foreign mid-run commits
Remove the record at workflows close: rejected, the push, re-trigger and Failure Path hand-back run after it
Temporary index for every commit: kept for the empty-own-set and ledger-row cases only, pathspec commits already isolate the index

summary: A wired-tracker run with no issue in the prompt warns and continues issue-less instead of stopping; a feat/ branch suffix is the FID verbatim and links an issue only when issues.jsonl has a feature row for it; workflows still never create tracker issues
description: Step 1 of /bkit-design, /bkit-plan, /bkit-build, /bkit-debug and /bkit-ship takes an issue id named in the prompt. With none, and a FID named or a feat/{FID} branch, bkit fids parse --branch takes the suffix verbatim as the FID for any lowercase slug (no all-digit check) and returns the embedded issue id only when .bkit/issues.jsonl holds a feature row keyed by that FID shape (Linear and Jira lowercased); otherwise issueId is null. A suffix that is not a lowercase slug exits 3 and Step 1 stops with a rename-or-name-an-issue message (never the Failure Path). With no issue the run sets ISSUE_ID empty, prints the no-issue warning (also the first line of every final message) and skips every issue-tied tracker read, label, comment and board call. A FID minted from the prompt is {branch-suffix}-{slug} with every all-digit word dropped. fids check and steps gate take --issue: an empty value accepts any slug, a non-empty value requires the FID to embed that same issue id. PR markers for a run with no issue carry only bkit:fid. bkit runs context (the /bkit-auto dispatch) keeps its strict branch parsing and stays issue-only.
rationale: After #490 made design and plan optional the issue was the last required input, and requiring it blocked /bkit-debug on red dev CI. This reverses the stop half of #486; the never-create half stays. A hand-named branch such as feat/upgrade-react-19 must run issue-less without renaming, so the branch suffix is trusted as the FID and an issue id inside it counts only when the repo already has a feature row for that issue; the all-digit rule stays on minted names, where a prompt word could otherwise read as an issue id.
alternatives: Keep the STOP: rejected, blocks dev CI repair
Auto-create an issue: rejected, #486 never-create rule
Reject any branch FID with an all-digit word: rejected, blocks hand-named branches such as upgrade-react-19
Trust an issue id embedded in any branch suffix: rejected, a numeric word in a hand-named branch would link an unrelated tracker issue

summary: A minted issue-less FID whose earlier run finished takes the first free -b, -c, ... suffix; only naming the FID in the prompt continues an earlier run
description: After minting {branch-suffix}-{slug} for a run with no issue, Step 1 runs bkit fids free --fid --workflow. It returns the minted name when no log folder in any month bucket uses it, or when that folder's last run of the workflow is IN_PROGRESS (continue); otherwise the first of {fid}-b ... {fid}-z with no finished run (exit 5 when all are used, exit 1 when the name has an all-digit word, which re-mints once). A FID taken from the prompt or the branch is never suffixed. fids check accepts the suffixed name as an ordinary slug.
rationale: Two unrelated incidents that mint the same name would otherwise share one log folder and attempt counter, so the second run started in SOAK mode against the first run's state. Continuity stays explicit: the human names the FID to continue.
alternatives: Always append a timestamp: rejected, unreadable FIDs and no continuity by name
Reuse the FID and reset the counter: rejected, mixes two runs in one log folder
Refuse a name already used: rejected, blocks a legitimate second incident

summary: The engine counts plan size and reads every Test first line: caps are 12 tasks per plan, 10 Test first tests and 3 test files per task; bkit tests plan-check writes the plan complexity verdict and the bkit-plan-complexity-check agent is removed; a Test first line no task bullet claims is never read as nothing to audit
description: One task-line reader in tests.ts serves tests green and the new tests plan-check. A task bullet is - [ ] **Task N followed by :, ., a dash, * or a space, so **Task N:** and **Task N — title.** both read. tests plan-check counts tasks, tests and distinct test files per task against MAX_TASKS_PER_PLAN / MAX_TESTS_PER_TASK / MAX_TEST_FILES_PER_TASK, writes a Verdict: SINGLE | SPLIT report, and exits 1 when a **Test first:** line sits outside every task bullet (or, with --children, when a sub-plan still breaks a cap). /bkit-plan Step 4 runs it on the draft, and Step 6 bkit-plan-update applies the quoted Unread lines with the review critiques. Complexity check and split are one step, Step 9: the engine count records SINGLE | SPLIT with no agent, an unread line still there means Step 6 or 8 wrote it and goes to the Failure Path, and on SPLIT it checks the split children and re-asks the split once. /bkit-plan has 11 steps. /bkit-build Step 3 runs it on the plan before any code and stops on an unread line. tests green audits every task it reads and reports each unread line as a plan-level test-first-unread gap, Fixable: false.
rationale: On the #650 build tasks of 8, 9 and 12 tests went test-first and the 20-test, 6-file task did not, so 10 tests and 3 files replaced the cap of 5. The complexity-check agent based its verdict only on two counts, so an agent added nothing and could contradict them. Gether plans writing **Task N — title.** were silently reported as having no Test first lines (Enforced: false, no gaps); widening the reader fixes those, and refusing to read an unclaimed Test first line as nothing to audit stops the next format drift passing silently.
alternatives: Keep the agent and override its verdict with the engine exit code: rejected, the agent had no judgement left to make
Hard-stop tests green on an unread line: rejected by the owner, the audit keeps going and records a gap so one bad line hides nothing else
Check over-cap tasks again in tests green at build time: rejected, the turn budget is already spent by then and plan time covers it
A cap of 5 tests per task: rejected, #650 tasks of 8-12 tests went test-first

Keep complexity check as its own step with a bkit-plan-update repair call: rejected, the repair belongs in Step 6 where bkit-plan-update already runs, and a step holding only a count is a condition on the split

summary: Prompts, workflows, rules.md and docs use normal English grammar: articles kept, singular or plural as the meaning needs; density comes from cutting filler, reasons and repetition. The Plural for general rules authoring rule is retired; § Notation carries a Grammar paragraph.
description: § Notation Grammar paragraph in .bkit/core/.bkit/prompts.md binds the same files Notation binds. Rules for counts: each {item} or one {thing} per {item} when the number matters; subject and pronoun agree. bkit-utility-compress-markdown keeps grammar words and its Good examples keep articles. Existing clipped text is not swept; it changes on its next edit, and shared rule and clause text is reworded in the #666 instructions.md pass and propagated by wording:sync.
rationale: Clipped plural text drifted back toward normal English after the plural rule landed on 2026-10-15: articles per 1,000 words in rules.md went from 8.8 to 17.6, in prompts 7.1 to 8.8, in workflows 20.9 to 24.2. The plural rule bound prompts only, and bkit-utility-compress-markdown both stripped articles and marked dropping them as Bad. No test checks style in local lines, so a style that fights the model default needs permanent policing. The token cost of normal grammar is about 0.05% of a run (rules.md is about 1.3% of a run's tokens; articles add about 5% of its words).
alternatives: Keep plural and widen it to all agent-read files with a ratchet test on net-new articles: rejected, it fights the model default on every edit and the saving is about 0.05% of a run
Switch to a singular rule: rejected, any fixed number rule drifts the same way; the meaning decides the number
Sweep every file to plain grammar now: rejected, #666 rewrites clause and rule text anyway, so a sweep first would change everything twice

summary: Every decision is written to docs/decisions.jsonl with bkit ledgers append by the step that makes it, at the moment it is made; a later change is a new row with the same key. @bkit-plan-update writes rows for decisions its merge adds or changes; the plan orchestrator writes a row for each open question the owner answers after close. Design writes no decision rows: plan-generate writes one per design ## Decisions item. Every prompt, workflow and rules.md line that writes ledger rows names bkit ledgers append.
rationale: Owner, 2026-10-23. The plan step in gether-life#1338 could not write its rows and nothing else did, so the build failed at its last task on rows no build agent may write. Writing at decision time removes that gap without a build-start check or rows carried in the plan.

summary: A plan lists every decision / deferral key written for it on one **Ledger rows:** line in Architecture & Component Changes (or None). Plan Step 10 runs bkit ledgers check on the final plan and takes the Failure Path when a listed key has no row. No runbook task writes or checks a ledger row, and the template no longer sends the build to docs/decisions.jsonl or docs/knowledge.jsonl.
rationale: Keys carry an issue prefix only optionally (jsonl.md § Key & References), so the check needs the plan to name its keys; one line is the smallest fixed place.

summary: Each repo's .bkit/*.jsonl holds only its own workflow rows, reported by the shipped `bkit stats` into a committed .bkit/stats.md; cross-repo data lives only in bkit's gitignored harvest/, built by the unshipped `pnpm harvest`
description: `bkit stats` (`.bkit/core/engine/commands/stats.ts`, shipped) reports only this repo's .bkit/stats.jsonl + .bkit/friction.jsonl + docs/deferrals.jsonl into a committed .bkit/stats.md. `pnpm harvest` (`scripts/harvest/bkit-harvest.mjs` + `scripts/harvest/ledgers.ts`, unshipped) copies every repo's stats + friction ledgers into gitignored harvest/, prunes every friction row and every chat/run row from the repos by one content gate (copy -> fsync -> read back -> prune), scans chats + run logs into harvest/stats.jsonl, checks outcome rows against run rows on run.parentSha, and writes harvest/stats.md. `bkit harvest`, `bkit analysis` and the chat-stats template are removed. bkit keeps no managed backup of harvest/.
rationale: Chat/run-log scanning reads one maintainer's machine across every repo, so its rows never belonged in one repo's ledger and it has no consumer use; a repo's own report needs only that repo's rows; comparing a repo's outcome rows with the scan's run rows checks the two writers agree. No managed backup of harvest/ by the maintainer's explicit choice. Design approved by the human in the issue #683 approach comment.

summary: #343 — the harvest MOVES consumer .bkit/friction.jsonl (prunes drained rows) instead of copying it; the prune is gated on byte-for-byte row content, NEVER on identity
description: Reverses #234's locked COPY-ONLY harvest decision for friction only; stats.jsonl is copied whole and its chat/run rows are pruned by the same content gate. Prune fires only after copy -> fsync -> read-back off disk. The central store moved .bkit/harvest/ -> harvest/ (repo root) and now ACCUMULATES across runs instead of being unlinked and rebuilt. Retired .claude/agents/utility-harvest-friction.md, which #234 said the CLI replaced but which was still live and still truncated the legacy .bkit/friction.md.
rationale: Friction is a work queue that must drain, so consumers start each cycle clean — the motivation for the reversal. #234's copy-only rule bought structural non-destructiveness ('copying, not moving, makes a harvest bug structurally non-destructive'); that property is preserved by ordering + the content gate rather than by never writing. The content gate is load-bearing, not caution: fold() collapses rows sharing an identity and keeps only the last, so an identity gate deletes every colliding row from the consumer while the store keeps one. Reproduced destroying a real consumer-a friction entry before the fix. Accumulation is a hard prerequisite: the old unlink-and-rebuild plus pruning would have made run 2 delete the store and re-copy from the emptied consumer, shredding every harvested row.
alternatives: Keep COPY-ONLY (rejected: friction never drains, consumers re-triage harvested rows). Gate prune behind --prune (rejected by owner: always-on chosen). Gate prune on identity (rejected: destroys fold-losers — proven data loss). Auto-commit harvest/ from the CLI (rejected: bkit commits data files at workflow close, not inside a utility verb; caller commits).

summary: Harvest prunes consumer friction only by byte-for-byte content after fsync + read-back, never clears or fold-rewrites the central store, keeps unparseable lines, and counts entities by fold
description: `scripts/harvest/ledgers.ts`: friction.jsonl is moved (copy → fsync → read back → prune by exact content), stats.jsonl is copied whole and its chat/run rows are pruned by the same content gate; the store at repo-root `harvest/` accumulates every distinct row; malformed consumer lines are kept; deferral/failure counts fold same-key rows; the path-derived repo slug is a loud last resort.
rationale: An identity-gated prune was a real data-loss bug (#343): `fold()` collapses rows sharing an identity, and friction keys truncated to ~68 chars gave two distinct entries one identity, so the prune deleted colliding rows the store never kept. A store that kept only fold winners would drop rows an earlier run already pruned (winners change between runs), and clearing it would delete the originals' only copy on the next run. Pruning against in-memory rows would trust an unconfirmed write. Pruning a half-written tail would delete a row never stored; re-reading at prune time keeps rows appended mid-harvest; temp-file + rename avoids a torn ledger. Friction is a work queue that must drain; stats are the consumer's own history. Harvested data is neither managed nor shipped, so it lives outside `.bkit/`. A raw line count reports one deferral as two and inflates with every triage pass. The old last-two-path-segments slug made the owner a directory on the harvesting machine and minted a new identity per clone location. Reasons moved out of code comments (owner rule 2026-10-10).
alternatives: Identity-gated prune — rejected: data loss.

summary: #663 — hiding old tool output inside a running agent (observation masking) was considered and is not possible: no host bkit runs on lets it clear earlier tool results
description: Observation masking (JetBrains, The Complexity Trap, NeurIPS 2025: one agent keeps running, old tool results become placeholders, the last few stay; about half the cost at an equal or better solve rate) is not a bkit lever. Old tool output leaves an agent's context only through the per-group fresh agent and the handover at about 160k (#668); #678 and #681 shrink tool output at its source.
rationale: Claude Code: a PostToolUse hook's updatedToolOutput replaces only the result that just arrived, never an earlier one; Claude Code clears older tool outputs itself only as the first step of compaction, which also summarises. The Messages API's clear_tool_uses_20250919 does exactly this, but bkit runs no model loop of its own; its agents run inside the host. Cursor, OpenCode and Codex not checked.
alternatives: PostToolUse hook trimming large Bash output to start, end and an outbox path (rejected: trims new output, not old; #650's waste was 167 grep calls of about 3kB each, which a size limit misses; risks cutting error lines). Per-subagent autoCompactWindow frontmatter as a backstop above the cap (not decided here: compaction also summarises; belongs to #668). Asking hosts for a clear-without-summary setting (not filed).

summary: The engine does tracker reads and writes; the tracker MCP is the fallback when a verb prints tracker.done false or exits 80
description: bkit verbs that produce a tracker comment post it themselves with --post (steps finish, workflows fail / handover / close / links, issues comment) and print tracker: {done, action, url, deduped} on success, {done:false, action, reason} on failure (reason = network | auth | scope | rate-limit | not-found | http-<n>), or {skipped} with no issue or tracker none. A failed post keeps the verb's own exit code; the agent then posts the printed comment through the tracker MCP. Pure tracker verbs exit 80 on failure. steps finish dedupes through engine-action rows in status.jsonl keyed workflow/run/step/subPlan/attempt/kind with a sha256 of the body; other --post verbs dedupe against the issue's last 5 comments. GitHub goes through gh with GH_TOKEN from BKIT_GH_TOKEN, Linear through its GraphQL API, Jira through the Rovo MCP server over HTTP.
rationale: Agents skipped comments the engine printed (friction design-summary-comment-not-posted): a printed comment the agent must remember to post is a write that silently does not happen. The engine posting it makes the write part of the step, and the dedupe makes a retried step safe. MCP stays as the fallback because the engine cannot reach a tracker in every runtime (no token, sandboxed network).
alternatives: Keep MCP primary and add a gate check that the comment was posted - REJECTED: the gate can only ask the agent, which is the party that forgot. Drop the MCP path entirely - REJECTED: runtimes without engine credentials would lose tracker writes.

summary: The engine reaches Jira through the Rovo MCP server over HTTP with BKIT_JIRA_API_KEY, not the Jira REST API
description: The engine's Jira client speaks MCP JSON-RPC to https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp with Authorization: Bearer ${BKIT_JIRA_API_KEY}: initialize, keep the Mcp-Session-Id, then tools/call; it reads SSE or JSON replies and sends a non-default User-Agent. cloudId is bkit.jira.site. Comments over 32,767 characters are split at line breaks, each part starting with ###### bkit:generated and _(part i/n)_. BKIT_JIRA_API_TOKEN is renamed BKIT_JIRA_API_KEY; install migrates .bkit/.env without hashing it.
rationale: The same token and server the agent's Jira MCP already uses work for the engine, so a consumer configures Jira once. The Atlassian API token for REST needs a separate email + token pair and different scopes. The key is a bearer API key, not a REST token, so the name follows what it is.
alternatives: Jira REST v3 with basic auth - REJECTED: a second credential and a second scope model to document and check. Keep the old variable name - REJECTED: it names the wrong credential type.

summary: The three tracker-carried bkit markers are h6 headings; detection is whole-line and heading-only
description: bkit:generated, bkit:ignore-earlier and bkit:blocked-by are `###### bkit:{name}` headings. Detection matches a WHOLE LINE in the heading form only: an HTML-comment marker already sitting in an issue is no longer honoured, and an inline prose mention of a token is never a marker. File-only markers (bkit:start/end, bkit:roadmap-*, bkit:tracker {name} start) are unchanged: they never cross a tracker API.
rationale: mcp__github__issue_read deletes every HTML comment from a body, so an HTML-comment marker could never survive a read — recorded in docs/knowledge.jsonl under github-mcp-issue-read-sanitises-bodies-killing-every-html-comment-marker, which also observed that a sanitised read begins at the comment's FIRST HEADING. A heading is therefore the one form with evidence of surviving. Whole-line detection is what lets the guard test narrow: an inline mention of a token in prose or a prompt is no longer a live marker, so describing the mechanism no longer arms it. The blocked-by encode is the case where sanitisation cost real data rather than a silent no-op, because design reads the body and writes it back. The dual-syntax legacy read and the raw `gh api` read mandate were both retired in f3e1d49e (#464); no live MCP round trip confirming the heading survives is cited for that retirement.
alternatives: Keep HTML comments and mandate raw gh api forever — REJECTED: makes the read path load-bearing on every future caller and blocks a bulk MCP tracker read. Backtick-escape the marker — REJECTED, already measured: the sanitiser runs on raw markdown and returns empty backticks. Infer bkit-ness from template heading shape — REJECTED: needs lockstep maintenance with every template heading and eats human comments sharing a heading. Read both syntaxes so legacy HTML-comment markers keep working — dropped in f3e1d49e; the heading form is the only one read.

summary: bkit verbs print key: value text by default and --json prints JSON; each verb's textOmit drops keys no workflow reads; context fetch writes a flat JSON array as a checked markdown table
description: renderText prints key: value lines, nested keys indented two spaces, arrays of flat objects as markdown tables; a string that would read as another type is quoted, and parseText reads the text back to exactly the --json object. textOmit keys appear under --json only: steps finish row (checks too when all pass, plus a top-level parentSha), steps done row, workflows start/fail row, workflows close row/counterRow/outcomeRow, clamp on tests run, context diff, run-block, ledger-scan and fetch; an audit test fails if a workflow or prompt code span names one. context fetch keeps the output as printed in {OUTBOX}/{name}.raw.{ext} and writes a table only when it parses back to the same values and types, else the output as printed with render: raw (<reason>) on stderr. TOON was measured and not adopted.
rationale: Measured with a local proxy, not the Anthropic token-counting API: bytes, and a punctuation-aware token count (each run of letters, each run of digits and each other non-space character counts as one); whitespace-split counts were also taken but say nothing for one-line JSON (35 JSON vs 288 text tokens over 10 verbs). Real outputs captured in a temp consumer (packed tarball, bkit install --claude --tracker=none) running 10 verbs in text and --json mode. All 10 verbs: 4631 -> 2927 bytes (-37%), proxy tokens 2020 -> 928 (-54%). Most of it is dropped keys: steps finish -80% bytes, steps done -96%, context fetch -75%, context run-block -73%, workflows start -24%; the format alone moves bytes -7% to +10% (list-blocks +10% and disk prune +3%, from indented multi-line values and table padding) but cuts proxy tokens on every verb (-19% to -57%) by dropping quotes, braces and commas. Context artifact from a real 20-row gh run list payload: fenced file 5091 -> 3319 bytes (-35%), proxy tokens 1898 -> 1007 (-47%); payload alone JSON 4575 bytes, markdown table 2803 (-39%), TOON 2490 (-46%) with the same proxy token count as the table (884 vs 885), so TOON buys bytes but no proxy tokens over a format every model already reads.

summary: The two plan reviewers split by what they read: review-1 reads the plan (tightness, task order, design coverage), review-2 reads the code (regression risk)
description: `bkit-plan-review-1` holds the plan-only checks: drift from source, design coverage, task dependency order, cycles and suggested scope expansion. `bkit-plan-review-2` holds the code-reading regression checks (compat boundaries, migration order, test coverage, mock-only coverage, unpassable checks). review-1 returns FAIL only for a task-order cycle no reordering fixes or a plan that contradicts its source design; every other gap is CRITICAL.
rationale: Reviewers that read the same input repeat each other's findings; splitting by input keeps two distinct lenses with one fewer agent.
alternatives: Keep three reviewers (tightness, dependency order, regression risk)

summary: One plan scope check, on Opus at medium effort, replaces the scope-check pair
description: `bkit-plan-scope-check` checks the plan template, Acceptance Scenario and Derived Test Matrix, and per-task scope, criteria and verification. It runs once, in parallel with the two reviewers.
rationale: On the same plans the Sonnet copy of the scope check raised 25 CRITICAL findings against Opus's 81, so the pair added cost without adding findings the Opus copy missed.
alternatives: Keep a cross-model pair of scope checks

summary: /bkit-plan runs one review round: the two reviewers and the scope check run in parallel on plan v1, then one update writes plan-v2-reviewed.md
description: Step 5 runs review-1, review-2 and the scope check in parallel; Step 6 applies all three reports in one pass.
rationale: A second round re-read a plan that the first round had already changed, for findings the scope check could raise on v1 just as well; one round removes a step and an update pass.
alternatives: Review, apply, then scope-check and apply again

summary: The build security reviewer (challenge-2) runs on every change; on a small change it runs alone
description: Build Step 10 sizes the change with `bkit challenge gate`; a small change skips `bkit-build-challenge-1` (bug-hunting) only.
rationale: A small diff can still open a security hole, and the security lens is the one that stays on the top model tier; the bug-hunting lens adds little on a diff that verify has just read whole.
alternatives: Skip the whole challenge on small changes
Run both reviewers on every change

summary: A build change is small when it changes under 300 lines AND under 10 files over origin/dev...HEAD, docs/plans/** excluded, measured again on every pass through Step 10
description: `bkit challenge gate` reads `diffNumstat` (the same range and excludes as the build diff artifact), appends a `challenge-gate` status row, and the outcome row carries `build.challenge.gate` for `bkit stats`.
rationale: Both limits must hold so a wide change of small edits still gets both reviewers; measuring on every pass keeps a round-2 challenge honest after fix tasks grew the diff.
alternatives: Lines only
Measure once per run

summary: Every bkit Claude Code subagent ships `autoCompactWindow: 300000` frontmatter; other hosts drop it; main-session compaction stays a consumer tip
description: All `.bkit/core/prompts/bkit-*.md` and the hand-authored `.claude/agents/utility-*.md` carry `autoCompactWindow: 300000` (plain integer; `300k` reads as 300 and is ignored). It only lowers the window: a lower repo / user setting and `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` still win; needs Claude Code v2.1.296+. `applyCodexAgent`, `applyOpencodeAgent`, `applyT3` (Cursor) and `applyAntigravityPrompt` drop it, each with a comment naming why. Per-host facts and sources: #690 and `.bkit/providers.md` § Context compaction.
rationale: A safety net against an agent running to the model's full window, not the cap: group size, the 160k handover and `maxTurns` stop an agent first. Per agent it cannot change the user's main session, so decision `549-compaction-threshold-is-a-tip-not-shipped` (repo-wide settings key stays a tip) stands. No other host has a working per-agent setting: Codex role files parse `model_auto_compact_token_limit` but discard it (openai/codex `core/src/agent/role.rs:37-48`); opencode has no agent field; Cursor has no setting; Antigravity agents run in the main session.
alternatives: Render `model_auto_compact_token_limit` into Codex role files (a no-op key that looks like a working setting)
Ship Codex's project-wide `.codex/config.toml` key (also changes the user's main Codex session)
opencode per-model alias with `limit.input` (untested end to end, one entry per model per provider)
Cursor `model: <id>[context=N]` (shrinks the whole window, valid values undocumented)

summary: Plan caps are package.json `bkit.tasks` (maxPerGroup 3, maxTestsPerGroup 15, maxTestsPerTask 10, maxTestFilesPerTask 3 by default); agents get the live values from `bkit repo info`
description: `CONFIG_DEFAULTS.tasks` holds the defaults; `readBkitConfig` reads each key and falls back per key on anything that is not an integer >= 1, and preflight advisory `bkit-tasks-invalid` names the bad keys. Install / upgrade seed the block like every other `bkit` setting (missing keys only). `tests plan-check` and `challenge merge` read the caps of the checkout they run in; the merge's four-group overflow is 4 x maxPerGroup. `bkit repo info` prints `tasks`; `/bkit-plan` and `/bkit-build` Step 1 hold the four values and pass them in Context to plan-generate, plan-update, convert and the challenge reviewers. Prompts and workflows name the held values, never a number; a workflow-shape test refuses a literal cap.
rationale: Owner, 2026-10-24: a consumer with a bigger or smaller agent context window needs different group sizes, and a constant forces a bkit release to change them. `repo info` already prints settings-derived facts at Step 1 of every workflow, so the caps reach agents without a new verb.
alternatives: Keep the constants in tests.ts (no consumer control)
A new `bkit settings` verb printing the caps (a second Step 1 call for one fact)
Read the caps from the plan-check report (no plan exists before plan-generate runs)

summary: A plan is one file of task blocks inside numbered groups; sub-plans and the Complexity Split step are gone
description: {FID}-plan.md holds every task as a marked block inside a group. bkit tests plan-check refuses a plan that breaks the format or the bkit.tasks caps. /bkit-build runs one fresh execute and verify agent per group from bkit context brief. No step writes {FID}-plan-N.md; old ones stay where they are and nothing reads them.
rationale: Sub-plans split by size after planning and handed each build agent a whole file; groups are drawn while planning, keep one file and one parser, and let each agent work from a small brief so no build subagent passes about 160k tokens.
alternatives: Keep sub-plans and add briefs per sub-plan
One execute agent per task

summary: No build subagent and no plan-generate agent should pass about 160k tokens of context; group size, the cap handover and maxTurns enforce it, workflows close measures it
description: The target is about 160k tokens per agent, not 120k. Groups are sized by the bkit.tasks caps; an execute agent that nears the cap hands over to a fresh one; autoCompactWindow 300000 is the safety net. workflows close records each agent type's context peak in run facts so bkit stats can check the cap.
rationale: A replay of 90 real agents showed 160k costs a few points more than 120k when a handover is cheap and stays about level with today when it is not (owner, 2026-10-24).
alternatives: 120k cap
No cap, compaction only

summary: The readguard hook does not point build agents at their group brief; #668 decision 13 is dropped
description: bkit-readguard.cjs is unchanged by #668. Build agents get the brief path in their prompt; nothing blocks or redirects a read of the full plan file.
rationale: Owner, 2026-10-24: keep it out of #668. A Claude-only hook nudge would also need equivalents on the other hosts.
alternatives: Readguard redirects full-plan reads to the brief (decision 13 as first written)

summary: Build challenge findings become plan tasks through bkit challenge merge and are fixed by the normal execute and verify loop; reconcile, remediate and challenge-tests agents are gone
description: The two reviewers write findings as task blocks. bkit challenge merge dedupes on location and severity, drops accepted findings, appends tasks in a new last group, writes LOW findings as deferral rows, and runs plan-check. Any finding with Fixable: false goes to the Decision Pause whatever its severity. The challenge runs at most two rounds.
rationale: Every fix gets the same test-first audit, verify and caps as planned work, with one code path; losing challenge-tests' extra edge-case sweep is accepted.
alternatives: Keep reconcile and remediate agents

summary: bkit workflows summary writes every workflow's summary from status rows and artifacts; the five summary agents are gone
