description: FAIL when a plan task is not done (build only), tests fail, a CRITICAL finding is unresolved or a FAIL is unanswered; a FAIL answered by a later fix step and a debug run that could not reproduce give CONCERNS; else PASS. bkit status resume prints where any workflow resumes.
rationale: Across 27 recorded summary steps every verdict was derivable from the step rows.
alternatives: Keep model-written summaries

summary: Rows from past runs naming removed steps or agents stay as written; new runs never write them, and readers keep parsing them
description: status.jsonl, .bkit/stats.jsonl and ledger rows that name sub-plans, complexity, briefs or removed agents are not rewritten. Readers (status, step-table, summary, telemetry) keep an old-row read path.
rationale: Ledgers are history; rewriting them loses what ran.
alternatives: Migrate old rows

summary: BAR-155 — two build-challenge reviewers split by role; bkit challenge merge combines their findings, no reconciler agent
description: /bkit-build Step 10 launches @bkit-build-challenge-1 (bugs, edge cases, error paths) and @bkit-build-challenge-2 (security: auth holes, exploits, data exposure) in parallel; on a small change only challenge-2 runs. Their findings are task blocks; bkit challenge merge dedupes them on location and severity and appends them to the plan. No reconciler agent runs.
rationale: Two reviewers with different briefs miss different things; merging task blocks is mechanical and needs no model.
alternatives: Keep @bkit-build-challenge-reconcile to merge the two reports

summary: bkit tests plan-check reads only marked task blocks in the one {FID}-plan.md; checklist lines outside a block are not tasks, and there are no sub-plans to check
description: plan-check parses the plan with parsePlanBlocks: a task is a <!-- bkit:task N start --> block inside a group, and a template checklist item such as the Gate 2 TEST FIRST line is never read as a task. A plan with no task markers is refused, naming the block format. plan-check checks the one plan file; no {stem}-N.md sub-plans exist.
rationale: Marked blocks make task text unambiguous, so the gate-line skip and the Unread hint for unlabelled bullets are no longer needed.
alternatives: Keep reading task bullets by label

summary: `.bkit/instructions.md` is the checked store with one master per section; bkit rules are copied word for word into the prompts that act on them, and the leaf `**Rules:**` line reads only below `bkit:end`
description: Masters: `.agents/rules.md` (template `.bkit/core/.agents/rules.md`) for rule text; the store for clause text and carrier lists; engine code and shipped settings for hook text and permissions; `prompts.md` / `workflows.md` for Special Behaviors and Authoring Rules. Each rule's `- carry:` line names the prompts whose agent acts on it (its prompt carriers plus the tool set); each named prompt holds the whole bullet in a `**bkit Rules:**` block after `**Contract:**`, in `rules.md` order, and no prompt holds a bkit rule its carry line does not name. The `rules-leaf` line reads `.agents/rules.md` below `<!-- bkit:end -->` (its `Universal Rules`, skipping `Orchestrator Rules`); workflows, entry files and the `utility-*` agents read all of `rules.md`. `pnpm instructions:sync` refreshes store copies from their masters and rewrites rule copies still in a retired wording.
rationale: The leaf line switches in the same change that copies the rules in, so no subagent is left without its rules, and a subagent no longer reads the ~6.6k-token bkit block of `rules.md`. A copy must be the whole bullet so an exception such as the Destructive git rebase carve-out cannot be dropped. The leaf reads everything below `bkit:end`, not only `## Project Rules`, because `## Project Settings` below it holds the MCP identifiers subagents need. The `utility-*` agents push and merge, so they read all of `rules.md`.
alternatives: Leaf reads only `## Project Rules` — rejected: subagents would lose `## Project Settings`.

summary: The plan and audit templates hold shape only; every rule for filling, reviewing or acting on them is a Contract bullet in the prompts that act on them
description: A template is copied into every plan and report it seeds, so each instruction line in it is paid for again in every copy and every later read. `docs/templates/bkit-plan.md` keeps headings, tables, placeholders, checkbox labels, owner callouts and the lines engine code parses (`**Ledger rows:**`, `- [ ] **Task N:**`, the Gate 2 `- [ ] **Test first:**` item). Its rules are labelled Contract bullets, worded the same in each plan and build prompt that acts on them; `.bkit/instructions.md` § Template Instructions names the carriers. Audit templates keep their probe steps and template-specific rules; the rules all 35 shared (read-only, instruction scope, example tools, evidence, Pre-Flight, credentials, permissions, anchor standards, previous run, gates, severity, report boxes) are Contract bullets in `bkit-audit-generate`. `bkit-build-plan-execute` alone ticks applicable Pre-Flight and gate boxes and never stops to ask; `bkit-build-plan-verify` ticks task boxes. Guarded by `.bkit/core/engine/audits/templates/template-shape.test.ts`.

summary: /bkit-build always works from {FID}-plan.md; with none, or one with no task blocks, bkit-build-plan-convert writes it first. Only convert reads build-input-{RUN}.md; every other build agent reads the plan or its group's brief
description: Step 2 writes build-input-{RUN}.md for every build: the session prompt, the issue text and the plan as it arrived. Only bkit-build-plan-convert reads it; the file stays as the record of what the run was given. Execute and verify read the group brief; install-skills, the challenge agents and diagnose read the plan. Run instructions in the session prompt beyond naming the issue (a redo, a resume, a constraint) are written once to {SESSION_DIR}/brief-note.md and reach every group's brief as its Deviations section through bkit context brief --note-file. Step 3 runs convert only when the plan check finds no plan or no task blocks. Convert works from the whole input file; where the plan and the issue disagree, the plan wins.
rationale: #663's lever is that no build subagent reads the whole plan: execute and verify get a 3-6KB group brief instead of a 100KB plan. The input file copies the plan in whole, plus the issue and its comments (54KB on #650 against a 30KB plan), so handing it to execute and verify put the full plan back in front of them beside the brief, with an older copy of the plan than the one convert rewrote. Their prompts never used it. The plan is the owner-approved artefact and already wins over the issue, so the issue text added tokens and no authority. The owner's run-specific words still reach the agents, through the brief's Deviations note, which is the channel #668 designed for them.
alternatives: Every build agent reads build-input-{RUN}.md beside the plan (the shape before this correction)
Pass the session prompt verbatim as the brief note on every run

summary: Sentences shared by 2+ prompts, 2+ workflows or 5+ audit templates, and header sentences workflows share with prompts, live once as clauses in `.bkit/instructions.md` § Clauses; `.bkit/core/engine/tools/instructions.ts` checks every copy and `pnpm instructions:sync` rewrites them in place
description: `.bkit/instructions.md` § Clauses holds one clause per shared sentence: canonical `text`, earlier wordings in `retired`, and a mode per surface (`required` / `where-used` / `repeatable` / `forbidden` / `if-verdict` / `if-bash` / `if-search` / `if-no-search`) for prompts, workflows, the `.agents/rules.md` managed block and the audit templates' managed block. The check (`.bkit/core/engine/tools/instructions.ts`, run by `.bkit/core/engine/tools/instructions.test.ts`) fails on a missing, duplicated or forbidden clause, a near-copy (80%+ similar, not equal), a retired wording, and any sentence the store does not list that is shared by `SHARED_MIN` files of one surface: 2 prompts, 2 workflows or 5 audit templates, each surface counted alone. It also fails on a clause no surface it applies to uses in that many files. `pnpm instructions:sync` (`.bkit/core/engine/tools/instructions.ts --write`) rewrites near-copies and retired wordings in place, so prompts carry no markers. Change a shared sentence only in `.bkit/instructions.md`: edit `text`, move the old wording to `retired`, run `pnpm instructions:sync`. A sentence in one prompt or one workflow stays local; a `### Shared lines` entry only records copies of a line that is not a sentence (for example a one-word step label) and says why it is kept.
rationale: Once a sentence appears in more than one prompt or workflow it should be owned and checked in one place (owner decision on #684, https://github.com/cbartens/bkit/issues/684#issuecomment-6390577228). A `### Shared lines` entry only records where copies sit; a clause is the master: sync rewrites every copy, near copies are flagged, retired wordings are rewritten, and a carrier missing it fails. The earlier cut-off of 5 prompts and 3 workflows recorded no reason for those numbers. Audit templates keep 5: #684 changed the prompt and workflow cut-offs only. Changing a shared sentence is one edit plus one command instead of a hand edit per copy (81878ecf); the check found real drift on its first run (81878ecf).
alternatives: Keep 5 prompts and 3 workflows, with lower-count copies recorded as `### Shared lines` entries — rejected on #684: those entries record copies but nothing keeps them in step. Markers in each prompt around the shared text — not used: sync finds copies by similarity and retired wordings so no markers are added (81878ecf); why markers were unwanted is not written down. Render-time assembly of prompt headers at `bkit install` — listed as deferred in `de-36-342-universal-untrusted-input-bullet-plus-glob-scoped-g`; #467 records no reason for choosing in-place sync over it.

summary: Every workflow input file dates its sections (description oldest, comments by posting time, plan / design / audit files by last-commit author date, session prompt newer than all, design Grill decisions newest); agents reading it apply newer-wins, and only `###### bkit:ignore-earlier` drops text.
description: `bkit workflows input` writes each human comment as its own dated section and dates each file section; every prompt whose agent reads a `*-input-*.md` file carries the `input-dates` clause from `.bkit/instructions.md`. A re-run's previous design or plan stays superseded context only, never a constraint. `/bkit-build` Step 3 runs `@bkit-build-plan-convert` when `newerThanPlan` > 0, so the plan absorbs later comments before any code and every later agent works from the plan.
rationale: Re-runs mixed comments the design or plan already settled with comments written to change it, and nothing told agents which to believe (owner decision on #691, 2026-10-25). Older text loses but is never dropped, so when nothing conflicts nothing is lost; that makes the rough edges acceptable: squash merges resetting author dates, undated comments counted as oldest, edited comments keeping their creation time. Author date, not committer date, because `bkit branches sync` rebases. The build folds newer comments into the plan first because the engine checks the plan's task blocks, test order and deliverables, and execute does not revise the plan.
alternatives: The plan always wins over the issue (the convert rule before) — rejected: wrong when the owner comments after the plan to change it. Dropping comments older than the design or plan — rejected: re-runs draft afresh, so anything only those comments said would be lost. A per-workflow anchor deciding which file comments are compared against — rejected for passing everything dated and letting the agent apply newer-wins.

summary: Every prompt, workflow and utility agent opens with three blocks, Protocol, Contract and Rules, each with a fixed lead-in; the CAUTION box and the header Code reads line are gone.
description: Protocol holds how to work through the file (`**Rules file:**` first, Order, No improv, Gates; in workflows also Narrate, Failures, Placeholders, Commands, Resume, Timeouts, CI wait turn-loop). Contract holds the deal between the agent and whoever runs it: inputs, outputs, mandate, what it writes or reports, No commits; a workflow's tracker groups sit in it. Rules holds `.agents/rules.md` bullets word for word, in rules.md order, Verify tools and External input included. Decision order: a rules.md copy goes to Rules, else a line about the deal to Contract, else Protocol. Clauses carry `- block:` and the check fails a clause outside its block, a missing or misordered block, a CAUTION box, and a rule copied into Protocol or Contract. Workflow lines moved unchanged.
rationale: The old split mixed three kinds of line under one CAUTION box, so where a line belonged was decided by habit, not meaning (owner decision on #692, 2026-10-25). Naming each block by what it holds makes placement checkable. The header Code reads line was a shortened copy of the R21 rule every carrying prompt already holds in full, so it is dropped rather than moved. `bkit` is dropped from `bkit Rules` because everything in these files is bkit's. `**Rules:**` is now the block label, so the rules-file pointer is relabelled `**Rules file:**`; the entry files keep `**Rules:**` because they have no blocks.
alternatives: Splitting Contract by how many prompts share a line (shared vs agent-specific) — rejected: `Read / Update / Create` is in most prompts yet is plainly part of the deal. Renaming only, keeping the CAUTION box in workflows — rejected: workflows are orchestrator prompts and take the same shape. Keeping the short header Code reads beside the full rule — rejected: two wordings of one rule in one prompt.

summary: Every point where a run can ask the owner has `ask` and a hard limit under `bkit.workflows.<workflow>.<point>`; headless or `ask: false` takes the recommendation and records any Accept as assumed, which ship asks the owner to confirm.
description: Points: design.grill (maxTurns 6), build.verify / challenge / tests, debug.fix / soak, ship.merge (maxAttempts 2), all ask true. A limit used up always goes to the Failure Path and a question never resets a count. Headless (GitHub Actions only) behaves as ask false everywhere. Hard blockers (test-order and other unfixable verify gaps, Fixable: false challenge findings) have no recommendation: asked in a session even with ask false, Failure Path headless. An assumed Accept is written `Decision: Accept (assumed)`, settles the item for the build, writes no decisions.jsonl row or TEST EXCEPTION, and is listed in the build summary. Ship asks Confirm / Reject in a session after Step 2; a rejection or a headless ship still merges, writes one needs-decision deferral per item and says so under a summary heading. Debug fix and soak count across every debug run of the feature with no run limit. bkit.loopPause is removed.
rationale: Owner decisions on #671, 2026-10-25. Replaces the #657 behaviour "Headless runs stop but stay in progress": every question cost a whole stopped run even when a recommendation existed, and in a session each pause reset the counts so pausing bought more attempts. The owner's approval point moves from before the build continues to ship.
alternatives: Keep headless stops (#657) — rejected: half the charged time of the longest step on #650 was waiting. Build unaffected tasks while waiting (#672) — closed as not planned, ask false removes the wait without slicing tasks. Reset counts on each answer — rejected: limits must be hard.

summary: No agent runs at xhigh: Opus agents that think run at high, Sonnet implementers and fix executors run at medium, and the Opus ledger / tracker / roadmap agents run at medium
description: `bkit-design-generate`, `bkit-design-update`, `bkit-plan-generate`, `bkit-plan-update`, `bkit-debug-failure-diagnose`, `bkit-debug-failure-soak` and `bkit-audit-generate` move from xhigh to high. `bkit-build-plan-execute`, `bkit-build-plan-gaps-remediate`, `bkit-debug-failure-remediate` and `bkit-ship-conflict-resolve` (Sonnet) and `bkit-utility-update-decisions`, `-deferrals`, `-failures`, `-knowledge`, `-roadmap`, `-tracker` (Opus) move from high to medium. Reviewers, challenge, verify, spike and both docs-sync agents stay at high. xhigh is reserved for a measured gain; a stuck bug goes to Fable by hand. The non-Claude effort mapping table is unchanged, so other hosts follow each agent's new row.
rationale: The goal is making Claude subscription and token budgets last longer. No effort level was ever measured on bkit tasks, and the ladder predates the 5.5 recalibration of effort. Anthropic recommends medium for well-specified agentic work and reserving xhigh and max for a measured quality gain. The owner's experience is that Opus at high reasons well enough for design, plan and diagnosis and that Sonnet at medium implements well. Ledger agents produce small, diffable jsonl edits, so a weak pass is cheap to catch. Reviewers stay at high because a missed bug ships unread.
alternatives: Keep the xhigh synthesizer tier
Keep fix executors at high because a failed fix costs another test-loop round
Measure each move with an A/B run before changing it
Raise the OpenCode/Codex columns one rung so non-Claude hosts keep their old thinking depth

summary: Superseded by `205-effort-opus-high-sonnet-medium-no-xhigh`: both docs-sync agents stay Sonnet at high; the Sonnet fix executors move to medium
The OpenCode effort column maps medium to `variant: max`, so every opencode agent from medium up runs at max; Claude, Cursor, Codex and Antigravity columns are unchanged
description: Only the medium row of the OpenCode column changes, from `high` to `max`. low stays `none`. The ollama gateway still writes no `variant:`. Cursor ignores `effort:` (its thinking is set by the pinned model name) and Codex stays identity with Default.
rationale: The opencode pins sit at or below their Claude tier and were chosen from parity-board scores measured with heavy thinking, so running them at `high` leaves them below the score that justified the pin, further than 'parity or just below'. They cost $0.03-$1.76 per task, so the extra thinking is cheap. The move matters more now that the Sonnet implementers and the ledger agents run at medium. Codex is subscription-paid and its models are nearest Claude, and its OpenAI column is still unprobed, so it is not tuned before a real probe.
alternatives: Keep OpenCode medium at `high` to stay inside the OpenCode Go 5-hour usage window
Raise Codex to one rung above Claude as well
Move Cursor Sonnet-tier agents from `composer-2.5` to `cursor-grok-4.5-high`

summary: #697 — rendering a nested JSON array as a markdown table was considered and is unsound: a table cell parses back to a scalar, so a flattened nested key cannot equal the input it came from
description: `bkit context fetch` writes a block's stdout as a markdown table only when the table parses back to the same values and types as the input object; the printed JSON is the fallback. Extending that to one level of nesting (option 6 of #697) cannot preserve the guarantee: with dotted keys `[{b:[{c:2}]}]` prints `| b.c |` / `| 2 |` and `parseText` returns `{ "b.c": 2 }`, never `{ b: [{ c: 2 }] }`, so `checkedTable` must refuse — which it already does (`item 0 key b is nested`).
rationale: `readTable` reads one scalar per cell; the row comparison in `checkedTable` is key-set plus value equality against the input rows, so a reconstructed nested object fails it on both value and reference. Teaching `readTable`/`parseText` to expand dotted keys back into objects is also unsound: a literal key containing a dot produces a byte-identical table (guaranteed collision), and the row compare would still be deep-equality rather than the identity the current contract asserts. Rendering each nested array as its own table below the main one is refused by the grammar (`parseText` returns null for stacked tables). The sound design already ships: refuse and write the output as printed, with `render: raw (<reason>)`, and `renderText`'s list/JSON path stays lossless.
alternatives: A deliberately designed lossless cell encoding (prefix + escaped JSON, deep-equality in `checkedTable`, dot-escaping in `keyText`/`markdownTable`) was not probed in depth: it is a new serialization layer rather than the proposed flattening, it loses the property that one column is one field, and it would need its own decision. No consumer block is currently refused by the nesting rule — every shipped block already prints a flat array or non-JSON text.

summary: A session-start advisory names only `.agents/rules.md`, delivered once per session at each host's earliest event — `SessionStart` on Claude Code and Cursor, the first tool call on opencode, Codex and Antigravity
description: One canonical advisory sentence rides every host, held as a language-specific part per side: `preflight-rules.sh` for the two shell hooks and `session-rules-advisory.js` for the JS hooks. Both parts declare plain `const` / `function` members with no `export` / `import`, because `renderParts` inlines a part's bytes into each host template and an `export` would make the rendered `.cjs` hooks invalid. Claude Code and Cursor splice the shell part into `bkit-preflight.sh` and merge it into the single JSON document that hook already writes (advisory alone on an IDE session, advisory plus the Linear guard result on a cloud session), written from a `printf` path that needs no `python3`; opencode, Codex and Antigravity have no session-start event, so a dedicated bkit hook per host emits the same sentence at the first tool call, once per session, on that host's advisory channel (opencode appends to the tool result, Codex `additionalContext`, Antigravity deny-once). The Codex hook registers as two single-value `PreToolUse` groups (`apply_patch`, `Bash`), the shape every shipped Codex matcher uses — alternation is unverified on that host. The advisory never names `AGENTS.md` and is a constant — no interpolation of issue or user content. Ideas 2-4 stay future work (deferrals `700-first-action-deny-gate`, `700-rules-content-hash-acknowledgement`, `700-provider-auto-load-rules`).
rationale: answered by owner: yes (recommended option A) for both open questions — advisory wording A (`[bkit] Read .agents/rules.md before any other action and follow all its rules.`) and per-host delivery A (SessionStart on Claude Code / Cursor; first tool call on opencode / Codex / Antigravity).
alternatives: Extend the GateGuard engine on the three non-session-start hosts — changes its per-file first-touch return value and the parity tests that assert it
Emit on Claude Code and Cursor only, and document the other three as a gap — fails the 'present across all providers' criterion
Inject the rules through provider auto-load config (opencode `instructions`, `CLAUDE.md` `@` import) — rejected on #700 as idea 4
One `export`ed helper module shared by the JS hosts — the part is inlined into CJS templates, so the rendered hooks stop parsing
Register the Codex hook on one `apply_patch|Bash` matcher — alternation is unverified on that host, where a matcher that never fires installs and exits 0 silently

summary: Engine tool-failure friction excludes shared routing exits and each verb's declared exit codes
description: The engine-level friction writer appends a tool-failure row only for a non-zero exit that is neither in SHARED_EXIT_CODES {0,1,2,80,81,82} nor declared in the failing verb's own exitCodes; undeclared codes, signal deaths and throws all write a row. The set is derived at runtime, never a literal list.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — a derived set is self-maintaining and excludes routine routing and usage exits (including exit 2, thrown by parseFlags and refuseUnsubstituted on ordinary authoring mistakes), so the row stays signal rather than noise.
alternatives: Option B — derived minus exit 2, keeping usage errors as signal, re-mutes the detector on every routine flag mistake in workflow prose; Option C — the literal {3,8,9,80,81} from the design grill Q5, writes rows on routine exits 1, 2, 4-7, 10-16 and 82.

summary: Friction by.step and dedup key use the failing command's own --step= else a noun-verb sentinel
description: The engine friction writer sets by.step to the failing command's own --step= value when it has one, else the <noun>-<verb> sentinel, and keys the row <noun>-<verb>/<step> over the same value. No step inference; the row is always admissible, since validate refuses an empty by.step.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — the engine layer has no intrinsic current-step value, and a degrade that never infers keeps the row admissible without drift.
alternatives: Option B — resumePoint inference of the run's current step (mis-names under group loops and retries); Option C — a BKIT_STEP env contract exported per workflow block (drift-prone prose work across every fenced block).

summary: The completeness start warning compares against the run immediately preceding in the same status.jsonl
description: The workflows start / resume warning reads the verdict of the run immediately preceding the one being started or resumed in the same status.jsonl, whatever its workflow, so a holey design run warns the plan run of the same FID.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — matches 'the previous run for that FID'.
alternatives: Option B — the last same-workflow run (misses a holey design warning the plan run); Option C — the last run carrying a stored completeness row (skips abandoned runs).

summary: The completeness warning fires on evidence holes and step holes only; unexercised calls are reported, never alarming
description: The verdict splits holes into evidence holes (a step recorded DONE missing its required journaled calls), step holes (a required step absent from a closed run) and unexercised (conditional or unreached calls). Only evidence holes and step holes make a run holey and trigger the start warning; the full report still lists every class. Sharpens the accepted Acceptance Scenario criterion 2.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — with every {BKIT} literal required and no watermark, a flat hole list is non-empty for a clean run, so a warning on any hole would fire on nearly every run and die of fatigue.
alternatives: Option B — a flat list with the warning on any hole (fires on nearly every run); Option C — split, but warn when unexercised exceeds a threshold (adds a magic number).

summary: engine-call rows stay in the run's status.jsonl with the MARK_ROWS reader fix in both copies
description: The per-command journal is engine-call rows in the run's status.jsonl, not a sidecar file. Both MARK_ROWS copies (commands/workflow/run-facts.ts and scripts/harvest/bkit-harvest.mjs) gain the new row types so step timing is unchanged; the accepted afterEnd / scan.rows shift is documented.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — settled by grill Q8; the sidecar's isolation is bought once by the reader fix.
alternatives: Option B — a sidecar engine-calls.jsonl beside status.jsonl (better isolation, but a new artifact kind in the docs / jsonl / harvest matrix, and it doubles the union-merge surface).

summary: A run with zero engine-call rows gets a steps-only preJournal verdict, with a journalSuspect heartbeat on the close path
description: A run holding no engine-call rows gets a steps-only verdict labelled preJournal rather than being flagged holey, so historical runs are not all flagged on the first resume after upgrade. The close path adds journalSuspect when the closing engine is itself journaling and recorded zero engine-call rows, so a dead journal is not mistaken for a historical run.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — avoids flagging every historical run at rollout while keeping an alertable signal on a dead journal.
alternatives: Option B — evaluate all runs uniformly (floods at rollout); Option C — carve out and write no completeness row when the journal is suspect (loses the only record of the suspect run).

summary: The completeness check reports every hole on every run; no pinned watermark or baseline
description: The generalised completeness check carries no pinned watermark or baseline and reports every hole it finds for a run. The advisory / fail-open posture and the advisory-to-blocking promotion gate (decision 384-tier3-promotion) are unchanged.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — settled by grill Q15; the warning's scope is set by the evidence-hole / step-hole split instead of a delta.
alternatives: Option B — reinstate the pinned-watermark delta of decision 384-tier3-promotion (needs a watermark artifact and a delta computation).

summary: Both MARK_ROWS copies plus the harvest parity test, the splitRuns / lastActivity audit and an unknown-row-type-inert test
description: Reader coverage for the two new status.jsonl row types is both MARK_ROWS copies (run-facts.ts and scripts/harvest/bkit-harvest.mjs), the parity test that pins them equal, the splitRuns / lastActivity audit, and one test asserting an unknown row type is inert in every reader, rather than an enumerated reader list.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — a missed reader is silent telemetry corruption, and an enumerated reader list is what the probe showed failing (total step minutes 1208.1 to 0.7 with MARK_ROWS unchanged).
alternatives: Option B — the two MARK_ROWS copies only (smallest change; risks a missed reader).

summary: engine-call rows carry no step; attribution is positional, and a call with no step in progress is reported unattributable
description: The engine-call row keeps grill Q11's shape with no step field. The check attributes a call to the step in progress (between two step-done rows); a call with no step in progress (after the run's terminator, or under a repeated step name) is named in an unattributable bucket rather than charged to a step.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — keeps the row shape verbatim and never invents an attribution.
alternatives: Option B — a self-describing step on the engine-call row (departs Q11 and still cannot cover the step-less calls); Option C — journal to a per-run sidecar ordered by at (departs Q8, loses the union-merge ride).

summary: The journal seam lands first, behind a flag, with the exit-code-passthrough test as its first commit
description: Build order for the mechanism: the commands/lib.ts runCommand seam lands first, behind a flag, with the exit-code-passthrough and one-stderr-line test as its first commit; the checker and the completeness command follow.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — the seam is the design's load-bearing guarantee, it is Unsettled by probe, and it carries the CLI-wide blast radius.
alternatives: Option B — the checker and the command first, the seam last (leaves the CLI-wide risk untested until the end); Option C — the seam in main() instead (departs the probe-verified runCommand seam and re-opens the classic-verb refactor).

summary: The friction write-to-harvest dogfood runs on bkit itself, not a scratch consumer
description: The write -> ledgers commit -> pnpm harvest path is verified end to end by building bkit and running the built CLI against bkit's own repo, forcing a non-zero exit and asserting the friction row in the run's own .bkit/friction.jsonl and in the harvested ledger.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A on bkit itself — exercises the write root, row shape, commit and harvest together in the repo that owns the mechanism.
alternatives: Option B — unit tests on the seam's row only (would not have caught the wrong write root or the refused step-less row).

summary: A run carries one completeness row per close; the read path takes the last and recomputes when rows follow it
description: workflows close appends one completeness row per close, so a run that closes more than once (the corpus's common shape) carries one per close. The read path takes the last stored row and recomputes when rows follow the stored verdict.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — every close is recorded, and the read path is defined for the corpus's repeated-close shape.
alternatives: Option B — only the first close of a run (a later close records nothing); Option C — write only when the run has no completeness row and never recompute at start (leaves a re-closed run's verdict stale).

summary: The follow-up is one issue and one plan; the eight workstreams become the plan's task groups
description: The engine run completeness mechanism is filed as one issue with one plan, its eight workstreams as the plan's task groups: WS-4 then WS-3 first (the journal seam behind a flag, exit-code-passthrough test first), WS-8 last. The Requires graph is a within-plan ordering, not a dependency between deliverables.
rationale: answered by owner: Option A — four of the eight workstreams are mechanical, WS-4 and WS-8 cannot ship alone (same-change mandate; CI-gated dist), and WS-1/2/5/6 share the Contract and CompletenessVerdict types and the completeness row contract.
alternatives: Option B — two issues by capability (journal + friction, then the completeness report), costing two full plan-build-ship cycles; Option C — the eight suggested issues (two cannot ship alone).

summary: The generalised check keeps the file name checks/status-holes.ts; the dispatch seam's row primitives go in a new leaf ledgers/journal.ts, and the active-run resolver goes in commands/lib.ts
description: The design left the module name open (checks/completeness.ts or the evolved checks/status-holes.ts). Settled: checks/status-holes.ts is evolved in place and keeps its name, so the [bkit-status-holes] log prefix stays truthful to the module, the package.json script bkit:audit:status and the CI step keep their path, and the docs/testing.md reference to the file stays valid. The seam's row builders (engine-call composition, friction composition, the derived exclusion set, friction dedup) go in a new leaf module .bkit/core/engine/ledgers/journal.ts, which imports only node:fs, node:path, ./status.js and ./telemetry.js. The active-run resolver (resolveActiveRun) goes in commands/lib.ts, which already holds statusLocation, statusRelPath, repoRoot and git.
rationale: Keeps the module identity (and its registered log prefix) while giving the seam logic a home that can be unit-tested in isolation. A seam module under commands/ could not import commands/workflow/locks.ts or fids.ts without cycling the engine's most-imported module (both import ../lib.js), so the resolver stays where those primitives already are reachable, and the row composition moves to a leaf with no command-layer imports.
alternatives: Rename the module to checks/completeness.ts with a new [bkit-completeness] prefix — REJECTED: it forces edits to package.json, the CI step, docs/testing.md and the docs/observability.md prefix list for no functional gain, and the prefix rule says a new prefix comes only with a new module. Put the whole seam inside commands/lib.ts — REJECTED: it would need the ledger row shapes in the engine's most-imported module, untestable in isolation. Put the seam in commands/workflow/journal.ts — REJECTED: lib.ts importing it would cycle (commands/workflow/locks.ts and fids.ts import ../lib.js).

summary: Promotion criteria for the generalised design / plan / build / debug / ship check: one release of fail-open signal without muting, with no pinned watermark
description: The check generalised by #699 covers all five workflows (design / plan / build / debug / ship), derives its expected step and command set from each workflow markdown at runtime, and reports every hole on every run. Its advisory / fail-open posture is unchanged: the CLI and the completeness verb always exit 0, the close and start call sites degrade on any error, and the check never blocks a workflow. Promotion criteria (advisory to blocking gate): one release of fail-open signal without muting, across the same corpus that made a day-one gate unshippable. The pinned watermark of this decision is no longer part of the criteria — decision 699-completeness-check-no-watermark replaces the delta against a watermark with the evidence-hole / step-hole split as the warning's scope, and deferral 384-promote-status-hole-detector-from-advisory-to-gate stays open until the release accrues.
rationale: The promotion gate is unchanged in posture and now carries an explicit scope: with every {BKIT} literal required and no watermark, a flat hole list is non-empty for a clean run, so the signal to accrue is the holey verdict (evidence holes plus step holes), not the raw delta.
alternatives: Flip to a blocking gate in this cycle — REJECTED: the design's constraint and the issue non-goal both hold the check advisory until one release of unmuted signal. Keep the pinned-watermark delta as a second promotion criterion — REJECTED: superseded by the no-watermark decision; a watermark artifact would have to be maintained for no signal the hole-class split does not already give.

summary: The plan-block verbs `tick`, `open` and `currency` live in a new `tasks` noun, not in `context` or `tests`
description: `bkit tasks tick --plan= --group= --tasks=` rewrites a plan's task line to `[x]`, `open` prints the group's tasks holding neither a `DONE` nor a `BLOCKED` line in the execute log (with `handover`), and `currency` prints each task whose plan-ref paths or symbols moved since `--base`, with its diff hunks. All three read the plan's task blocks through `parsePlanBlocks` (`.bkit/core/engine/commands/workflow/plan-blocks.ts`); none keeps a second task store.
rationale: answered by owner: A — a new `tasks` noun (Recommended)
alternatives: Fold `tick` into `tests` beside `plan-check`
Fold the verbs into `context` beside `brief` / `diff`
Keep the plan tick in the verifier and expose only `open` / `currency`

summary: `bkit tests green` always emits `verdict` plus a `fixable` and a `logLine` per gap — no flag gates it
description: `verdict` is `PASS` with no gaps, `FAIL` when any gap is `fixable: false`, `CONCERNS` when every gap is `fixable: true`, and `null` when any gap needs a diff read (`delete-still-referenced`, `test-changed`, `red-mismatch`, or the row state `Changed since red = added lines only`) — those four reads stay with the verifier. The mapping moves out of `bkit-build-plan-verify.md` § Process 8 and 10 into one table in `tests.ts`, so the prompt names no kind→`Fixable` mapping and no verdict mapping. A `fixable: null` gap makes the report `verdict` null even beside an unfixable gap, so the verifier applies its mapping to every gap.
rationale: answered by owner: A — always
alternatives: Gate the keys behind `--verdict`
Leave the mapping in the prompt and emit only the raw gap kinds
Have the engine decide the four diff reads too

summary: A plan's `Derived Test Matrix` carries a `Task` column; `bkit tests plan-check` refuses an unmapped row, a row naming two tasks, a test-bearing task no row names and a header with no column — a plan with no matrix section is not refused
description: The column is the mapping `plan-check` reads. A plan whose text carries no `Derived Test Matrix` section yields no `matrix` problem whatever its tasks name, because the refusal is on a row and issue-form and converted plans carry no table. With the table present the check runs both ways: a header without the column is one `matrix` problem naming the column to add, never one problem per row; a `Task` cell naming no task, an undefined task, or two or more tasks is one problem at the row; a test-bearing task no row names is one problem at its task line, and an `n/a`-only task needs no row. The bidirectional half survives an in-build append because `challenge merge`'s `appendTasks` and build Step 5's `Fix now` writer each write a matrix row for the tasks they add, and build Steps 3 and 7 route a `matrix` / `supersession` problem to `@bkit-build-plan-convert` like a `markers` problem, so a pre-column plan has a recovery path. The template `docs/templates/bkit-plan.md` and the `plan-scenario-detail` clause carry the column, so new plans are born compliant. The same change adds the `supersession` kind, refusing a task `DELETE` with no `Supersession Inventory` row.
rationale: answered by owner: A — the `Task` cell as a fourth column in the Derived Test Matrix
alternatives: Infer the mapping from the row's `Target file` plus its test words
Check nothing and leave the mapping to `bkit-plan-scope-check`
Report the missing column once per row instead of once per plan
Refuse every plan whose `Derived Test Matrix` section is absent — huge fixture blast radius, and an issue-form plan could never pass
One-directional check only (rows must name a task) — a plan could then evade the criterion by naming no rows

summary: A `not-green` gap is `fixable: true` in `bkit tests green`, the mapping moved verbatim from the verifier prompt
description: `not-green` is the gap a fix executor closes, so the engine emits `fixable: true` for it, exactly as `bkit-build-plan-verify.md` Process 8 does today. This settles a contradiction inside the issue: its `Tasks` Task 1 `DONE WHEN` lists `false, false, null` for a `not-green` / `no-red` / `test-changed` fixture, while the prompt maps `not-green` to `Fixable: true`. The plan reproduces the prompt's mapping, not the issue's value order, and the deviation is recorded in the plan.
rationale: answered by owner: A — `not-green` → `fixable: true` (the prompt's mapping, moved verbatim)
alternatives: `not-green` → `fixable: false`, following the issue's literal value order — every failing test would turn `FAIL` and the build would stop in a Decision Pause instead of handing the gap to a fixer

summary: Any `fixable: null` gap makes `bkit tests green`'s report `verdict` null, even beside an unfixable gap — `null` outranks `false`
description: The report's `verdict` is `null` as soon as one gap needs a diff read (`delete-still-referenced`, `test-changed`, `red-mismatch`, or the row state `Changed since red = added lines only`). An unfixable gap beside a diff-reading one does not make the report `FAIL`: the engine abstains, and the verifier applies its own mapping to every gap, then rolls the result up into its artifact header. The verifier still reaches `FAIL` from the decided gap lines.
rationale: answered by owner: A — any `fixable: null` gap makes the report `verdict` null, in line with the issue's Edge Case and its Task 1 `DONE WHEN` fixture
alternatives: An unfixable gap wins: any `fixable: false` makes the report `FAIL`, else `null` — the engine would pre-decide a verdict while a diff-reading gap is still unread

summary: The `no-red` "work already landed" exemption stays in the verifier prompt as an override of the engine's `no-red` `fixable: false`
description: The engine maps every `no-red` gap to `fixable: false`. The verifier keeps its override: `no-red` on a task the plan-currency report classifies `Broken` with work already landed, and the execute log records `DONE — TASK {N}: already landed`, is no gap. The exemption is stated beside the four diff reads so it is not read as part of the deleted kind→`Fixable` table.
rationale: answered by owner: A — keep the exemption in the prompt as a verifier override of the engine no-red fixable: false
alternatives: Teach `tests green` to suppress the `no-red` gap itself — pushes a plan-currency classification into the test-first audit
Let the regression stand and declare it — a passing build would start pausing on work that already landed

summary: The verify artifact's `Verdict:` header is the verifier's post-judgement roll-up, and each gap log line carries the verifier's decided `Fixable` where the engine printed `null`
description: `tests green` prints `fixable: null` and `verdict: null` when a gap needs a diff read. The verifier decides those gaps from the diff it reads, appends each `logLine` with its decided `Fixable: true` or `Fixable: false` in place of the engine's `null`, and writes the header as the roll-up over its decisions: any decided `false` → `FAIL`; else any decided `true` → `CONCERNS`; else `PASS`. The header never carries `null`.
rationale: answered by owner: A — the header is the verifier post-judgement roll-up and each gap line carries the decided Fixable in place of the engine null
alternatives: Copy the report's `null` verdict into the header and widen `steps finish` to accept it — breaks the step contract and the header readers
Keep assembling the gap log line by hand in the prompt — that is the prose this change removes
Have the engine decide the four diff reads — they are judgement (a different thing with the same name; an added line inside a planned test)

summary: A red whose test gained added lines only emits a `test-changed` gap with `fixable: null`, so `green` exits 1 on that row
description: Today the `added` branch beside `onlyAddsLines` sets the row's `changed` to `added lines only` and emits no gap. The engine now pushes the same `test-changed` gap the non-added branch does, with `fixable: null`, and the verifier reads its diff: added lines inside a planned test or in setup it runs → `Fixable: false`; added lines only outside every planned test → no gap. The row joins `testOrderOnly`.
rationale: answered by owner: A — reuse the existing test-changed kind; the row changed cell added-lines-only picks the diff read
alternatives: A new kind (`red-added-lines`) joining `TEST_ORDER_GAPS` and the prompt's four reads — widens four lists for one row state the report already names
Leave the row gap-free — the verifier never sees a case `#701` explicitly puts in the engine's output

summary: `bkit tasks tick` requires one of `--tasks` / `--green` and exits 2 without one — the group-wide no-flag default is dropped
description: A `tick` call must name what it ticks: `--tasks={NUMBERS}` for the numbers the verifier judged satisfied, or `--green` to tick every gap-free task in the group (narrowed by `--tasks=` when both are passed). Neither flag present exits 2, with the usage line naming both. This supersedes the plan's recommended option A for this question (keep the no-flag default and document its only caller in `--help`).
rationale: answered by owner: B — require one of `--tasks` / `--green`, exit 2 otherwise
alternatives: Keep the group-wide no-flag default and name its only intended caller in the verb's `--help` — the plan's recommendation; a caller that forgets `--tasks=` would tick tasks no agent judged satisfied

summary: `bkit tasks currency` diffs `{base}..{against}` with `--against` defaulting to `origin/dev`, not `{base}..HEAD`
description: The verb matches each task's plan-ref paths and needles against `git diff --name-only {base}..{against}` and `git diff {base}..{against} -S{needle} --name-only`, defaulting `--against` to `origin/dev`, and the plan-current prompt calls it with `--base={BASE_SHA} --against=origin/dev`.
rationale: answered by owner: A — {base}..{against}, with --against defaulting to origin/dev
alternatives: `{base}..HEAD` — loses dev's movement and over-matches the branch's own work
Diff both ranges and merge the hunks — two signals in one output a caller cannot attribute

summary: `bkit tasks tick` requires `--group` and one of `--tasks` / `--green`; it ticks inside the named group only, and the holistic verify runs one tick per group
description: `tick` refuses a call with no `--group` or with neither `--tasks` nor `--green` (exit 2), so no caller can tick by default. Inside the named group: `--tasks={NUMBERS}` ticks exactly those numbers (a number outside the group exits 2), `--green={REPORT}` ticks the group tasks the `tests green` report does not gap, and both together intersect. The holistic build Step 9 buckets the numbers the verify artifact judged satisfied per group and runs one `tick` per group instead of a single cross-group call. Supersedes the earlier answer that made `--group` optional.
rationale: answered by owner: B — one tick per group, `--group` required (revised from A so no implicit default remains)
alternatives: `--group` optional, so `tick --tasks=` with no `--group` ticks named tasks across groups — an implicit default the owner removed

summary: `bkit tasks currency`, and plan-current's Process 6-7, judge `{base}...{against}` — the three-dot range, matching `branches scan-diff`'s `{base}...HEAD`
description: `currency` compares with `git diff {base}...{against}` (three dots = merge-base(base, against)..against), with `--against` still defaulting to `origin/dev`. Three dots is byte-identical to two dots when `{base}` is an ancestor of `{against}` — the normal case, now that design and plan worktrees are based on `origin/dev` — and correct when it is not. `{BASE_SHA}` is the plan's anchor `baseSha`, resolved by build Step 4's `bkit branches anchor-read --field=baseSha --against=origin/dev`; a plan anchored on a local `dev` commit ahead of `origin/dev` (this plan's anchor, `5c94780ac`, was one) would give a two-dot range whose endpoints are inverted, so `git diff` would report unpushed `dev` work as movement — false matches. This also lines `currency` up with `branches scan-diff`, which already uses `diff <base>...HEAD`.
rationale: answered by owner: yes — change the range to three-dot so `currency` matches `branches scan-diff`'s established form
alternatives: Keep the two-dot `{base}..{against}` — identical in the normal case, inverted whenever the anchor is not an ancestor of `origin/dev`

summary: The CI advisory step keeps the module's own exit-0 CLI as its surface; the bkit completeness check verb is the ad-hoc reader
description: Which surface the CI advisory step invokes is settled as Option A: the advisory step keeps the module's own exit-0 CLI (`tsx .bkit/core/engine/checks/status-holes.ts docs/plans/*/logs/*/status.jsonl`) as its CI surface, generalised so each file's workflow is inferred from its own rows, and `package.json` `bkit:audit:status` is left unchanged. The new `bkit completeness check --workflow= --file=` verb is the maintainer's ad-hoc reader for a single run; the module's `main()` keeps its caller. The design named both surfaces and left the choice to the plan.
rationale: answered by owner: A — the advisory step runs on every static-lane build of a clean tree, so it must not depend on dist/ being built (the CLI is tsx); the verb is the maintainer's ad-hoc reader and its --workflow-optional path is still exercised by TASK 10's tests. One surface per job, no duplicated entry point.
alternatives: B — repoint bkit:audit:status at bkit completeness check --file= per file, so the verb is the only surface (the sweep then needs a shell loop and the module's main() loses its only caller); C — both surfaces: the CLI for the corpus sweep and the verb for one file, kept in step by a shared assertion.

summary: Check Capability Register runs `check-at HEAD` on every event; on a pull request HEAD is GitHub's test merge of the PR into its base, the tree a squash merge lands
description: The step runs `bash scripts/graphify/bkit-graphify.sh check-at HEAD` with no REGISTER_REV. A push checks the pushed commit; a pull_request checks the default checkout, GitHub's test merge of head into base. That is the tree a squash merge puts on the base, so the PR verdict is the post-merge push run's verdict (708). On a PR red the step adds a `::error` naming the base: a branch behind it merges the base in, runs `pnpm graph:refresh`, commits and pushes. The graphify release (`spec`), the script `check-at` runs and the register it judges all come from that one tree. Owner decision on 444, 2026-10-28.
rationale: A head-commit check differs from the merge-ref check only when the PR is behind its base, and that is exactly when two branches' registers merge line by line into a file no rebuild of the merged code produces: the head is green, the squash lands, the dev push reds. A merge-ref red is clearable by the author (sync with the base, refresh, commit), so it is a real signal, not a false one. Checking the head also split tooling from verdict: CI installed the merge ref's pinned release while `check-at` ran the head's own script, whose version gate rejected it after a GRAPHIFY_SPEC bump on dev.
alternatives: Keep `check-at` on the PR head and fail when the head does not contain the base (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`) — REJECTED: forces a sync on every behind PR, including ones whose merge yields a correct register. Keep the head check and record the gap — REJECTED: leaves the 708 failure mode open for any PR shipped behind dev, which `bkit-ship.md` Step 4 allows (`prs update-branch --only-if-required`). Residual gap either way: CI does not re-run a PR when its base moves after the last run.

summary: Superseded by `capability-register-gates-pull-requests-at-the-merge-ref`: the PR gate checks GitHub's test merge, not the PR head
A rule in `.bkit/instructions.md` is identified by its `### {name}` heading, not by its position in `.agents/rules.md`
description: Local-line tags (`[scope-discipline]`), clause `- rule:` and `- tags:` lines and drift prose name rules by their `### {name}`. Names are kebab-case and unique across `## Rules` and `## Project Rules`. `checkRules` still pairs entries with rules.md bullets by order and text, but no longer checks an ID against a position, so a rule inserted mid-list needs no edit to any other entry. `checkCoverage` fails on a tag or clause that names no rule.
rationale: Positional `R{nn}` / `P{nn}` IDs forced every later rule to be renumbered whenever a rule was inserted mid-list (about 760 references for one insertion). A missed reference still looked like a valid ID and silently pointed at another rule, and references in `CHANGELOG.md` and plan logs went stale. A name survives moves, explains itself, and a typo fails the check.
alternatives: Fixed append-only numbers (new rule takes the next unused number wherever it sits): short tags, but unreadable without a lookup

summary: Lite paste-prompt workflows are retired; each phase runs its full workflow, and only build's ending is configurable
description: Issue #541's inspiration-style copy-paste prompts (`design:lite` to `ship:lite`) and the `.bkit/lite.md` payload are removed in #715. Every phase runs its full workflow. `/bkit-build` alone varies its ending through `package.json` `bkit.workflows.build.publish`: `remote` and `local` both default `true`; `local: false` holds the branch and worktree without pushing, opening a PR or running CI. Consumer lines below `bkit:end` in `.bkit/lite.md` survive as a consumer-owned stub through the install migration that replaces `migrateShortcutsToLite`.
rationale: #650 and #705 removed the gap lite workflows filled, and a second implementation of each workflow drifts with no test able to catch it. The retained value (worktree isolation, plan convert, verify, gaps, holistic verify, challenge, tests) stays in the one workflow, so only delivery varies.
alternatives: Keep the lite prompts and size the challenge down (second implementation, untested drift) - rejected. Keep `.bkit/lite.md` as a managed doc carrying a retirement notice (still ships a managed lite block) - rejected.

summary: Workflow labels keep phase transitions and next:* hints; the `:lite` suffix and every lite workflow name are retired
description: `next:*` hints and workflow labels name only the five full workflows (`next:design|plan|build|debug|ship`, `bkit:design|plan|build|debug|ship`). The `:lite` suffix, `next:<phase>:lite` hints and the lite names in the audit, roadmap and tracker prompts are removed. Label arithmetic already clears every `next:*` on a workflow label write and needs no change.
rationale: Lite workflows no longer exist, so a label pointing at one mis-routes the issue. The label arithmetic stays as it is: its generic `next:*` removal already clears a stale lite hint.
alternatives: Keep `:lite` labels as reserved-but-unused names (a label rule naming a workflow nothing can start) - rejected.

summary: `/bkit-build` ending is configurable through `bkit.workflows.build.publish` (`remote` / `local`, both `true` by default)
description: `package.json` `bkit.workflows.build.publish` holds `remote` and `local`. `remote` accepts only `true`; anything else takes the default and `bkit check` raises `bkit-build-publish-remote`. `local` accepts `true` or `false`; an invalid value takes the default and raises `bkit-build-publish-invalid`. A LOCAL run resolves `publish.local`; every other runtime resolves `publish.remote` and coerces a resolved `false` to `true` with a warning. A plain-text `publish=true` / `publish=false` token in the session prompt overrides config for that run. `false` skips branch push, PR creation, CI dispatch and docs sync, keeps the worktree and branch, releases the lock, records ending `held` and `publish: false` in the close row and telemetry, leaves the issue `In review` with a 'built locally, not published' comment, and prints `Publish: held` in the summary. `true` keeps the existing push, PR and `/bkit-ship` handoff.
rationale: The worktree, plan convert, verify, gaps, challenge and tests are the value a user wants; publishing is the only part some runs do not need. Making the ending a setting keeps one workflow implementation and one test suite, while the per-run token covers a one-off.
alternatives: A separate `bkit ship --batch` verb (a second landing workflow that drops the per-feature checks) - rejected. A per-run flag only, no config default (every run must restate its ending) - rejected. String values `pr` / `local` (the earlier sketch; contradicts the issue's final `true`/`false` vocabulary) - rejected.

summary: Lite workflows are retired; `.bkit/lite.md` becomes a consumer-owned stub and the five full workflows are the only path
description: Delete the `.bkit/core/.bkit/lite.md` source, its manifest entry and canonical-docs list entry, the README tier-table rows, the `.agents/docs.md` index row, and every rules / prompt / README guidance line naming a lite workflow. `migrateRetiredLite` replaces `migrateShortcutsToLite`: it strips the managed block from a consumer's `.bkit/lite.md`, appends consumer lines from a `.agents/shortcuts.md` managed block, writes the merged lines under a retired-lite stub heading, deletes either file when no consumer content remains, leaves a file with no single managed block in place and logs the fix, and is idempotent. The change lands in `docs/migrations.md`. Historical ledgers, `CHANGELOG.md` and closed issues keep their mentions.
rationale: A lite workflow skips the gates, worktree isolation, PR, CI and audit trail, and a second implementation of each workflow drifts with nothing testing it. Removing it leaves one tested path; the publish setting covers the real need to hold a build locally.
alternatives: Move the consumer section into `.bkit/prompts.md` (that doc holds model pins, not workflow guidance) - rejected. Keep `.bkit/lite.md` as a managed doc with a retirement notice (still ships a managed lite block) - rejected. Delete the consumer section outright (destroys consumer edits) - rejected.

summary: README and README charts quote bkit's own compression-tool measurements; every other public figure names an outside source
description: The README token section and the bkit-tokens chart keep bkit's own transcript measurements (cost split over more than 400 transcripts, per-tool saving, repeat-read and shell-read shares) because the comparison publishes its method, scripts and 95% ranges so a reader can re-run it on their own transcripts. Transcript counts are rounded down (more than 400), not exact. Every other public README or chart figure names an outside source until bkit has measured its own runs under the current workflow shape; readers are pointed at bkit stats for their own numbers.
rationale: Owner decision 2026-10-28: the compression comparison is a deliberate exception to the outside-sources-only rule for public numbers.
alternatives: Drop all bkit-measured figures from the README token section

summary: The machine-wide tests lock admits a fixed number of heavy runs (default 1, `BKIT_TEST_SLOTS` overrides); live load never decides who runs
description: Each holder of the `tests` lock exports `BKIT_TEST_WORKERS` = cores / slots for its runner. Slot 1 is `tests.lock`, slot k > 1 `tests.<k>.lock`, so runs with different slot settings still meet on slot 1. An invalid `BKIT_TEST_SLOTS` falls back to 1 with one stderr note.
rationale: Load average lags (two agents checking at once both see a quiet machine), counts unrelated work, and RAM reads differ per OS; a fixed slot count is predictable and explainable.
alternatives: Live load-average / memory-pressure gate; hardware-derived slot formula from performance vs efficiency cores and RAM.

summary: `bkit tests run` waits up to `--lock-wait-s` (default 60) for the tests lock, then exits 81 naming the holder; workflows end the turn and re-run the block
description: 81 is `EXIT.AGENT_WAIT`. Every `tests run` block in `bkit-build.md` and `bkit-debug.md` routes exit 81 to end-turn + re-run, pinned by `local-gate-audit.test.ts`. A raw `pnpm test` in bkit's repo waits (`LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S`, default 3600) and prints the holder once a minute.
rationale: An agent tool call has a hard timeout; a lock wait longer than it reads as a hang. 60 s matches `bkit runs dispatch`'s poll budget.
alternatives: Wait the full stack-lock default (3600 s) inside the tool call; fail the gate as FAIL.

summary: Single-file runs, nested runs, watch mode and CI never take the tests lock
description: `bkit tests red` / `green`, `bkit:test:file`, a raw `vitest run` whose every filter is an existing test file, a run under a live `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_OWNER_tests`, vitest watch mode, and `CI=true` / `CI=1` take no lock. A filter that is not a file path (`integration.test`) or no filter is a heavy run.
rationale: A single file uses about one core; queuing an agent's write-test-then-fix loop behind a multi-minute gate costs more than the load. A watch session would hold the lock for hours.
alternatives: A small separate light-run pool; watch mode taking the lock.

summary: The stack-lock template is renamed `bkit-machine-lock.sh` and gains named, machine-wide locks; no migration
description: Optional `[name]` on every function; named locks live at `~/.cache/bkit/machine-lock/<name>.lock` with no repo prefix; `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_OWNER_<name>` lets children skip; `run "<who>" [--lock <name>] -- <cmd>`. The unnamed stack lock keeps its lock file path, function and env names, so an adopted copy and the new script exclude each other. Named-lock holder lines name the caller's checkout; the stack lock's names the script's checkout.
rationale: Extends the one existing flock implementation instead of adding a second script. Copies are copy-and-own: consumers keep theirs at their own paths; `syncTemplateCopies` prunes the old name from `.bkit/templates/` and the upgrade report prints `removed:`.
alternatives: A second lock script; a TypeScript lock in the engine (no flock in Node).

summary: Locks are taken in one order — tests, then other named locks, then the unnamed stack lock — and the script refuses the reverse
description: Asking for `tests` while the shell or a live parent holds any other lock, or for a named lock while holding the stack lock, is refused at once with a message naming the order; `run` exits 73. Pending human confirmation as plan Open Question 3 (default: enforced).
rationale: One fixed order means two runs can never each hold one lock and wait forever for the other; enforcing it makes the order testable instead of a header comment.
alternatives: Document the order in the script header only.

summary: `bkit tests run` executes the packaged `getTemplatesRoot()/scripts/ci/bkit-machine-lock.sh`, never a consumer's copy
description: First engine verb to execute a copy-and-own template. `.bkit/templates` ships in `package.json` `files`; `getTemplatesRoot()` resolves under dist, tsx and node_modules layouts. Under `CI` the engine skips the script and runs the gate directly. Pending human confirmation as plan Open Question 1 (default: packaged copy).
rationale: One source of truth versioned with the engine; a consumer may edit, move or delete their adopted copy. `template-path-refs.test.ts` forbids workflows and prompts, not the engine, from naming template paths.
alternatives: The consumer's synced `.bkit/templates/` copy (absent before install); an engine-owned second copy under `.bkit/core/`.

summary: The lock script's `run` exits 75 when the wait gives up and 73 when the lock cannot be taken; the engine maps them to 81 and 4 only alongside the script's own log line
description: Functions keep returning 1 on every refusal so existing `|| exit 1` callers are unchanged. 73 covers an unwritable lock dir, no `/usr/bin/perl` (plan Open Question 2, default refuse), an unnameable stack and a lock-order refusal. A gate that itself exits 75 with no give-up line in the log stays a FAIL.
rationale: The engine must tell a lock outcome from the gate's own exit; sysexits `EX_TEMPFAIL` (75) and `EX_CANTCREAT` (73) are outside the codes test runners use, and the log line removes the remaining ambiguity.
alternatives: A two-phase engine holder process kept alive across the gate; parsing log text alone.

summary: bkit's own heavy vitest runs take the tests lock from a vitest global setup holding `run --lock tests -- cat` on a piped stdin
description: `vitest.test-lock.ts` decides heavy vs light from `project.vitest.config.filters`, spawns `bash scripts/ci/bkit-machine-lock.sh run … --lock tests` whose command waits on stdin, resolves on its ready line and exports `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_OWNER_tests`; teardown closes stdin; vitest dying closes the pipe so the lock frees within a second. `maxWorkers` comes from `BKIT_TEST_WORKERS` only when present (plan Open Question 4, default).
rationale: A global setup runs once per run in the main process; `vitest.setup.ts` runs per file in every worker. Config load cannot take the lock without every IDE / `vitest list` load queuing.
alternatives: Take the lock at config load with top-level await; take it in `vitest.setup.ts`.

summary: Every full gate bkit ships outside a workflow block runs through `bkit tests run`: the pre-push hook template's push gate and the subagent prompts' gate steps
description: `.bkit/templates/.husky/pre-push` (and bkit's adopted `.husky/pre-push`) runs `pnpm bkit tests run --gate=bkit:gate:static-unit-integration --gate=bkit:gate:static-unit --log=…`; exit 81 stops the push naming the holder. The gaps-remediate, debug-failure-remediate, plan-verify, debug-failure-soak and ship-conflict-resolve prompts run their gate the same way and re-run on exit 81. Pinned by `husky-pre-push.integration.test.ts` and `local-gate-audit.test.ts`. Pending human confirmation as plan Open Question 6 (default A).
rationale: Success Criterion 1 covers every full gate on the machine; raw `pnpm bkit:gate:*` calls in consumer repos never take the tests lock, so pushes and subagent gates overlap other agents' gates.
alternatives: Route the hook only and leave the prompts raw; narrow Success Criterion 1 to `bkit tests run` gates with a blocking deferral; wrap the hook's gate in the packaged script's `run --lock tests` with the 3600 s wait.

summary: The lock script's `run` exits 75 when the wait gives up and 73 when the lock cannot be taken; the engine maps 75 to 81 only when the give-up line names the `tests` lock and this run, and 73 to 4 only alongside a refusal line
description: Functions keep returning 1 on every refusal so existing `|| exit 1` callers are unchanged. 73 covers an unwritable lock dir, no `/usr/bin/perl` (plan Open Question 2, default refuse), an unnameable stack and a lock-order refusal. `classifyLockExit` in `tests.ts` reads exit 75 as a lock wait only when the log's `[machine-lock]` give-up line names the `tests` lock and the engine's own `<who>`; a gate's own 75, or a nested lock's give-up inside the gate, stays a FAIL. 81 is the shared `EXIT.AGENT_WAIT` and stays out of the verb's `exitCodes`.
rationale: The engine must tell a lock outcome from the gate's own exit; sysexits `EX_TEMPFAIL` (75) and `EX_CANTCREAT` (73) are outside the codes test runners use, and matching the lock name plus the engine's own `<who>` removes the case where a consumer gate's nested stack lock gives up.
alternatives: A two-phase engine holder process kept alive across the gate; parsing log text alone; matching any give-up line.

summary: bkit's own heavy vitest runs take the tests lock from a vitest global setup holding `run --lock tests -- cat` on a piped stdin; with no TTY the wait is capped at 60 s
description: `vitest.test-lock.ts` decides heavy vs light from `project.vitest.config.filters` / `.watch`, skips under a `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_OWNER_tests` pid an injected `alive(pid)` probe confirms, spawns `bash scripts/ci/bkit-machine-lock.sh run … --lock tests` whose command waits on stdin, resolves on its ready line and exports `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_OWNER_tests`; teardown closes stdin; vitest dying closes the pipe so the lock frees within a second. When stdin is not a TTY and `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S` is unset, the holder waits 60 s, then the setup throws naming the holder (plan Open Question 7, default A). `maxWorkers` comes from `BKIT_TEST_WORKERS` only when present (plan Open Question 4, default).
rationale: A global setup runs once per run in the main process; `vitest.setup.ts` runs per file in every worker. Config load cannot take the lock without every IDE / `vitest list` load queuing. An agent tool call has a ~10-minute ceiling, so a no-TTY run must give up with a holder line well before it.
alternatives: Take the lock at config load with top-level await; take it in `vitest.setup.ts`; keep the 3600 s wait for every run; cap every run at 60 s.

summary: `bkit tests run` waits up to `--lock-wait-s` (default 60) for the tests lock, then exits 81 naming the holder; workflows end the turn and re-run the block
description: 81 is `EXIT.AGENT_WAIT`. Every `tests run` block in `bkit-build.md` and `bkit-debug.md` routes exit 81 to end-turn + re-run with no re-run ceiling (plan Open Question 9, default), pinned by `local-gate-audit.test.ts`. A raw `pnpm test` in bkit's repo waits `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S` (default 3600) from a terminal and at most 60 s with no TTY, printing the holder once a minute.
rationale: An agent tool call has a hard timeout; a lock wait longer than it reads as a hang. 60 s matches `bkit runs dispatch`'s poll budget.
alternatives: Wait the full stack-lock default (3600 s) inside the tool call; fail the gate as FAIL; cap exit-81 re-runs and then take the Failure Path.

summary: The engine never executes the lock template; consumers copy `bkit-machine-lock.sh`, customise it and wire it into their `package.json` gate scripts like every other template
description: Plan Open Question 1 answered: neither the packaged copy (A), the synced `.bkit/templates/` copy (B) nor an engine-owned copy (C). Copy-and-own like the stack lock (`.bkit/templates.md` § Local stack lock): `cp .bkit/templates/scripts/ci/bkit-machine-lock.sh scripts/ci/`, then wrap `bkit:gate:*` scripts as `bash scripts/ci/bkit-machine-lock.sh run --lock tests -- <gate>`. bkit's own repo does the same in its `package.json`.
rationale: answered by owner: the consumer must copy the script and customise it and add it into package.json same as all the other templates
alternatives: A) engine runs the packaged `getTemplatesRoot()` copy; B) engine runs the consumer's synced `.bkit/templates/` copy; C) engine-owned second copy under `.bkit/core/`.

summary: Locks are taken in one order — tests, then other named locks, then the unnamed stack lock — and the script refuses the reverse
description: Asking for `tests` while the shell or a live parent holds any other lock, or for a named lock while holding the stack lock, is refused at once with a message naming the order; `run` exits 73. Confirmed by the owner as plan Open Question 3, option A.
rationale: answered by owner: A
alternatives: Document the order in the script header only.

summary: Shipped pre-push hook and subagent prompts keep calling `pnpm bkit:gate:*` raw; the lock lives inside the consumer's wrapped gate scripts, so every caller queues
description: Plan Open Question 6 answered with a new option D: no change to `.bkit/templates/.husky/pre-push` or the five prompts that run gates raw; plan TASKS 7 and 8 drop. Follows from `724-engine-runs-packaged-lock-template` (consumer wraps `bkit:gate:*` in `bkit-machine-lock.sh run --lock tests`). A wrapped gate that gives up waiting exits 75 to raw callers; only `bkit tests run` maps 75 to 81. Success Criterion 1 holds in repos that wire the script.
rationale: answered by owner: D
alternatives: A) hook and prompts call `bkit tests run`; B) hook only; C) neither, narrow SC 1 with a Blocking deferral.

summary: `bkit-machine-lock.sh` waits 60 s, not 3600 s, when stdin is not a TTY and `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S` is unset, then exits 75 naming the holder
description: Plan Open Question 7 answered with option A-prime: the short no-TTY default lives in the lock script, not only in bkit's vitest global setup, so pushes, subagent prompts and agent tool calls in every repo that wires the script see the holder before an agent tool timeout (~10 min). Terminal runs keep the 3600 s default; an explicit `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S` always wins.
rationale: answered by owner: A-prime
alternatives: A) vitest global setup only sets the 60 s wait; B) always 60 s; C) keep 3600 s, documented.

summary: The bkit-cloud router's bkit:auto kill switch reads every tracker, GitHub included, through one bkit issues fetch path
description: The router's kill-switch re-read of bkit:auto moves off gh issue view onto bkit issues fetch for GitHub, Linear and Jira alike: one implementation, one test. GitHub gains a dependency on the npm registry and pnpm install for this check.
rationale: answered by owner: A — one bkit path for all trackers; with an unreadable label failing closed (grill Q1) both paths fail the same way, and drift between two copies of the safety-critical check is the larger long-term risk.
alternatives: B — keep gh issue view for GitHub and bkit for Linear / Jira (two paths drift, two tests); C — bkit for all with a gh issue view fallback on GitHub (fallback rarely exercised).

summary: The bkit-cloud codex job runs openai/codex-action with sandbox danger-full-access and allow-bots true, proven by live dispatches before the template ships
description: The codex job passes sandbox: danger-full-access and allow-bots: true to openai/codex-action, matching what the claude and opencode jobs can do on the runner. Before the template ships, the build runs three live dispatches: one workflow_dispatch, one workflow_run from a human push, one from a bot-authored commit. Each asserts the actor check passes and that git push, gh pr comment and one tracker verb succeed; the codex job summary line records them.
rationale: answered by owner: A — parity with the claude and opencode jobs; bkit phases push and comment mid-run, which the action's default workspace-write sandbox and bot-actor refusal may block (spike C11 blocked: no OPENAI_API_KEY, no live runner).
alternatives: B — a named permission-profile in a committed codex-home/config.toml allowing network (narrower; one more consumer-owned file); C — action defaults plus a post-step that pushes (safest; breaks phases that push or comment mid-run).

summary: The bkit-cloud codex job trusts the checkout through a codex-home config.toml written at run time, not a committed file
description: A step before openai/codex-action writes $RUNNER_TEMP/codex-home/config.toml with [projects."$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"] trust_level = "trusted" and passes that directory as codex-home, so codex exec loads the project config.toml and .codex/agents/*.toml subagents. The live dispatch asserts a hyphenated bkit subagent from .codex/agents/*.toml actually spawned, which also proves the trust table survives the action's Resolve Codex home, write-proxy-config and drop-sudo steps (spike C10 blocked).
rationale: answered by owner: A — the only option whose trust key tracks the runner's real workspace path; the action rejects --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust and -c projects.* under protected safety-strategy, and an untrusted project degrades subagent-spawning phases while the job goes green (spike C7).
alternatives: B — committed config.toml hard-coding the runner workspace path (breaks silently on self-hosted runners or a renamed repo); C — no trust (subagent phases degrade, project config and hooks absent).

summary: preflight-tracker.sh records 'not verified' and exits 0 when a Cursor or Claude session under GitHub or Jira has no resolvable issue id
description: When the session-start tracker guard finds no issue id (Cursor @cursor sessions, whose GITHUB_ISSUE_ID injection and checkout branch are unverified), it writes a 'not verified' line into session context and exits 0 rather than HARD STOPping. Such sessions run unguarded.
rationale: answered by owner: A — a HARD STOP would block every @cursor background session under GitHub / Jira, making the Cursor-own-triggers path settled in grill Q3 unusable; a prompt-scoped stop is not implementable because the SessionStart payload carries no prompt (spike C12 blocked).
alternatives: B — HARD STOP (fail closed; every @cursor session under GitHub / Jira blocked); C — HARD STOP only when the prompt names bkit-{command} (not implementable today).

summary: `bkit-machine-lock.sh` waits 60 s, not 3600 s, for every lock (the unnamed stack lock included) when stdin is not a TTY and `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S` is unset, then exits 75 naming the holder
description: Plan Open Question 7 answered with option A-prime: the short no-TTY default lives in the lock script, so pushes, subagent prompts and agent tool calls in every repo that wires the script see the holder before an agent tool timeout (~10 min). Applies to every lock the script takes, the unnamed stack lock included (a plan Breaking Change). Terminal runs keep the 3600 s default; an explicit `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S` always wins.
rationale: answered by owner: A-prime; the stack-lock scope accepted by the owner
alternatives: A) vitest global setup only sets the 60 s wait; B) always 60 s; C) keep 3600 s, documented; tests lock only, stack lock keeps 3600 s.

summary: `bkit-machine-lock.sh run` takes an optional `<who>`; when absent it reads `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WHO`, else `npm_lifecycle_event`, else `run`
description: `bkit tests run` passes its run identity to a consumer-wrapped gate through `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WHO` (and the wait through `LOCAL_STACK_LOCK_WAIT_S`), so the copy-and-own wiring `run --lock tests -- <gate>` needs no `<who>` argument and the engine can match the give-up line to its own run.
rationale: answered by owner: accepted
alternatives: Required `<who>` argument in every consumer wrap; engine matches the give-up line on the lock name only.

summary: Every secret bkit-cloud.yml reads uses its BKIT_-prefixed .bkit/.env name: BKIT_OPENAI_API_KEY gates the codex job, BKIT_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY the claude job
description: Every variable bkit uses lives in .bkit/.env under a BKIT_ name (.bkit/.env.example), even when the same vendor key is also used elsewhere, and the bkit-cloud router reads its repo secrets under those same names. The codex job is gated on BKIT_OPENAI_API_KEY (added to .bkit/.env.example), not OPENAI_API_KEY — superseding grill Q7's vendor name.
